INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Seventy Fifth 
Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No. 26) of the Department of 
Higher Education, Ministry of Education for the year 2026-27.  
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the estimated 
expenditure of the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India projected under 
various Demands for Grants for the upcoming financial year needs to be voted by Parliament. 
As a sequel thereto, Demands for Grants of the relevant Ministries/Departments stand 
referred to concerned Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee to make a close 
scrutiny thereof under Rule 270 of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the 
Council of States (Rajya Sabha). While making scrutiny of the Demands for Grants, the 
Committee has made an appraisal of the performance, programmes, schemes and policies of 
the Department of Higher Education vis-a-vis expenditure made out of Consolidated Fund of 
India in the current financial year. 
 
3. The Budget allocations of the Ministry of Education have been sought under two 
demand Numbers, i.e, Demand No. 25 pertains to the Department of School Education and 
Literacy and Demand No.26 pertains to Department of Higher Education. In this Report, a 
scrutiny of Demand No. 26 pertaining to the Department of Higher Education of the Ministry 
of Education for the Financial Year 2026-27 has been made by the Committee. While 
scrutiny of Demand No. 25 pertaining to Department of School Education and Literacy is 
covered in Report number 376th of the Committee. 
 
4.  During the course of examination of Demands, the Committee heard the views of the 
Secretary, Department of Higher Education and other Senior Officers of the Department in its 
sitting held on 18th February, 2026. The Department also made available inputs from various 
organizations/agencies, namely, University Grants Commission (UGC); All India Council for 
Technical Education (AICTE), NAAC, IGNOU, JNU, DU, IIT Delhi etc under the 
administrative control of the Department of Higher Education.  
 
5. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has mainly relied 
upon the following documents:- 
(i)  Detailed Demands for Grants (2026-27);  
(ii) Annual Report for the year 2025-26; 
(iii) Annual Plan for the year 2026-27; 
(iv) Appropriation Accounts for the year 2025-26; 
(v) Detailed Explanatory Note (Demand-wise) on the Demands for Grants (2026-
27) pertaining to the Department and Organizations/Institutes under its 
administrative control along with a brief synopsis of the Scheme/Item for which 
Demand is being raised;  
(vi) Output Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF) 2026-27, relating to all 
Schemes under the Department; 
(vii) National Education Policy, 2020;

CHAPTER 1  
INTRODUCTION 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT OF HIGHER EDUCATION 
1.1 Higher education plays a pivotal role in the growth, stability and overall progress of a nation 
and its society. It serves as the cornerstone for the development of human capital, fostering 
intellectual advancement, innovation and socio-economic transformation. The Higher 
Educational Institutions (HEIs) act as centres of excellence where knowledge is created 
preserved and disseminated. HEIs equip students with advanced skills, critical thinking abilities 
and professional competencies necessary to meet the evolving demands of a globalized and 
technology-driven world. In essence, higher education not only drives economic growth and 
employment generation but also shapes the moral, intellectual and cultural fabric of society. It is 
in this backdrop, the Committee on Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports considered 
the Demand for Grants 2026-27 of the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education. 
1.2 The Ministry of Education (MoE) is the apex body responsible for framing and implementing 
the National Education Policy, overseeing educational programmes at all levels, and developing 
systemic educational infrastructure across the country. The Department of Higher Education is 
responsible for the overall development of the higher education sector in India, encompassing 
universities, colleges, and institutions of national importance. 
The Ministry of Education comprises of two Departments: 
(i) Department of School Education and Literacy (DoSEL); and  
(ii) Department of Higher Education (DoHE) 
1.3 Mission and Vision of the Department 
Mission: 
 Provide greater opportunities of access to higher education with equity to all eligible 
persons, particularly to vulnerable sections. 
 Expand access by supporting existing institutions, establishing new institutions, and 
supporting State Governments and non-Government Organizations/Civil Society. 
 Initiate policies and programmes for strengthening entrepreneurship, research and 
innovations and encourage institutions to engage in stretching the frontiers of knowledge. 
 Promote the quality of higher education by investing in infrastructure and faculty, 
promoting academic reforms, improving governance and institutional restructuring. 
Vision: To realize India's human resource potential to its fullest in the higher education sector 
with equity and excellence.

CHAPTER 2 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMAND FOR GRANTS 2026-27 FOR THE 
DEPARTMENT OF HIGHER EDUCATION 
2.1 The Committee considered the Demands for Grants (2026-27) of the Department of Higher 
Education in its meeting held on 18th February, 2026. The Demands for Grants (2026-27) of the 
Ministry of Education has been presented to Parliament under the following Demand Numbers: 
Demand No.25 - Department of School Education and Literacy 
Demand No.26 - Department of Higher Education 
This Report pertains to the Demands for Grants (Demand No. 26) relating to Department of 
Higher Education.

Short Analysis of budget allocated to the Department 
2.9 A consistent upward trend is observed in the overall budget allocation for the Department of 
Higher Education. The allocation in BE 2026-27 at Rs. 55,727.22 crore is higher than the BE 
2025-26 by Rs. 5,649.27 crore (11.28%). This significant increase is attributable to the following 
factors: 
 Substantially enhanced allocations for Autonomous Bodies such as Central Universities 
(+4.49%), IITs (+6.82%), NITs (+10.07%), and IIMs (+15.92%), reflecting the growing 
requirements of academic and research infrastructure. 

9 
 
 Increased allocations under flagship schemes such as PM-ONOS (Rs. 2,200 crore), 
MERITE (Rs. 300 crore, 36.36% over BE 2025-26), Centres of Excellence in AI (Rs. 250 
crore, 25% increase), and PM Research Fellowship (Rs. 600 crore). 
 New allocations for PM Research Chair (Rs. 200 crore) and CoE in AI for Education (Rs. 
100 crore) introduced in BE 2026-27.

World Class Institutions 
3.2 Under the World Class Institutions scheme, the selected institutions are granted the status of 
“Institute of Eminence (IoE)”. It is a Central Sector Scheme aimed at establishing world-class 
institutions each in the public and private sector, by providing an enabling regulatory 
environment that allows them to achieve the highest levels of global excellence in teaching and 
research. The scheme grants selected institutions significant regulatory and administrative 
autonomy to facilitate their rise in global rankings. One of the major objectives of the scheme is 
that the institutions should appear in top-500 of any of the renowned global education ranking 
frameworks in a period of ten years of becoming an IoE.  
The following institutions have been granted the IoE status as of 2026: 
 Public Institutions (08): IIT-Delhi, IIT-Bombay, IIT-Madras, IIT-Kharagpur, IISc 
Bangalore, Banaras Hindu University, University of Hyderabad and University of Delhi. 
 Private Institutions (04): Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Birla Institute of 
Technology & Science, O.P. Jindal Global University and Shiv Nadar University.

recognised ranking parameters, along with a robust monitoring framework. The

across 350 target institutions.

States with low GER in technical education and specifically in the North Eastern Region, 
ensuring that the scheme's benefits flow equitably across geographies and not merely to 
already well-resourced engineering institutions. 
3.48 The Committee recommends a comprehensive stakeholder consultation with State 
Governments and affiliated technical universities that should be completed before 
finalizing the project design, to ensure state ownership and co-investment in the project's 
outcomes. 
Malaviya Mission Teacher Training Programme (MMTTP) 
3.49 The Malaviya Mission Teacher Training Programme (MMTTP) was re-launched in 
September 2023 as a successor to the PMMMNMTT (PM's Mission for Mentoring the Nation's 
Teachers) scheme. It aims to build competencies in faculty through exposure to Indian values, 
updated knowledge and skills, and alignment with NEP 2020. The total financial outlay for FY 
2023-24 to 2025-26 is Rs. 361.59 crore.  
3.50 At present, 151 MMTTCs have been identified across the country for conducting many 
training programmes for teachers, major among them are as under: 
 Nurturing Future Leadership Program: to build faculty leadership capacity across 
different levels to create a strong pool of potential leaders for generational transition. 
NIEPA is the coordinating agency, and 33 HEIs (16 IIMs; 8 IITs; 9 Pvt. HEIs) have been 
identified as NFLP Host Institutions. 
 Capacity Building Program on Specific Learning Disabilities: to address the issue of 
learning disabilities among a set of students and to create awareness among teachers and 
to sensitize them for teaching the student with specific disabilities, including learning 
disabilities to reverse their underrepresentation.  
 Capacity Building Programme for Promoting Positive Mental Health Resilience & 
Wellbeing in HEIs: aims at sustained faculty capacity building in Higher Education 
Institutions (HEIs) by creating a platform to share best practices and collaborate with 
experts on student mental health and wellbeing. It seeks to foster an institutional 
ecosystem where the wellbeing of both students and faculty is prioritized.  
 Capacity Building Programme on Cyber Security: This 5-day onlineprogramme offers 
Basic and Intermediate cyber-security training for educators, equipping them with skills 
to promote digital security and resilience in educational institutions. The programme is 
being hosted by IIT Madras.  
 Capacity Building Programme on Artificial Intelligence: This 5-day online 
programme equips faculty and academic leaders with AI skills to enhance teaching, 
promote research, and support NEP 2020 goals. The program is being hosted by IIT 
Ropar.

Centres of Excellence (CoEs) in Artificial Intelligence (AI) 
3.71 Artificial Intelligence is rapidly transforming sectors such as healthcare, agriculture, 
education, manufacturing, and public service delivery. Staying ahead in this domain is not 
merely a matter of technological advancement, but one of strategic importance. To establish 
India as a global leader in use of AI for public services, the Government of India announced 
establishing Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Union Budget 2023-24. 
Following the announcements, three Centres of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence were 
established at IISc Bangalore (Healthcare), IIT Kanpur (Sustainable Cities), and IIT Ropar 
(Agriculture) with total budget outlay for the three CoEs of Rs. 990 crore. These dedicated 
Centres of Excellence are necessary to create focused platforms for high-quality research, 
innovation, and skill development in this critical domain. They will enable collaboration between 
academia, industry, and government, ensuring that AI solutions are aligned with national 
developmental priorities.  
3.72 To further the vision of “Make AI in India and Make AI work for India”, a fourth CoE in AI 
for Education was announced in Budget 2025-26 with a total outlay of Rs. 500 crores and 
established at IIT Madras. This CoE aims to establish Centres of Excellence to promote 
interdisciplinary research, innovation, and capacity building in Artificial Intelligence 
applications for the education sector. It will support development of indigenous, scalable AI-
based solutions for improving teaching, learning outcomes, and educational governance. 
Separately, Rs. 17.00 cr was allotted for it in RE 2025-26 and Rs. 100.00 cr is allocated in BE 
2026-27 for this purpose.

Pradhan Mantri Vidyalaxmi Scheme (PM-VL) 
3.88 PM Vidyalaxmi (PM-VL) was approved by the Union Cabinet on 6th November 2024 as a 
new Central Sector Scheme. Its objective is to ensure that no meritorious student is denied the 
opportunity to pursue higher education due to financial constraints. The scheme facilitates 
collateral-free and guarantor-free education loans to students securing merit-based admission in 
top Quality Higher Education Institutions (QHEIs), identified through NIRF rankings. More than 
917 QHEIs have been identified, covering over 22 lakh students annually. 
Key features of the scheme are as under: 
 Collateral-free and guarantor-free education loans covering full tuition fees and course-
related expenses. 
 Credit guarantee of up to 75% of outstanding default for loans up to Rs. 7.5 lakh. 
 Interest subvention of 3% during moratorium period on loans up to Rs. 10 lakh for 
students with annual family income up to Rs. 8 lakh. 
 Total outlay: Rs. 3,600 crore for 2024-25 to 2030-31, covering an estimated 7 lakh 
students. 
 Dedicated online portal operational since 25th February 2025; all 12 Public Sector banks, 
20 leading private banks, 24 Regional Rural banks integrated on single portal. 
 Loans are made accessible through a simple, transparent, student-friendly and entirely 
digital application process; PM Vidyalaxmi Digital Rupee App (CBDC Wallet) for 

56 
 
disbursing interest subvention; the amount is credited to CBDC wallet of the beneficiary, 
then can be redeemed into bank account. 
 As on 22.01.2026, 25,385 grievances received on portal and 23,623 has been resolved. 
 Average Turn Around Time (TAT) for loan sanction ahs been reduced to less than 9 
days. 
 Simple 2-page application format (reduced from earlier 7-8 pages).

University Grants Commission (UGC) 
4.1 The University Grants Commission (UGC), established under an Act of Parliament in 1956, 
is a statutory body responsible for the coordination and maintenance of standards in universities 
throughout India. UGC provides financial assistance to eligible universities and colleges, 
promotes autonomous colleges, and advises on matters related to higher education. UGC is also 
responsible for introducing and implementing various academic reforms, including CHOICE-
Based Credit System (CBCS), Four-Year Undergraduate Programme (FYUP), academic 
autonomy, and curriculum reforms under NEP 2020. Its role and functions include coordination 
between universities; maintenance of standards; promotion of research; granting recognition to 
universities; disbursing scholarships/fellowships; framing regulations for higher education; 
promoting quality assurance through NAAC; and overseeing SWAYAM, ABC, and NIRF 
frameworks. 
4.2 Key initiatives undertaken by UGC: 
 154 Non-Technology Post-Graduate MOOCs developed for SWAYAM (2017 onwards); 
415 universities have adopted SWAYAM Credit Framework Regulations 2021; 4,55,956 
students earned credit transfers through SWAYAM (2021-2024). 
 Framework for Universities to conduct examinations for SWAYAM Courses notified 
(August 2024); 191 Universities adopted. 
 SWAYAM Outreach Workshops conducted at 8 locations (Jan-Mar 2025), with 
participation of over 7,000 stakeholders. 
 Guidelines for Incorporating Indian Knowledge in Higher Education Curricula released. 
 Mulya Pravah 2.0 introduced – focusing on human values and professional ethics. 
 Guidelines for Transforming Higher Education Institutions into Multidisciplinary 
Institutions (2022). 
 UGC (Institutions Deemed to be Universities) Regulations 2023 notified. 
 Foreign Higher Educational Institutions Regulations 2023 – facilitating branch campus 
establishment.

MISCELLANEOUS 
Research and Innovation 
5.1 Research and innovation are at the heart of any vibrant higher education system. Universities 
are not only places for teaching but also spaces where new ideas are explored, tested, and 
transformed into solutions for real-world problems. Strong research culture helps institutions 
contribute meaningfully to national priorities such as healthcare, agriculture, technology, and 
sustainable development. It also enhances academic excellence and global standing. By 
encouraging curiosity, critical thinking, and collaboration with industry, research-driven 
institutions prepare students to become innovators and leaders. In a rapidly changing world, 
continuous investment in research and innovation is essential to ensure long-term growth, 
competitiveness, and self-reliance for the nation. Key stats with regard to research and 
innovation scenario in HEIs in the country: 
 In the last 5 years, 2021 to 2025, over 1.1 Lakh patents have been filed by educational 
institutions of the country. Around 3,000 patents have been granted to centrally funded 
institutions under the Department of Higher Education during this period. 
 The IRINS (Indian Research Information Network System), which is a part of NMEICT 
has on boarded more than 1,800 higher education institutions and provided access to the 
comprehensive research profiling platform to them. The portal hosts more than 37.89 
lakh publications and approximately 2.75 lakh researcher profiles, including Assistant 
Professors, Associate Professors, and Professors. Collectively, these publications have 
garnered over 3.9 crore citations, reflecting the vast research footprint of Indian 
academia. 
 Research and innovation are central to institutional benchmarking within the Indian 
higher education ecosystem. Research & Innovation is a key criterion for Accreditation 
under National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC). Research is also among 
the five core weighted parameters of the National Institutional Ranking Framework 
(NIRF) for ranking Indian HEIs. 
 Around 6000 Institutions/Universities have established R&D Cells to catalyse 
multidisciplinary/ trans-disciplinary and translational research culture. 16,408 IICs have 
been set up in HEIs to develop a culture of research and innovation in Indian HEIs. 
 Presently 8,412 start-ups are incubated at HEIs and it is targeted to 50,000 start-ups by 
2030.

schemes: 
 PMRF: 3,688 scholars admitted; 10,300 journal publications; 7,966 conference

 SPARC: 28 partner nations; research under 12 thematic areas aligned with G20 priorities; 
75.36% efficiency (DRDO evaluation, 2025). 
 STARS: Focuses on science education-research integration; allocation maintained at Rs. 
40 crore.

5.4 The Committee recognizes that strengthening research and innovation ecosystems is 
central to India in achieving a knowledge-driven economy. The Committee recommends 
that the Department, in coordination with DST, DBT, CSIR, and ANRF (Anusandhan 
National Research Foundation), develop a unified National Research Mission for higher 
education with a five-year rolling budget, clearly delineating the roles of each agency to 
avoid duplication and ensure synergistic investment. A target of increasing India's GERD 
(Gross Expenditure on R&D) from 0.64% of GDP to at least 1.5% of GDP by 2030 should 
be embedded in this Mission. 
5.5 IIT data shows 9,393 patents applied and 5,733 granted between 2019 and 2025, but 
commercialization of these patents remains limited. The Committee is of the view that a 
Technology Transfer and Commercialization Office be established as a central facilitation 
body, interfacing with the private sector, DPIIT, and Start-up India may be established, to 
convert publicly-funded research into market-ready products and processes. 
5.6 While CFIs like IITs and IISc have world-class research infrastructure, State 
universities - which account for over 80% of enrolled students - have negligible research 
capacity. The Committee recommends that a dedicated 'State University Research 
Enhancement Fund' under PM-USHA with an annual outlay of at least Rs. 500 crore to 
develop Research and Innovation Clusters should be established at State universities, with 
matching contributions from State Governments. 
5.7 Consistent with NEP 2020's vision of multidisciplinarity, the Committee recommends 
that as per UGC notified guidelines Multi-Disciplinary Research Centres in every Central 
University should be established by 2027, covering at least three convergence areas such as 
AI and healthcare, sustainability and urban planning, or materials science and agriculture 
to facilitate establishing seed centres. 
5.8 The Committee notes that the Department does not currently publish a consolidated 
research output report mapping budget allocations to publications, patents, and citations 
across schemes. The Committee recommends that the Department should introduce an 
Annual Research Outcomes Report covering PMRF, SPARC, STARS, CoE-AI, MERITE, 
and all research-linked schemes, enabling Parliament and the public to assess the return on 
India's research investment in higher education.

5.13 The Committee emphasizes that a well-structured scholarship and fellowship 
ecosystem is essential to ensure that no deserving student is denied access to higher 
education due to financial constraints. To facilitate this, the Department currently operates 
multiple scholarship schemes — CSSS, SSS-JKL, CSIS, PMRF, UGC-JRF/SRF, NET-JRF, 

71 
 
and PM Vidyalaxmi — through different portals with separate application processes. The 
Committee recommends that a Single Integrated Scholarship Portal under the National 
Scholarship Portal (NSP) 2.0 should be developed, where a student can apply for all eligible 
schemes simultaneously through a single form and single KYC process, with automated 
eligibility matching and DBT disbursement. 
5.14 The Central Sector Scholarship Scheme (CSSS) provides Rs. 12,000 per annum for the 
first three years, a rate that has remained static for several years despite rising cost of 
education. Similarly, UGC fellowship stipends for PhD scholars were last revised in 2019. 
The Committee recommends an immediate upward revision of all scholarship and 
fellowship amounts - at minimum linked to CPI inflation - and thereafter indexed 
automatically every three years. 
5.15 Prestigious fellowships like PMRF are limited to scholars at IITs, IISc, and a select list 
of institutions. The Committee recommends introduction of a dedicated Post-Doctoral 
Fellowship Scheme for researchers at accredited State universities and government 
colleges, with at least 2,000 fellowships per year at an enhanced stipend of Rs. 75,000 -
85,000 per month, to stimulate a research culture beyond the elite institutions. 
5.16 The Committee notes that UGC fellowship data shows year-on-year increase in SC, 
ST, and OBC fellowship holders; however, the proportion relative to enrolled population in 
these categories remains unclear. The Committee recommends that the Department should 
conduct a comprehensive gap analysis - mapping the number of eligible 
SC/ST/OBC/PwD/Minority students enrolled in PhD programmes against the number 
actually receiving fellowships - and take corrective action to bridge the gap at the earliest. 
STEM, MOOC and ICT Initiatives

strengthen the quality, accessibility and global competitiveness of higher education in the

fostering innovation, research capability and technological self-reliance. Simultaneously, 
MOOCs and digital learning platforms have expanded access to high-quality academic resources 
beyond geographical boundaries, particularly providing accessible education to rural and remote 
areas in the country, enabling flexible and lifelong learning opportunities. ICT initiatives, 
including virtual laboratories and digital repositories, have enhanced teaching-learning 
processes, improved outreach and contributed to building a future-ready and knowledge-driven 
education ecosystem.

5.19 The Committee notes that while overall STEM enrolment is growing, female 
participation in engineering and technology courses remains disproportionately low (42.6% 
as per AISHE 2021-22). The Committee is of the view that AICTE and UGC should jointly 
develop Gender Parity in STEM Action Plan with institution-specific targets for female 
enrolment and offer scholarships exclusively for women in STEM at postgraduate and 
doctoral levels in all HEIs. 
5.20 Many government degree colleges and State university-affiliated colleges lack 
functional STEM laboratories, forcing students to learn from textbooks alone. The 
Committee recommends that PM-USHA's Phase 3 should prioritise laboratory 
modernisation and equipment grants for STEM disciplines, with a minimum of Rs. 50 lakh 
per institution for science lab upgradation and Rs. 1 crore for engineering workshops, 
covering at least10% of HEIs. 
5.21 AICTE's Model Curriculum in AI, Data Science, and Robotics is a commendable step; 
however, adoption across the 10,000+ AICTE-approved institutions is limited. The 
Committee recommends that AICTE mandate updated STEM curriculum adoption as a 
condition for annual approval renewal, with a three-year implementation timeline. Faculty 
retraining through MMTTP should be specifically aligned with the updated STEM 
content. 
5.22 The Committee emphasizes that India's STEM innovation potential is constrained by 
geographical concentration of research in metropolitan and Tier-1 city institutions. The 
Committee recommends a STEM Research Cluster programme to establish 50 STEM 
Research Clusters at government institutions in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities over a period of 
five years, with seed funding of Rs. 5-10 crore each under a dedicated scheme, focusing on 
applied research relevant to local industries, agricultural and environmental challenges. 
5.23 Of India's 45,000+ colleges, only a fraction has implemented SWAYAM credit transfer 
despite 415 universities adopting the framework. The Committee recommends that UGC 

73 
 
should take necessary steps mandating all affiliated colleges to allow students to earn at 
least 20% of their total academic credits through SWAYAM courses, with a phased 
implementation timeline starting from academic year 2026-27. Non-compliance should be 
flagged during NAAC accreditation assessment. 
5.24 The Committee appreciates SWAYAM Plus, with 89 industry partners and 4.8 lakh 
enrolments, which has demonstrated strong industry appetite for skilling through the 
MOOC model. The Committee recommends that SWAYAM Plus should target more  
industry partners and enrolments, with specific campaigns in MSME and manufacturing 
sectors where skilling gaps are acute. Completion certificates from SWAYAM Plus should 
be recognised under the National Credit Framework (NCrF). 
5.25 The Committee observes that despite India's linguistic diversity, the majority of 
SWAYAM courses are in English or Hindi while a significant proportion of India's student 
population learns best in their mother tongue. The Committee recommends that by 2027-
28, at least 500 SWAYAM courses be made available in each of the 22 Scheduled 
Languages, with dedicated funding for translation, dubbing, and regional language content 
creation, and involvement of regional language universities and State governments in 
content development.

5.33 The Committee notes the recent policy reforms enabling reputed foreign universities 
to establish campuses in India. While recognising the potential benefits in terms of global 
exposure and academic collaboration, the Committee underscores the need for robust 
regulatory oversight. It recommends that clear safeguards be instituted to ensure that such 
institutions reinvest a reasonable portion of their surplus within India. The Committee 
further is of the view that course curricula maintain an appropriate balance between global 
standards and Indian academic, cultural, and developmental contexts. Therefore, periodic 
performance reviews, including assessment of academic quality, research output, fee 
structures, student diversity, and compliance with national regulations, should be made 
mandatory. A transparent monitoring mechanism must be established to ensure 
accountability and alignment with national higher education priorities.

1. The Committee notes with appreciation the 11.28% increase in BE 2026-27 (Rs. 
55,727.22 crore) over BE 2025-26. However, it observes that actual expenditure in 2024-
25 (Rs. 45,576.52 crore) fell short of the BE by nearly Rs. 4,500 crore. The Committee is

(para 2.12)

percentage of GDP stood at 4.06% (2022-23), which is significantly below the NEP 2020 
target of 6% of GDP. The Committee recommends that the Government should take 
concrete, time-bound steps to progressively increase the education budget, with a clear 
roadmap to achieve at least the 6% target by 2030. 
(para 2.13)

regarding the issue of delayed submission of Utilisation Certificates by

efficacious. 
(para 3.64) 
 
42. The Committee observes that both the National Apprenticeship Training Scheme 
(NATS) and the Prime Minister’s Internship Programme aim to enhance employability 
and provide structured industry exposure to youth. In view of this, the Committee 
recommends that the Department undertake a comparative assessment of the objectives, 
duration, certification standards, stipend structures, and post-internship employment 
outcomes under both programmes to avoid duplication and ensure optimal utilisation of 
public resources. The Committee further recommends convergence of data systems, 
harmonization of quality standards, and integration with industry demand mapping so 
that both initiatives function in a complementary manner and contribute effectively to 
long-term skill development and sustainable employment generation. 
(para 3.65) 
 
43. The Committee notes that third-party evaluation by IPE Global (November 2025) 
has recommended continuation of the scheme. The Committee, therefore, is of the view 
that Study in India be continued beyond its sunset date of 31st March 2026, in light of 
the positive Third Party Evaluation by IPE Global (November 2025). 
(para 3.68) 
 
44. The Committee notes that AE under SII in 2023-24 was Rs. 7.50 crore over BE of 
Rs. 25.00 crore and AE in 2024-25 was Rs. 13.00 crore over BE of Rs. 20.00 crore.  The 
Committee is of the view that resource utilization under SII should be reviewed and 
necessary steps should be taken to strengthen the marketing and outreach components, 
including digital campaigns in target countries. 
(para 3.69) 
 
45. The Committee recommends that the Office of International Affairs (OIA) capacity 
at participating HEIs be strengthened through dedicated grants under SII for 
recruitment of international relations staff and development of English-
medium/multilingual support infrastructure. The Committee also recommends that 
steps should be taken under SII towards increasing the number of students from 
ASEAN, Africa, and the Pacific Island nations — regions where India has significant 
diplomatic interests — and set country-specific annual enrolment targets. 
(para 3.70) 
 
46. The Committee is of the view that the three AI-CoEs (IISc – Healthcare; IIT 
Kanpur – Sustainable Cities; IIT Ropar – Agriculture) should publish their annual 
impact reports detailing research outputs, startups supported, government applications 
developed, and societal outcomes achieved. For the newly established CoE in AI for 
Education at IIT Madras (total outlay Rs. 500 crore), the Committee recommends that a 

84 
 
clear implementation plan with phase-wise milestones, covering: development of AI-
based pedagogical tools; deployment in Government schools and HEIs; faculty/teacher 
training in AI tools; and accessibility of AI products in regional languages should be 
developed to support further the higher education scenario in the country. 
(para 3.74) 
 
47. The Committee recommends that the CoEs should build strong linkages with 
AICTE's AI curriculum initiative, UGC's multidisciplinary education guidelines, and 
NMEICT's digital platforms to avoid duplication and ensure that AI solutions developed 
under the CoEs are rapidly scaled through existing delivery channels. 
(para 3.75) 
 
48. The Committee recommends that equity considerations be built into AI-CoE 
research mandates, specifically requiring that solutions developed in healthcare and 
agriculture CoEs are accessible and appropriate for use in rural, tribal, and low-
resource settings. 
(para 3.76) 
 
49. The Committee notes the BE 2026-27 allocation of Rs. 2,200 crore is about 10% 
higher than the allocation made in FY 2025-26 to provide for increase in subscription 
charges and foreign exchange fluctuations. The Committee welcomes PM-ONOS as a 
landmark initiative providing equitable access to 13,000+ international journals for over 
6,500 Government HEIs from 1st January 2025. The Committee recommends that an 
institutional uptake report should be published showing (a) institution-wise downloads; 
(b) discipline-wise usage; and (c) research output by ONOS-subscribing institutions in 
order to justify the effectiveness of the scheme. The Committee also recommends that 
PM-ONOS be extended to Government-aided private HEIs and to all NAAC-accredited 
institutions in a phased manner, given the scheme's significant value in democratizing 
research access. 
(para 3.78) 
 
50. The Committee recommends that PM-ONOS include provisions for Open Access 
publishing support to enable Indian researchers to publish in high-impact international 
journals, which currently requires Article Processing Charges (APCs) that are a 
significant barrier for researchers at less-resourced institutions. 
(para 3.79) 
 
51. The Committee notes the absence of a multi-year financial plan for PM-ONOS 
beyond the current three-year subscription (2025-2027). It recommends that the 
Department negotiate long-term agreements with publishers to secure predictable 
subscription costs, and place the financial sustainability plan before the Committee. 
(para 3.80) 
 
52. The Committee notes that out of 3,215 approved projects under all phases of 
RUSA/PM-USHA, only 1,566 (48.7%) have been completed. With the scheme now 
extended up to March 2028, the Committee recommends that a project-completion 

85 
 
calendar for the remaining 1,649 projects should be chalked-out, with State-wise 
timelines and accountability provisions in completing the approved projects. 
(para 3.84) 
 
53. The Committee also recommends that quarterly review meetings with Chief 
Secretaries and Higher Education Secretaries of States/UTs with the highest project 
backlogs should be convened and action-taken reports thereon be placed before the 
Committee for its consideration. 
(para 3.85) 
 
54. The Committee further recommends that PM-USHA's third phase fund releases be 
made contingent on satisfactory utilization of previously released funds and submission 
of audited Utilization Certificates (UCs). States with pending UC backlogs should be 
sensitized to submit UCs before making any fresh allocations. 
(para 3.86) 
 
55. The Committee recommends that a formal Third Party Evaluation of PM-USHA 
(Phase 3) outcomes be conducted by an independent institution by December 2026, 
covering access, quality, equity, and governance improvements, and the report be 
shared with the Committee. 
(para 3.87) 
 
56. The Committee appreciates that the average turn-around-time (TAT) for loans 
sanctioned under the PM-Vidyalaxmi scheme has been reduced to 9 days. The 
Committee recommends that the Department of Higher Education and Department of 
Financial Services should regularly coordinate through the IBA with all banks to 
further reduce the turn-around-time (TAT) for loan sanction and their timely disbursal. 
It further recommends that the Department set a target of covering at least 5 lakh 
students under the interest subvention component by 2027-28, with annual milestones, 
and submit the progress to the Committee. 
(para 3.90) 
 
57. The Committee is of the view that the list of QHEIs be reviewed and expanded 
periodically to include more State Government and Government-aided institutions, 
particularly those in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, to ensure that first-generation learners in 
smaller towns are also able to access collateral-free education loans to pursue their 
higher studies. 
(para 3.91) 
 
58. The Committee recommends that State-wise and social category-wise 
(SC/ST/OBC/Minority/Female/PwD) data on applications, sanctions, and disbursements 
under PM Vidyalaxmi on a quarterly basis should be published, to monitor equitable 
access to loan facilities under the PM Vidyalaxmi Scheme. 
(para 3.92) 
 

86 
 
59. The Committee notes that 1,762 grievances on the PM Vidyalaxmi portal remain 
unresolved (out of 25,385 received as of 22.01.2026). It recommends that a zero-pending-
grievance target within 10 working days be strictly enforced and that banks failing to 
comply be sanctioned under the scheme framework for better implementation of the 
scheme. 
(para 3.93) 
 
60. The Committee recommends that the PM Vidyalaxmi CBDC Wallet mechanism be 
thoroughly evaluated for user accessibility, particularly for students in rural areas with 
limited smartphone access, and that offline disbursement alternatives be developed, if 
needed. 
(para 3.94) 
 
61. The Committee notes that several schemes including Startup India Initiative in 
Higher Educational Institutions, IMPRINT, and IMPRESS have been concluded. The 
Committee is of the view that the Department should compile and share comprehensive 
third-party evaluation reports for all concluded schemes with the Committee, covering 
outcomes achieved, gaps left, and lessons learned to calibrate future scheme design. 
(para 3.96) 
 
62. The Committee recommends that before discontinuing any scheme, a sunset review 
be conducted at least two years in advance, allowing adequate time for beneficiaries to 
transition and for making alternative institutional arrangements. 
(para 3.97) 
 
63. The Committee notes that there is mismatch in data furnished by the Department 
regarding few schemes in table provided in Annexure II of replies of Questionnaire Part 
– II, and Document X (Details of Schemes/ Programmes currently under operation along 
with note on physical and financial targets fixed and achievements). The Committee 
expresses its concern over the casual approach being taken while furnishing data/ 
information to the Committee which is disappointing to the Standing Committee of the 
Parliament. The Committee, therefore, directs the Department that correct reply/ figure 
with due diligence and after proper vetting by the authority concerned be furnished for 
its consideration. 
(para 3.98) 
 
64. The Committee notes with concern the critical vacancy situation in UGC — 516 out 
of 763 sanctioned non-teaching positions are vacant (67.6% vacancy rate). This severely 
impacts UGC's capacity to discharge its statutory functions, including monitoring 
thousands of universities, processing grant proposals, and implementing NEP 2020. The 
Committee recommends that UGC should take all necessary steps to fill up vacant 
positions in a time-bound manner, with a target of at least 75% vacancy reduction by 
March 2027. 
(para 4.5) 
 
 

87 
 
65. The Committee recommends that UGC expedite its work on academic credit 
recognition for SWAYAM courses, increasing the number of universities implementing 
credit transfers beyond the current 415 institutions. A nationwide campaign involving 
State Higher Education Departments should be launched in order to make this 
efficacious. 
(para 4.6) 
 
66. The Committee appreciates fund utilisation by the UGC and notes that allocation 
for UGC in BE 2026-27 (Rs. 3,709 crore) includes both the Commission's own funds and 
grants channelled to universities. The Committee recommends clear sub-head-wise 
reporting on UGC's own institutional expenditure versus grants disbursed to 
universities, to ensure accountability at the Commission level. 
(para 4.7) 
 
67. The Committee is of the view that, in order to bridge the employability gap, the 
UGC should move beyond general internships and adopt a structured industry-
integrated curriculum model keeping in view the current market demands. 
(para 4.8) 
 
68. The Committee notes consistent under-utilisation of funds vis-à-vis Budget 
Estimates (AE Rs. 352.25 crore over BE Rs. 420 crore in 2023-24, AE Rs. 137.50 crore 
over BE 400 crore in 2024-25 and AE 103.87 crore over BE Rs. 200 crore in 2025-26), 
which adversely affects the functions and intended outcomes. The Committee is of the 
view that realistic budgeting may be done during the budget allocation, monitoring 
should be strengthened and procedures should be streamlined to ensure efficient 
utilisation of public resources and achievement of developmental objectives within the 
financial year. 
(para 4.14) 
 
69. The Committee notes that only 20 posts have been filled up on regular/ permanent 
basis in the last six years. The Committee is of the view that for an important regulatory 
body such as AICTE the vacant posts (133 out of 209 sanctioned posts i.e. 63.6%) in 
critical middle and senior administrative layers may hamper the AICTE’s operations 
and the broader technical landscape as it regulates over 10,000 technical institutions. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that vacancies may be filled on priority through 
direct recruitment and lateral entry where appropriate, at the earliest. 
(para 4.15) 
 
70. The Committee recommends that AICTE's model curriculum in emerging 
technologies (AI, Data Science, Robotics, Semiconductor Manufacturing) be updated at 
least every two years in consultation with all stakeholders including industry, and that 
adoption of these curricula be tracked and incentivized through accreditation. 
(para 4.16) 
 

88 
 
71. The Committee recommends that AICTE develop a formal mechanism to track 
graduate employment outcomes from AICTE-approved institutions, and publish an 
annual Graduate Employability Report to inform policy on technical education quality. 
(para 4.17) 
 
72. The Committee appreciates Central Universities for their efficient and judicious 
utilisation of allocated funds, reflecting sound financial management and effective 
implementation of programmes. 
(para 4.22) 
 
73. The Committee notes that despite 16,507 faculty and 11,943 non-faculty posts filled 
in mission mode (September 2022 to July 2025), significant faculty vacancies persist 
across Centrally Funded Institutions (CFIs). The Committee recommends that a 
consolidated, annually updated vacancy register of all CFIs be prepared to keep a track 
on vacancy positions in order to fill up such vacancies timely. 
(para 4.23) 
 
74. The Committee recommends that the IIT mentorship programme for newer 
institutions be formalised under a structured scheme with dedicated funding, 
documented outcomes, and reporting obligations, given its potential to improve quality 
across the broader HEI ecosystem. 
(para 4.24) 
 
75. The Committee recommends that IGNOU's digital infrastructure be upgraded to 
support hybrid and blended learning, and that IGNOU be encouraged to develop 
courses in regional Indian languages in line with NEP 2020's multilingualism objectives. 
Allocation for IGNOU (Rs. 160 crore in BE 2026-27) should be reviewed upward given 
its mandate to serve 35+ lakh learners. 
(para 4.25) 
 
76. The Committee recommends that IISERs, which represent a unique integration of 
science education and research, receive enhanced and stable funding, as their allocation 
has shown a declining trend (Rs. 1,459.30 crore in 2024-25 actuals; Rs. 1,319 crore in BE 
2026-27). The Committee is of the view that this trend of declining allocation be 
reviewed to ensure IISERs' research infrastructure needs are adequately met. 
(para 4.26) 
 
77. The Committee is of the view that Central Universities and other premier 
institutions strengthen and properly structure their alumni engagement frameworks, 
with defined roles in mentoring, research funding, infrastructure support, and 
endowment creation. Further, the Committee is also of the view that the Department 
may consider incentivising alumni contributions through transparent governance 
mechanisms. 
(para 4.27) 
 

89 
 
78. The Committee notes the issue of significant increase in fees in certain Central 
Universities, including the University of Delhi, and recommends a detailed justification 
linking fee revision to ensure affordability. 
(para 4.28) 
 
79. The Committee further recommends enhanced budgetary support for the 
NITTTRs, with clear norms for teacher training eligibility, including consideration of 
integrated B.Ed. and discipline-specific teacher education pathways. 
(para 4.29) 
 
80. During its study visit to Pune, the Committee undertook a tour of the Bhandarkar 
Oriental Research Institute (BORI). The Committee was extremely impressed by the 
work done by BORI, which currently hosts 5 of the 14 Indian manuscripts that have 
been recorded in the UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register. The Committee notes 
that other institutions may similarly be doing good work in the preservation of Indian 
heritage and knowledge systems. The Committee recommends that the Ministry identify 
and consider supporting such institutions with funding. 
(para 4.30) 
 
81. The Committee note that despite budget allocations of Rs. 100 crore (2024-25) and 
Rs. 25 crore (2025-26), no expenditure has been booked under National Digital 
University. The Committee is of the view that a concrete, time-bound implementation 
roadmap may be submitted to the Committee for its consideration at the earliest, 
covering the legal/regulatory framework, governance structure, technology platform, 
content partnerships, and learner enrolment targets. 
(para 4.34) 
 
 
82. The Committee recommends that NDU be positioned as a complementary rather 
than competing platform to SWAYAM and IGNOU, with a clear differentiation in 
mandate - preferably focused on credit-bearing online degree programmes and micro-
credentials for working professionals. 
(para 4.35) 
 
83. The Committee recognizes that strengthening research and innovation ecosystems is 
central to India in achieving a knowledge-driven economy. The Committee recommends 
that the Department, in coordination with DST, DBT, CSIR, and ANRF (Anusandhan 
National Research Foundation), develop a unified National Research Mission for higher 
education with a five-year rolling budget, clearly delineating the roles of each agency to 
avoid duplication and ensure synergistic investment. A target of increasing India's 
GERD (Gross Expenditure on R&D) from 0.64% of GDP to at least 1.5% of GDP by 
2030 should be embedded in this Mission. 
(para 5.4) 
 
84. IIT data shows 9,393 patents applied and 5,733 granted between 2019 and 2025, but 
commercialization of these patents remains limited. The Committee is of the view that a 

90 
 
Technology Transfer and Commercialization Office be established as a central 
facilitation body, interfacing with the private sector, DPIIT, and Start-up India may be 
established, to convert publicly-funded research into market-ready products and 
processes. 
(para 5.5) 
 
85. While CFIs like IITs and IISc have world-class research infrastructure, State 
universities - which account for over 80% of enrolled students - have negligible research 
capacity. The Committee recommends that a dedicated 'State University Research 
Enhancement Fund' under PM-USHA with an annual outlay of at least Rs. 500 crore to 
develop Research and Innovation Clusters should be established at State universities, 
with matching contributions from State Governments. 
(para 5.6) 
 
86. Consistent with NEP 2020's vision of multidisciplinarity, the Committee 
recommends that as per UGC notified guidelines Multi-Disciplinary Research Centres 
in every Central University should be established by 2027, covering at least three 
convergence areas such as AI and healthcare, sustainability and urban planning, or 
materials science and agriculture to facilitate establishing seed centres. 
(para 5.7) 
 
87. The Committee notes that the Department does not currently publish a consolidated 
research output report mapping budget allocations to publications, patents, and 
citations across schemes. The Committee recommends that the Department should 
introduce an Annual Research Outcomes Report covering PMRF, SPARC, STARS, 
CoE-AI, MERITE, and all research-linked schemes, enabling Parliament and the public 
to assess the return on India's research investment in higher education. 
(para 5.8) 
 
88. The Committee emphasizes that a well-structured scholarship and fellowship 
ecosystem is essential to ensure that no deserving student is denied access to higher 
education due to financial constraints. To facilitate this, the Department currently 
operates multiple scholarship schemes — CSSS, SSS-JKL, CSIS, PMRF, UGC-
JRF/SRF, NET-JRF, and PM Vidyalaxmi — through different portals with separate 
application processes. The Committee recommends that a Single Integrated Scholarship 
Portal under the National Scholarship Portal (NSP) 2.0 should be developed, where a 
student can apply for all eligible schemes simultaneously through a single form and 
single KYC process, with automated eligibility matching and DBT disbursement. 
(para 5.13) 
 
89. The Central Sector Scholarship Scheme (CSSS) provides Rs. 12,000 per annum for 
the first three years, a rate that has remained static for several years despite rising cost 
of education. Similarly, UGC fellowship stipends for PhD scholars were last revised in 
2019. The Committee recommends an immediate upward revision of all scholarship and 
fellowship amounts - at minimum linked to CPI inflation - and thereafter indexed 
automatically every three years. 

91 
 
(para 5.14) 
 
90. Prestigious fellowships like PMRF are limited to scholars at IITs, IISc, and a select 
list of institutions. The Committee recommends introduction of a dedicated Post-
Doctoral Fellowship Scheme for researchers at accredited State universities and 
government colleges, with at least 2,000 fellowships per year at an enhanced stipend of 
Rs. 75,000 -85,000 per month, to stimulate a research culture beyond the elite 
institutions. 
(para 5.15) 
 
91. The Committee notes that UGC fellowship data shows year-on-year increase in SC, 
ST, and OBC fellowship holders; however, the proportion relative to enrolled 
population in these categories remains unclear. The Committee recommends that the 
Department should conduct a comprehensive gap analysis - mapping the number of 
eligible SC/ST/OBC/PwD/Minority students enrolled in PhD programmes against the 
number actually receiving fellowships - and take corrective action to bridge the gap at 
the earliest. 
(para 5.16) 
 
92. The Committee notes that while overall STEM enrolment is growing, female 
participation in engineering and technology courses remains disproportionately low 
(42.6% as per AISHE 2021-22). The Committee is of the view that AICTE and UGC 
should jointly develop Gender Parity in STEM Action Plan with institution-specific 
targets for female enrolment and offer scholarships exclusively for women in STEM at 
postgraduate and doctoral levels in all HEIs. 
(para 5.19) 
 
93. Many government degree colleges and State university-affiliated colleges lack 
functional STEM laboratories, forcing students to learn from textbooks alone. The 
Committee recommends that PM-USHA's Phase 3 should prioritise laboratory 
modernisation and equipment grants for STEM disciplines, with a minimum of Rs. 50 
lakh per institution for science lab upgradation and Rs. 1 crore for engineering 
workshops, covering at least10% of HEIs. 
(para 5.20) 
 
94. AICTE's Model Curriculum in AI, Data Science, and Robotics is a commendable 
step; however, adoption across the 10,000+ AICTE-approved institutions is limited. The 
Committee recommends that AICTE mandate updated STEM curriculum adoption as a 
condition for annual approval renewal, with a three-year implementation timeline. 
Faculty retraining through MMTTP should be specifically aligned with the updated 
STEM content. 
(para 5.21) 
 
95. The Committee emphasizes that India's STEM innovation potential is constrained 
by geographical concentration of research in metropolitan and Tier-1 city institutions. 
The Committee recommends a STEM Research Cluster programme to establish 50 

92 
 
STEM Research Clusters at government institutions in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities over a 
period of five years, with seed funding of Rs. 5-10 crore each under a dedicated scheme, 
focusing on applied research relevant to local industries, agricultural and environmental 
challenges. 
(para 5.22) 
 
96. Of India's 45,000+ colleges, only a fraction has implemented SWAYAM credit 
transfer despite 415 universities adopting the framework. The Committee recommends 
that UGC should take necessary steps mandating all affiliated colleges to allow students 
to earn at least 20% of their total academic credits through SWAYAM courses, with a 
phased implementation timeline starting from academic year 2026-27. Non-compliance 
should be flagged during NAAC accreditation assessment. 
(para 5.23) 
 
97. The Committee appreciates SWAYAM Plus, with 89 industry partners and 4.8 lakh 
enrolments, which has demonstrated strong industry appetite for skilling through the 
MOOC model. The Committee recommends that SWAYAM Plus should target more  
industry partners and enrolments, with specific campaigns in MSME and 
manufacturing sectors where skilling gaps are acute. Completion certificates from 
SWAYAM Plus should be recognised under the National Credit Framework (NCrF). 
(para 5.24) 
 
98. The Committee observes that despite India's linguistic diversity, the majority of 
SWAYAM courses are in English or Hindi while a significant proportion of India's 
student population learns best in their mother tongue. The Committee recommends that 
by 2027-28, at least 500 SWAYAM courses be made available in each of the 22 
Scheduled Languages, with dedicated funding for translation, dubbing, and regional 
language content creation, and involvement of regional language universities and State 
governments in content development. 
(para 5.25) 
 
99. The Committee notes with satisfaction that allocation under NER BE has been 
enhanced from Rs. 4,020.85 crore in NER BE 2025-26 to Rs. 4,424.16 crore in NER BE 
2026-27, an increase of Rs. 403.31 crore (10.03%). This increase demonstrates sustained 
Government commitment to improving higher education access and quality in the North 
Eastern States through targeted investments in existing institutions and new scheme 
deliveries. The Committee is of the view that the Department of Higher Education 
should publish a detailed NER spend report covering institution-wise utilization under 
all schemes, not just the dedicated NER budget line, to capture the full picture of 
investment in the NER higher education. 
(para 5.28) 
 
100. The Committee recommends that a dedicated monitoring cell should be set up for 
NER institutions, given the unique challenges of geography, connectivity, and social 
contexts in these States. Regular review meetings with NE States' education Secretaries 
should be institutionalized for better monitoring of HEIs in NER. 

93 
 
(para 5.29) 
 
101. The Committee recommends that NE institutions and universities should be 
provided targeted additional support for infrastructure development, faculty 
recruitment, and research capacity, given that these institutions cater to socially and 
geographically disadvantaged student populations. The Committee also recommends 
that a special component of PM-USHA be carved out for North Eastern States with 
relaxed matching-grant requirements, recognizing the fiscal constraints of smaller NE 
States. 
(para 5.30) 
 
102. The Committee notes the recent policy reforms enabling reputed foreign universities 
to establish campuses in India. While recognising the potential benefits in terms of 
global exposure and academic collaboration, the Committee underscores the need for 
robust regulatory oversight. It recommends that clear safeguards be instituted to ensure 
that such institutions reinvest a reasonable portion of their surplus within India. The 
Committee further is of the view that course curricula maintain an appropriate balance 
between global standards and Indian academic, cultural, and developmental contexts. 
Therefore, periodic performance reviews, including assessment of academic quality, 
research output, fee structures, student diversity, and compliance with national 
regulations, should be made mandatory. A transparent monitoring mechanism must be 
established to ensure accountability and alignment with national higher education 
priorities. 
(para 5.33)

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Seventy Sixth 
Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No. 25) of the Department of 
School Education & Literacy for the year 2026-27.  
2. In accordance with the constitutional provisions under Article 113, the estimated 
expenditure of the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India projected under 
various Demands for Grants for the upcoming financial year needs to be voted by Parliament. 
As a sequel thereto, Demands for Grants of the relevant Ministries/Departments stand 
referred to concerned Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee to make a close 
scrutiny thereof under Rule 270 of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the 
Council of States (Rajya Sabha). While making scrutiny of the Demands for Grants, the 
Committee has made an appraisal of the performance, programmes, schemes and policies of 
the Department of School Education and Literacy vis-a-vis expenditure made out of the 
Consolidated Fund of India in the current financial year. 
3. The Budget allocations of the Ministry of Education have been sought under two 
Demand Numbers, i.e, Demand No. 25 pertains to the Department of School Education and 
Literacy and Demand No.26 pertains to Department of Higher Education. In this Report, a

CHAPTER 1 
INTRODUCTION 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT OF SCHOOL EDUCATION AND LITERACY 
1.1 School education forms the bedrock of a nation’s intellectual, social and economic 
development. School serves not merely as institutions of learning but as structured 
environments where children are nurtured to think critically, act responsibly and contribute 
meaningfully to the society. A strong school education system ensures the development of 
literacy, numeracy and cognitive skills, which are indispensable. Investing in school 
education yields long-term dividends in the form of a skilled workforce and sustainable 
economic growth. In essence, the quality and accessibility of school education directly 
influence the trajectory of national progress. It is in this backdrop, the Committee on 
Education, Women, Children, Youth and Sports considered the Demand for Grants 2026-27 
of the Department of School Education and Literacy, Ministry of Education. 
1.2 The Ministry of Education (MoE) is the apex body responsible for framing and 
implementing the National Education Policy, overseeing educational programmes at all 
levels, and developing systemic educational infrastructure across the country. The 
Department of School Education and Literacy decides the policy and programmes relating to 
school education, adult education and digital education with focus on quality, equity and 
inclusion. 
The Ministry of Education comprises of two Departments: 
(i) Department of School Education and Literacy (DoSEL); and  
(ii) Department of Higher Education (DoHE) 
1.3 Vision and Mission 
Vision: To develop a comprehensive and holistic school education system anchored in the 
constitutional values of equality, justice, and social cohesion that prepare every child in India 
to be a creative, critical thinker and a responsible global citizen, in alignment with the vision 
of NEP 2020. 
Mission: To ensure universal access to quality schooling from Balvatika to Grade XII, 
promote foundational literacy and numeracy, reduce dropout rates, bridge gender and social 
gaps, and nurture innovation through technology-integrated learning, thereby enabling every 
child to realise his/her full potential. 
1.4 Objectives of the Department 
 To formulate the National Policy on school education and ensure its implementation. 
 To ensure planned development, universal access, and improvement in quality of 
school education across the country. 
 To provide special attention to disadvantaged groups — economically deprived, 
females, SC/ST/OBC, and minorities. 
 To provide financial assistance in the form of scholarships and other support to 
deserving students. 

2 
 
 To administer the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 
2009. 
 To implement the National Education Policy 2020 at school level through curriculum, 
pedagogy, and assessment reforms. 
 To promote digital education, foundational literacy and numeracy, and innovation in 
school education. 
 To encourage international cooperation in education, including with UNESCO and 
foreign governments. 
1.5 Autonomous and Regulatory Bodies under the Department 
The following Autonomous Bodies and Institutions are under the administrative control of 
the Department of School Education and Literacy, involved in policy formulation, curriculum 
development, teacher training, and implementation of various schemes: 
 National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) 
 Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS) 
 Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS) 
 National Bal Bhawan (NBB) 
1.6 The Department of School Education and Literacy also administers the Right of Children 
to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009, as amended from time to time. The Act 
mandates the appropriate Government to provide free and compulsory elementary education 
to every child of the age group of 6 to 14 years in a neighbourhood school. 
1.7 The major Legislative and Policy Framework under the Department of School Education 
and Literacy are as follows: 
 Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 
 National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 
 National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCF-SE) 2023 
 National Curriculum Framework for Foundational Stage (NCF-FS) 2022 
 National Food Security Act, 2013 (for PM POSHAN)

crore in BE 2025-26 for Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS), AE as on 13th  February

that in Samagra Shiksha alone, the largest scheme run by the Department, AE is Rs.

9 
 
recommends identifying the specific administrative, procedural and inter-governmental 
bottlenecks responsible for under-utilisation in CSS schemes. 
2.12 In backdrop of the Actual expenditure by the Department of School Education and 
Literacy during the FY 2025-26 and Rule 56(3) of General Financial Rules (GFR), 
Ministry of Finance, the Committee recommends the Department to adhere to Rule 
56(3) of GFR and to streamline its expenditure during FY 2026-27 to optimize the 
utilization of funds allocated to it and to avoid piling up of expenditure during the last 
quarter of the financial year. 
2.13 The Committee observes that the Department had projected Rs. 98,331.90 crore to 
the Ministry of Finance for BE 2026-27, against which the actual allocation in BE 2026-
27 stands at Rs. 83,562.26 crore which is a shortfall of Rs. 14,769.64 crore i.e. 15.02% 
compression. The Committee is of the view that the Department should project the 
shortfall, if required, at the time of Revised Estimates so that the scheme does not suffer 
due to shortage of funds. 
2.14 The Committee is of the view that the capital expenditure, which stands at a 
negligible amount of Rs. 0.85 crore in BE 2026-27, should be substantially increased to 
support critical infrastructure requirements, particularly for schools in Aspirational 
Districts, LWE-affected areas, and tribal areas. 
2.15 The Committee welcomes the steps taken by the DoSEL in pursuance of the 
recommendation given in 363rd Report and a MoU has been signed with the State of 
Kerala for implementation of PM SHRI Scheme. The Committee, therefore, reiterates 
its recommendation from 363rd Report to resolve the issue expeditiously and amicably 
with the States of Tamil Nadu and West Bengal. Further, the Committee is of the view 
that SNA-SPARSH, now being rolled out in States/UTs, should be expanded to all States 
expeditiously to enable just-in-time release of funds, improved monitoring, and 
enhanced transparency in fund utilization. 
2.16 The Committee is of the view that a dedicated Outcome Budget document be 
prepared for the DoSEL, linking every rupee of expenditure to measurable learning 
outcomes, enrolment targets, and quality indicators, aligned with the SDG 4 
framework. 
2.17 The Committee is of the view that public expenditure on education, both Centre 
and States, as a percentage of GDP should be placed on a time-bound roadmap with 
clearly defined annual milestones to achieve the NEP 2020 target of 6% by 2030.

MAJOR SCHEMES/ PROGRAMMES OF THE DEPARTMENT 
3.1 In the course of the meetings, the Department has informed about the numerous schemes

Pradhan Mantri Innovative Learning Programme (DHRUV) 
3.2 The Pradhan Mantri Innovative Learning Programme (DHRUV), introduced in 2019 
under the aegis of the Department of School Education and Literacy, Ministry of Education, 
is a pioneering national initiative for the early identification and nurturing of gifted and 
talented students across the country. The programme is envisaged as a first-of-its-kind 
national framework for gifted students to enhance their skills through specialized training, 
personal mentorship and exposure to leading institutions and experts. By fostering curiosity, 
creativity and innovative thinking, DHRUV aims to develop future leaders, researchers and 
innovators who can contribute to national development. The initiative also promotes a culture 
of excellence in learning and encourages young minds to pursue knowledge, research and 
problem-solving for societal progress. The guidelines for the scheme are presently being 
finalised after extensive stakeholder deliberations.

School Education and Literacy that the initial allocation of Rs 55 crore was sought at the BE 
stage in FY 2025-26, envisaging that a pilot of the scheme will be launched in select 
States/UTs during FY 2025-26. However, extended deliberations with subject matter experts 
and stakeholders for firming-up the scheme guidelines resulted in limited time being 
available for executing the pilot. The allocation was accordingly revised to Rs 5 crores at RE 
stage in FY 2025-26 to cater for preliminary activities involved in the pilot, such as 
information dissemination, test material development and teacher training and sensitization 
for identification of giftedness. Further, it was informed that the scheme has not seen any 
actual financial utilization since its announcement, as the appraisal and approval process as 
per extant Department of Expenditure guidelines are currently in progress. 
3.5 The Committee notes that the scheme was announced in 2019 but no actual 
expenditure has occurred under the Scheme till date. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that long-pending approval of the DHRUV scheme must be expedited and 
a timeline should be set for operationalization of the scheme. The Committee is also of 
the view that allocation of Rs. 50 crore in BE 2026-27 should be utilised productively 
and the Department should ensure that no carry-forward of unspent balances is taken 
into subsequent years. 
 
3.6 The Committee is of the view that a transparent and scientific methodology for 
identification of gifted and talented children must be developed, ensuring 
representation from all States/UTs and socio-economic backgrounds, including 
SC/ST/OBC/Female and rural communities. A special outreach should be undertaken 
by the Department for girl children and children from disadvantaged communities to 
ensure equitable access to mentorship under DHRUV. 
 
3.7 The Committee is of the view that the scheme should incorporate provisions for 
identifying gifted children in the domains of visual arts, performing arts, sports, and 
traditional knowledge in addition to STEM fields. In this regard, State Governments 
should be involved as implementation partners with the role of States in identification 
and nomination of candidates. 
 
3.8 The Committee is of the view that a digital platform should be created for the 
scheme to facilitate mentor-mentee interaction, tracking progress of the beneficiaries, 
and dissemination of knowledge resources in real time. The Committee is also of the 
view that annual performance reviews and independent evaluations of outcomes should 
be built into the scheme design from the inception so that proper monitoring could be 
done. 
 
National Means cum Merit Scholarship Scheme (NMMSS) 
3.9 The National Means-cum-Merit Scholarship Scheme was launched in the year 2008 with 
the objective of awarding scholarships to meritorious students from economically weaker 
sections to arrest the dropout rate at the Class VIII level and encourage them to continue 

12 
 
secondary education up to Class XII. The scheme provides scholarships of Rs. 12,000 per 
annum (Rs. 1,000 per month) per student at the Class IX stage, continuing up to Class XII, 
subject to the fulfilment of eligibility criteria. Scholarships are awarded to selected students 
of class IX every year and their continuation or renewal in classes X to XII for study in State 
Government, Government-aided and Local body schools under the scheme. As per the 
guidelines of the NMMSS, the beneficiary students should get a minimum of 60% marks in 
class-X for continuation of scholarship (relaxable by 5% for SC/ST candidates) for class-XI 
and class-XII. 
3.10 The Committee was informed that to ensure fair access to NMMSS test for students 
from diverse backgrounds, the NMMSS examination is not conducted at Central level but at 
the State-level. Each State/UT is assigned the task of conducting its own test, at State level in 
different languages as per the prescribed syllabus for Class VIII.  
3.11 The scheme is administered through the National Scholarship Portal (NSP), which 
operates on the PFMS platform, which was developed for streamlining and fast tracking the 
release of Scholarships and assuring the delivery of scholarships with efficiency, 
transparency and reliability across Ministries/Departments of the GOI. AII the qualified 
candidates across all States/UTs submit their applications for scholarship through NSP, which 
gets verified at two levels, i.e. at Institute Nodal Officer (L1) and District Nodal Officer (L2). 
Those applications which are finally verified at two levels are considered for sanction of 
scholarship amount. Aadhaar Payment Bridge (APB) gateway is used for disbursal of 
scholarship through NSP in DBT mode. The rate of successful payments under APB system 
is approximately 95% every year. 
3.12 As per the Evaluation study report of Institute of Economic Growth, 2025 the scheme 
has been successful in ensuring that the students continue to meet the continuation/renewal 
criteria to continue their scholarships in class-XI and class-XII. At the same time, this criteria 
has motivated the beneficiary students for better academic performance in class-X and class-
XII examination. As per the study, the scheme is effective and benefiting the meritorious 
students of economically disadvantaged sections in continuation of higher education and it 
has been strongly realized that this scholarship scheme should be continued in future with the 
prescribed policy changes and recommendation. This scheme is not only preventing school 
dropouts and early marriage of girl-children but also improving equity and quality in 
education. Overall, the enhanced outlay aligns with the objectives of the National Education 
Policy 2020 by promoting equity, reducing dropout rates, and ensuring continuity of 
education at the secondary level and achieving the objective of 100% GER in secondary 
education by 2030.

3.17 The Committee observes that the scholarship amount of Rs. 12,000 per annum has 
remained unchanged since the launch of scheme. The Committee is of the view that the 
scholarship amount should be revised to at least Rs. 24,000 per annum (Rs. 2,000 per 
month), factoring in inflation and the actual cost of living for students in urban, semi-
urban, and rural areas. The Committee also observes that for the year 2024-25, a toal of 
1,942,199 candidates appeared of which only 97,754 (5%) candidates were selected. The 
Committee, therefore, is of the view that the total number of scholarships sanctioned 
(1,00,000 per year) should be substantially increased in line with the large number of 
eligible students appearing in the examination every year. 
3.18 The Committee observes that AE under NMMSS in 2025-26, as on 13th February 
2026, stands at Rs. 27.36 crore against an allocation BE of Rs. 374 crore in BE stage 
which is only 7.31% utilisation with less than seven weeks remaining in the financial 
year. The Committee recommends the Department to identify the reasons for the 
exceptionally low utilisation of NMMSS funds in 2025-26, including (a) number of 
applications received, verified at L1 and L2 levels, and sanctioned as of 13th February 
2026; (b) the number of applications pending at each stage of the NSP; and resolve the 
bottlenecks on priority so that eligible students are not deprived of scholarships they 
have already qualified for.

examination within the prescribed timeline should be subjected to a constant 
monitoring mechanism with corrective action protocols. The Committee is also of the

view that the States which have historically shown low utilization rates should be 
provided dedicated capacity building support to ensure full utilization of their quota. 
3.20 The Committee recommends that the National Scholarship Portal (NSP) should be 
completely made multilingual and accessible to students in all regional languages to 
reduce barriers to application and encourage participation from remote areas. The 
Committee also recommends that the verification and disbursal process should be 
streamlined to ensure that renewals are processed within 30 days of the commencement 
of the academic year, preventing disruption to students' studies. 
Atal Tinkering Labs (ATL) Scheme 
3.21 The Atal Tinkering Labs (ATL) Scheme is a flagship initiative of the Department of 
School Education and Literacy (DoSEL), Ministry of Education, announced in the Union 
Budget 2025-26. The scheme aims to establish 50,000 ATL in Government schools to foster 
a spirit of innovation, scientific temper, creativity, and problem-solving skills among school 
students from Class VI to XII, in alignment with the objectives of the National Education 
Policy 2020. The ATL programme seeks to create a nation of innovators by providing hands-
on learning experience through modern tools such as, AI, 3D printers, robotics kits, 
electronics, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and other STEM-related equipment. The 
scheme is being positioned as a transformative intervention to develop a future-ready 
workforce. 
3.22 The experience of ATL 1.0 as a pathway to attract students to science and technology - 
has been used as evidence to scale this pedagogy systematically through ATL 2.0. Selection 
of ATL schools under ATL 2.0 prioritizes higher secondary government schools (classes 6–
12) as Hubs, which will then be mapped to nearby Spoke schools, ensuring that students from 
surrounding government, government-aided and even private schools can also benefit from 
the ATL ecosystem. ATL 2.0 proposes a more rigorous monitoring architecture building on 
ATL 1.0’s third-party assessment, which showed that 97.5% of existing ATLs were 
operational and that schools reported clear gains in 21st-century competencies. Under the 
new scheme, key performance indicators (KPIs) will be defined for both Hub and Spoke 
schools covering frequency and quality of ATL sessions, project completion, participation in 
competitions, mentorship engagement and inclusion of girls and disadvantaged groups. 
3.23 In response to a query of the Committee during the meetings, the Department of School 
Education and Literacy has informed that for national skill development and entrepreneurship 
linkages, the scheme explicitly plans to: 
 Leverage the Mentor India/Mentor of Change ecosystem and explore onboarding 
World Skills and National Skills Competition mentors as ATL mentors in 
collaboration with MSDE, thus connecting school-level innovation with national skill 
standards. 
 Build structured innovation pathways from ATLs to higher education institutions 
(IITs, NITs, engineering colleges, other HEIs of eminence) through formal mapping 
of Hub ATLs to local HEIs for mentorship, lab visits and knowledge exchange. 
 Institutionalize synergy with Dept of Science and Technology’s (DST) 
INSPIRE-MANAK scheme so that student awardees can use ATL infrastructure to 
convert ideas into workable prototypes and connect ATLs with DST’s NIDHI 
incubation ecosystem for incubation and scale-up of promising student innovations.
