3.26 The Committee recommends that given the massive scale-up from Rs. 500 crore 
(RE 2025-26) to Rs. 3,200 crore (BE 2026-27), a comprehensive national implementation 
framework, including clear norms for equipment procurement, teacher training, and 
school selection should be prepared before the funds are released to participating 
schools. The Committee also recommends that priority should be given to schools in 
aspirational districts, tribal areas, and educationally backward regions for 
establishment of ATLs to ensure equitable access to innovation infrastructure. In this 
regard, the scheme should include a structured maintenance and renewal budget to 
ensure sustainability of ATL operations beyond the initial setup phase. 
3.27 The Committee recommends that a dedicated trained teacher/facilitator must be 
mandated for every ATL, with specialised training programmes conducted through 
respective SCERTs and DIETs. The State-wise targets for ATL establishment should be 
set with clear timelines, and progress should be tracked through PRABANDH portal or 
equivalent monitoring mechanism. 
3.28 The Committee is of the view that the scheme’s convergence with CBSE's existing 
ATL network and NITI Aayog's Atal Innovation Mission framework should be ensured 
to avoid duplication of efforts and infrastructure. 
3.29 The Committee recommends that annual ATL competitions and innovation fests 
should be organised at district, State, and national levels to showcase student talent and 
sustain engagement with special emphasis on female students. In this regard, gender-
inclusive design principles be incorporated in ATL activities, with specific incentives for 
girl students to participate in innovation challenges.

3.38 The Committee notes that there is persistent gap between the fund allocation and 
actual utilisation under Samagra Shiksha – for example 2025-26 BE of Rs. 41250 crore 
vs AE of Rs. 22634 crore as of 13.02.2026. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Department of School Education and Literacy should introduce a stricter release-
linked-to-expenditure mechanism and review the fund utilisation pattern of States/UTs 
on monthly basis in order to make the scheme efficacious. 
3.39 The Committee notes that the dropout rate for some States is persistently above the 
national average which is a matter of concern. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Department should identify at least ten districts with the highest secondary 
dropout rates in each of the States where secondary dropout exceeds 15% and prepare 
a district-specific intervention plan in collaboration with the State government under 
Samagra Shiksha that address the locally-dominant factors of dropout.  
3.40 The Committee is of the view that the target of universal school infrastructure 
(100% schools with toilets, drinking water, electricity, ramps, and libraries) should be 
achieved on a time-bound basis. In this regard, the Committee is of the view that special 
attention is needed for ramp availability which is currently 87.7% in 2024-25 and 
playground access which is currently 79.9%. 
3.41 The Committee notes that some States lag behind in closing the gender gap with 
respect to gross enrolment. In this regard, the Committee recommends that  gender gap 
in enrolment at secondary level must be addressed through targeted incentives, with 
special focus on States like Bihar, Jharkhand, and Madhya Pradesh where girls' 
dropout rates remain high. 
3.42 The Committee notes that the NIPUN Bharat Mission has seen some successes but is set to 
be wound up this Financial Year. The Committee recommends that it be extended for another 5 
years till 2032, with its ambit broadened to include children from Grades 3 to 5, with a focus on 

24 
 
oral reading fluency in addition to basic literacy and numeracy. The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry seek to increase the annual budgetary allocation from Rs. 2,500 
crores to Rs. 6,000 crores to enable the Missions’s expanded focus and to enhance funding for 
Early Childhood Care and Education, teaching-learning materials, and capacity-building 
support for teachers. This increase would expand reach from 2.5 crore to 6 crore children 
annually while maintaining the Rs. 1,000 per-child investment and keeping total expenditure 
under 1% national school education budgets.  
 
3.43 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry consider a census assessment for all 
Grade 5 students (Government and private) to diagnose system health and enable early course 
correction post the completion of the expanded NIPUN Bharat Mission. The Ministry may also 
consider the use of Personalised Adaptive Learning (PAL) products, leveraging advances in 
technology to support education among children. 
 
3.44 The Committee notes that the NEP calls for universal Early Childhood Care and 
Education. The Committee notes that it is particularly important for the Ministry and the WCD 
Ministry to work on education for 5-year–old children, whose health requirements for 
vaccinations, etc. have largely concluded and who are ready to learn. The Ministry should 
develop a focused package for 5-year-olds with special attention to their educational needs, and 
ensure that any such learning protocol is universalized across Bal Vatikas and Anganwadis. 
 
Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN) 
3.45 Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN), earlier known as the National 
Programme of Mid-Day Meals in Schools (MDM), is one of the largest school nutrition 
programmes in the world. It is a rights-based Centrally Sponsored Scheme under the National 
Food Security Act, 2013. The primary objective of the scheme is to improve the nutritional 
status of children enrolled in Classes I to VIII and Balvatika in Government and Government-
aided schools, while simultaneously enhancing school attendance, enrolment, and retention 
rates. 
3.46 The scheme is one of the foremost rights based Centrally Sponsored Scheme 
implemented in partnership with the States and Union Territories (UTs) for providing one hot 
cooked and nutritious meal to all children studying in Bal Vatika (just before class-I) and 
classes I to VIII of Government and Government-aided schools.  The Scheme covers about 
11 crore children in more than 10.35 lakh schools and more than 24 lakh Cook-cum-Helpers 
are engaged for preparation of the meals in all the States/ UTs. The main objectives of the 
Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman Scheme are to address two of the pressing problems 
for the majority of children in India, viz. hunger and education: 
i. Improving the nutritional status of children studying in classes Bal Vatikas (just 
before class I) and I – VIII in Government and Government-Aided Schools. 
ii. Encouraging poor children, belonging to disadvantaged sections, to attend school 
more regularly and help them concentrate on classroom activities. 
iii. Providing nutritional support to children of elementary stage in drought-affected areas 
during summer vacation and during disaster times. 
3.47 The Committee was informed during the course of meetings that the Department of 
School Education and Literacy has put in place an automated system of data collection for 
real time monitoring of PM POSHAN. Such data (on number of meals served on that day and 
reasons if meals not served) is being continuously captured from schools. Under this system, 

25 
 
States/UTs have set up a suitable system of data collection (i.e. Interactive Voice Response 
System (IVRS)/SMS/Mobile Application/Web Application) from schools on daily basis for 
purpose of monitoring and timely follow up action. Daily email alerts are sent to States/UTs 
regarding number of schools which have reported data on that particular date and schools 
where meals have not been served. It is being implemented in all the States and UTs. A 
comprehensive Management Information System (MIS) has been developed for PM 
POSHAN Scheme. States/UTs are submitting data on specific fields on MIS. Based on the 
data collected, various drill down reports are made available for real time monitoring of the

3.50 The Committee was informed by the Department that the NITI AAYOG has conducted 
the evaluation of PM POSHAN Scheme through an independent third-party agency. The 
study concluded that the PM POSHAN scheme is important not just for improving child 
nutrition, but also for boosting learning outcomes, promoting social equity, empowering 
communities, and supporting the holistic development of India’s next generation and 
therefore, strongly recommended for continuation of PM POSHAN Scheme. 
3.51 The Committee observes that in 2022-23, AE under the scheme was Rs. 12,680.97 
crore which exceeded the BE of Rs. 10233.75 crore and came nearly to the RE of Rs. 
12800 crore. In 2023-24, AE had fallen to Rs. 8,457.72 crore against a BE of Rs. 11,600 
crore. Further, in 2024-25, AE was Rs. 9,903 crore against a BE of Rs. 12,467.39 crore 
and in 2025-26, as on 13th February 2026, AE is Rs. 6,639.22 crore against a BE of Rs. 
12,500 crore. The pattern shows year-on-year divergence between the allocations and 

28 
 
the actual utilization by the schools. The Committee recommends that the Department 
should introduce a quarterly fund release schedule for PM POSHAN that is fixed at the 
beginning of the financial year to monitor the fund utilisation systematically. The 
Committee further recommends that the SNA-SPARSH model, currently being piloted 
under Samagra Shiksha, may be extended to PM POSHAN as a priority, so that funds 
flow in response to demonstrated expenditure rather than in bulk tranches that either 
arrive too late or too close to year-end for orderly utilisation. 
3.52 The Committee notes that the cooking cost norms under PM POSHAN were 
increased by 9.5% with effect from 01.05.2025. In this regard, the Committee is of the 
view that a comprehensive review of cooking cost norms should be conducted at least 
once every two years, factoring in CPI-linked inflation to ensure nutritional adequacy of 
meals. 
3.53 The Committee notes persistent decline in the number of beneficiaries from 12.16 
crore in 2022-23 to 10.99 crore in 2024-25. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Department of School Education and Literacy should examine whether this reflects 
genuine reduction in eligible enrolment or gaps in scheme coverage, and take corrective 
measures accordingly. 
3.54 The Committee notes that PM-POSHAN has not been implemented in the State of 
West Bengal in full spirit for last two years. The Committee recommends that the Union 
and State Governments work together to resolve all issues expeditiously. 
3.55 The Committee is of the view that the role of Anganwadi Centres in complementing 
PM POSHAN for children aged 3-6 years should be formally integrated with clear 
responsibilities defined for School Education and WCD departments at State level. 
Strengthening Teaching-Learning and Results for States (STARS) 
3.56 The Strengthening Teaching-Learning and Results for States (STARS) Project is a 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme approved by the Cabinet in October 2020, implemented with 
World Bank assistance. The project aims to improve measurable educational outcomes and 
support school-to-work transition for improved labour market outcomes. Implemented in six 
States - Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, and Rajasthan - 
the STARS project is aligned with NEP 2020's vision of quality-based learning outcomes. 
The project was originally approved for five years up to FY 2024-25 and has been extended 
for two additional years till March 2027. 
3.57 The key focus areas under the STARS Project include Foundational Learning and Early 
Childhood Education (ECE); Strengthening of Learning Assessment Systems; Teacher 
Development and Improvement of Classroom Practices; Governance and Decentralized 
Service Delivery; and School-to-Work Transition and Vocational Education. The expected 
outcomes of the STARS Project are as follows: 
 Increase in students achieving minimum proficiency in grade 3 language in select 
states 
 Improvement in secondary school completion rate in select states 
 Improvement in governance index scores in select states 

29 
 
 Strengthened learning assessment systems with fully operational National assessment 
centre and state assessment centres 
 Partnerships developed to facilitate cross-learning between states 
 State-level improved service delivery by Strengthening Early Years Education, 
Improving Learning Assessment Systems, Improving Teacher Performance and 
Classroom Practice, Strengthening Governance and Decentralized Management for 
Improved Service Delivery, and Skill education and training. 
3.58 The Committee was informed that under the STARS Project, institutions such as 
SCERTs, DIETs, and BRCs/CRCs are being strengthened 
to enhance academic support, teacher professional development, mentoring, and evidence-
based planning, with the district positioned as the primary unit for implementation and 
monitoring. The Project is also driving major assessment reforms through the establishment 
of an independent National Assessment Centre and State Assessment Cells, alongside 
adoption of competency-based assessments supported by online item banks.  Further,  the  
Project  is  institutionalizing  performance- based governance by incentivizing improvements 
in governance related PGI indicators, strengthening systems for teacher deployment, 
attendance, school inspection, and planning, and ensuring the eﬀective use of UDISE+ for 
accurate, validated, and publicly accessible data, thereby supporting a shift toward outcome-
oriented monitoring and governance. Main achievements of the scheme are as under: 
 National Assessment Centre-PARAKH (Performance Assessment, Review and 
Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic Development) was set up in NCERT as per the 
mandate under STARS on 8th February 2023. 
 Under the STARS scheme, states have launched impactful school readiness initiatives 
to strengthen early childhood education such as Pahile Paule initiative in Maharashtra 
engaging over 14 lakh children and forming 2.5 lakh mothers' groups across 70,000 
schools in School Readiness Melas, Pehli Shikshak-Maa program in Himachal 
Pradesh resulting in up to 40-47% improvements in cognitive, language, and socio-
emotional skills, Responsive Parenting Kit in Rajasthan distributed to over 25,000 
early learning centers. 
 All six STARS states have established State Assessment Cells. These Assessment 
cells have developed learning outcome-based online item banks, as well as teacher 
training modules for Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation (CCE) and 
classroom-based assessment. They have also conducted teacher training on CCE and 
classroom-based assessment. 
 Increase in secondary school completion rate among the six STARS states from 
79.95% to 93.53% in FY 2022-23.(UDISE report 2022-23) 
 Increase in students achieving minimum proficiency in grade 3 language in six 
STARS states from 44.17% in NAS 2021 to 70.33% in PARAKH Rashtriya 
Sarvekshan (PRS) 2024.

reform. The Committee is also of the view that the Department should assess whether 
the STARS framework can be expanded to additional States as a domestic scheme 
(without external financing) given its demonstrable impact on learning outcomes and 
inform the Committee for its consideration. 
3.61 The Committee appreciates that all six STARS States have established State 
Assessment Cells that have been an effective centre of learning. The Committee 
recommends that the State assessment systems strengthened under STARS should be 
integrated with the national PARAKH framework to ensure comparability and 
sustainability of assessment practices. 
3.62 The Committee notes that the project is concluding its initial implementation phase 
in March, 2027. With regard to this, the Committee is of the view that the transition 
plan for STARS-supported States after the project closure should be clearly defined, 
ensuring that gains made under the project are not lost. The Committee recommends 
that the teacher training activities supported under STARS should be linked to the 
DIET CoE programme under Samagra Shiksha for continuity. 
3.63 The Committee is of the view that the project's outcomes on learning levels, teacher 
performance, and school governance should be independently evaluated by a third 
party before project closure. Further, the Department should explore a possible 
successor scheme or additional financing for scaling up evidence-based education 
interventions. 
PM Schools for Rising India (PM SHRI) 
3.64 PM Schools for Rising India (PM SHRI), earlier known as the Exemplar Schools 
scheme, is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme launched in 2022. The scheme aims to develop and 
upgrade more than 14,500 model schools across the country that will serve as exemplars of 
the National Education Policy 2020 in action - providing high-quality, equitable, and 
inclusive education to students across diverse backgrounds. These schools are expected to 
lead educational transformation in their respective regions and showcase best practices. A 
total of 13,076 schools have been selected as PM SHRI schools from 33 States/UTs along 
with KVS/NVS/NCERT. The total cost of the project is Rs. 27360 crore spread over a period 
of 5 years which includes central share of Rs. 18128 crore. 

31 
 
3.65 The Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) of PM SHRI schools are assessed on their 
ability to deliver high-quality, equitable, inclusive, and joyful education, while addressing the 
diverse socio-cultural, multilingual, and academic needs of students and ensuring their active 
participation in the learning process in accordance with the vision of NEP 2020.

training is done through District Institutes of Education and Training (DIETs). There is 
financial provision of up to ₹3.00 lakh per DIET for capacity-building programmes of PM

New India Literacy Programme (NILP/ULLAS) 
3.73 The New India Literacy Programme (NILP), branded as ULLAS (Understanding of 
Lifelong Learning for All in Society) / Nav Bharat Saaksharta Karyakram, is a Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme of Adult Education for the period 2022-27. The scheme is designed to 
impart foundational literacy and numeracy skills to all persons above 15 years of age who are 
not literate. It covers five components: Foundational Literacy and Numeracy, Critical Life 
Skills, Vocational Skills, Basic Education, and Continuing Education. The scheme is 
implemented in a hybrid mode through volunteerism based on the vision of making Bharat 
'Jan Jan Saakshar', driven by Kartavyabodh (a sense of duty) and Janbhagidari (collective 
responsibility), utilising School/HEIs platforms and community engagement through 
volunteerism. Volunteers include students of Schools, Teacher Education Institutions of 
NCTE, Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) etc. to teach the non-literates. The scheme is 
aligned with the recommendations of NEP 2020 on Adult Education and Lifelong Learning. 
More than 2.37 crore learners from 33 States/UTs have participated in the literacy test under 
the scheme. 
3.74 The scheme has five components, namely; Foundational Literacy and Numeracy, 
Critical Life Skills, Basic Education, Vocational Skills, and Continuing Education. The 
scheme covers basic reading, writing and numeracy, digital literacy, financial literacy and life 
skills relevant to daily life. Learning content is provided in regional languages through 
learner-friendly primers, digital platforms, and community learning centres to ensure 
universal access and inclusivity. A dedicated Mobile App of ULLAS was launched on 
29.7.2023 for registering learners and volunteer teachers and also enables teaching learning 
process by providing access to primers available in 27 languages. As on date, more than 3.14 
crore Learners and 46.98 lakh Volunteer Teachers (VTs) have been registered on Mobile App 
of ULLAS till date. 

34 
 
3.75 The Committee was informed, during the course of meetings that the implementation of 
ULLAS since 2022-23 has resulted for the first time in declaration of ‘Full Literacy’ by 
States/UTs. Till now 6 States & UTs – Ladakh, Mizoram, Tripura, Goa, Chandigarh and 
Himachal Pradesh have declared Full Literacy. The Literacy rate as per PLFS 2023 stands at 
80.9% as in 2023-24.

3.78 The Committee observes that flat allocation of Rs. 160 crore for four consecutive 
years from 2024-25 to 2026-27 for ULLAS is inadequate given the scale of adult 
illiteracy in the country. The Committee is of the view that a significant enhancement in 
allocation is required to commensurate with the estimated 25+ crore functionally 
illiterate adult so that the target of making all adults above 15 years of age literate by 
2030 is achieved. 
3.79 The Committee recommends that FLNAT (Foundational Literacy and Numeracy 
Assessment Test) should be conducted twice annually across all States, and results 
should be disaggregated by gender, social category, and age group. 
3.80 The Committee observes that several large States such as Maharashtra, Gujarat, 
Haryana, Karnataka and Jharkhand have shown low or no release of funds under the 
scheme. The Committee is of the view that the Department should examine and address 
implementation bottlenecks in these States on priority. 
3.81 The Committee is of the view that the volunteer teachers under ULLAS should be 
provided at least token compensation/incentives to sustain their motivation and 
engagement. Further, the scheme should leverage technology platforms such as mobile 
apps, community radio, and local language digital content to reach learners in remote 
areas for better output. 
3.82 The Committee is of the view that the Community Learning Centres (CLCs) 
established under the scheme should be mapped and monitored for functionality, with 
linkages to NIOS for certification.

Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS) 
4.1 Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS) was established in 1965 as a registered 
autonomous body under the Ministry of Education to cater to the educational needs of 
children of transferable Central Government employees. The KVS operates Kendriya 
Vidyalayas (KVs) - Central Government schools providing education from Class I to XII - 
across India and abroad. KVS schools follow the CBSE curriculum. The organisation is fully 
financed by the Government of India and is India's largest chain of centrally-managed 
schools, with a presence in every State and UT. 
4.2 The main objectives of Kendriya Vidyalayas are as under: 
 to cater to the educational needs of the children of transferable Central Government 
employees including Defence and Para-Military Personnel by providing a common 
programme of education. 
 to provide, establish, endow, maintain, control and manage schools for the children of 
transferable employees of the Government of India, floating population and others 
including those living in remote and undeveloped locations of the country and to do 
all acts and things necessary for or conducive to the promotion of such schools. 
 to pursue excellence and set pace in the field of school education; 
 to initiate and promote experimentation and innovativeness in education in 
collaboration with other bodies like the CBSE, NCERT etc., and 
 to develop the spirit of national integration and create a sense of ‘Indianness’ among 
children.

Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS) 
4.12 Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS), established in 1986, is an autonomous organisation 
under the Ministry of Education, registered under the Societies Registration Act 1860. NVS 
establishes, runs and operates Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas (JNVs) - fully residential 
schools providing quality education from Class VI to XII – all over the country primarily for 
talented rural children, with at least 75% seats reserved for rural students. JNVs are free-of-
cost institutions targeting socially and economically backward gifted students who lack 
access to accelerated learning due to financial, social and rural disadvantages, where students 
receive food, lodging, uniform, books, and stationery at the expense of the Government. As 
per the policy of Government of India, one JNV is to be established in each district of the 
country. Keeping in view with this policy, JNVs has been sanctioned all over the country, 
except the State of Tamil Nadu, which has not yet accepted the Navodaya Vidyalaya Scheme. 
4.13 The main objectives of Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas are as under: 
 to provide good quality modern education to the talented students predominantly from 
rural areas irrespective of socio-economic status. 
 to nurture and promote the talent and creativity of the students 
 to develop integrated personality of the students under residential co-educational 
setup through value orientation and ultimately developing students to be good human 
beings and an asset to our Nation. 
 to make JNV as an excellent pace setting school in the District.

National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) 
4.24 The National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT), established in 
1961, is an autonomous organisation set up to advise and assist the Ministry of Education and 
State Governments in formulation and implementation of education policies. NCERT's core 
mandate encompasses curriculum development, preparation of textbooks, teacher education, 
research in education, and academic support to States. NCERT has recently developed new 
textbooks for Classes I-VIII aligned with the NCF-SE 2023 and NEP 2020 vision of 
competency-based, experiential, and multidisciplinary learning. NCERT is currently pursuing 
Deemed-to-be University status. 
4.25 The major objectives of NCERT are as follows: 
 to undertake, promote and coordinate research in areas related to school education and 
teacher education; 
 to prepare and publish model textbooks, supplementary reading material, newsletters, 
journals and develop educational kits, multimedia digital materials, etc.; 
 to organise pre-service and in-service training of teachers and teacher educators; 
develop and disseminate innovative educational techniques and practices; collaborate 
and network with state educational departments, universities, NGOs and other 
educational institutions; 
 to act as a clearing house for ideas and information in matters related to school 
education; and 
 to act as a nodal agency for achieving the goals of Universalisation of Elementary 
Education.

National Bal Bhawan (NBB) 
4.38 National Bal Bhawan (NBB), established in 1956, is an autonomous body fully financed 
by the Ministry of Education, Department of School Education and Literacy. It serves as a 
non-formal educational institution for children in the age group of 5 to 16 years. The 
institution was envisioned to promote learning through creative thinking, imagination and 
engaging activities for children. Its primary objective is to nurture and develop the creative 
abilities and skills of children by providing training in a wide range of activities such as art 
and craft, music, dance, stitching, handicrafts, weaving, clay modelling, science, museum 
activities, literacy, home management and physical education through a non-formal learning 
approach. It provides opportunities for cultural activities, fine arts, performing arts, science 
experimentation, and technology exploration, with special focus on children from 
economically weaker sections. 
4.39 The vision of National Bal Bhawan is as follows: 
 to let every child fully participate, contribute and strive towards a creative, humane, 
innovative and joyful World in all its Wonder. 

45 
 
 to provide opportunities that ignite curiosity and celebrate possibilities through 
immersive dynamic experiences in visual arts, scientific activities and physical 
activities. To foster values that mould self-confident, holistic and responsible citizens 
of the world.

MISCELLANEOUS 
ICT, AI and Digital Learning Initiatives 
5.1 Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and digital education occupy a 
central place in the implementation of NEP 2020. The Department of School Education and 
Literacy has made significant investments in ICT infrastructure, digital content, and AI-
integrated learning through its schemes. Key initiatives include the ICT component of 
Samagra Shiksha, PM e-VIDYA, DIKSHA (Digital Infrastructure for Knowledge Sharing), 
e-Pathshala, and the newly announced AVGC Content Creator Labs in secondary schools. 
The Finance Minister in her Budget Speech 2026-27 announced support to the Indian 
Institute of Creative Technologies, Mumbai, for setting up AVGC Content Creator Labs in 
15,000 secondary schools and 500 colleges. 
5.2 The Committee was informed during the course of meetings about the key digital 
initiatives undertaken in the field of ICT and Digital learning by the Department, are given as 
under: 
 DIKSHA (Digital Infrastructure for Knowledge Sharing): Serves as a comprehensive 
digital National platform for school education with digital learning content in multiple 
languages, accessed by crores of students, parents and teachers. It provides access to 
NCERT textbooks, energized digital textbooks with QR code integration, interactive 
learning materials, teacher professional development course and assessment tools. It 
acts as ‘One Nation, One Digital Platform’ under PM eVidya inititative. 
 PM e-VIDYA: Multi-mode platform integrating PM e-VIDYA DTH channels (One 
Class One Channel), online content, and digital textbooks. 
 NIPUN Bharat Digital Resources: Various FLN-focused digital content for 
foundational stage learners has been created under NIPUN Bharat. 
 AI in Curriculum: Budget Speech 2026-27 announced regarding specific measures for 
embedding AI in education curriculum from school level initiated in consultation with 
NCERT, CBSE, and IIT Madras. 
 AVGC Content Creator Labs: Announced in Budget 2026-27 - 15,000 secondary 
schools to get AVGC labs, linked to IICT Mumbai. 
 e-Jaadui Pitara (e-JP): Launched in February 2024, e-JP is a blend of technology and 
education to foster play-based pedagogy beyond classroom walls. This web based 
mobile application currently has more than 1,000 stories and includes songs, lullabies, 
riddles and activities available in 14 different languages. The application has 1lakh+ 
users till date. 
 NCERT: NCERT is conducting AI training programs that focus on foundational AI 
concepts, AI ethics, data literacy and the practical use of AI tools for lesson planning 
and assessments. Over 46,000 teachers have participated in AI awareness workshops 
and training. The Completion rate for teacher AI modules on the DIKSHA platform is 
63.23%.

OBSERVATIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE 
1. The Committee observes that against a combined fund allocation of Rs. 62,660 crore 
in BE 2025-26 for Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS), AE as on 13th  February 
2026 stands at Rs. 32,296.54 crore which is barely 51.5% of the BE and only 60.1% 
of the RE of Rs. 53,730.02 crore in the same financial year. The Committee further 
notes that in Samagra Shiksha alone, the largest scheme run by the Department, AE 
is Rs. 22,633.88 crore against a BE of Rs. 41,250 crore which is 54.9% utilisation of 
allocated funds with less than six weeks left in the financial year. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends identifying the specific administrative, procedural and inter-
governmental bottlenecks responsible for under-utilisation in CSS schemes. 
(para 2.11) 
 
2. In backdrop of the Actual expenditure by the Department of School Education and 
Literacy during the FY 2025-26 and Rule 56(3) of General Financial Rules (GFR), 
Ministry of Finance, the Committee recommends the Department to adhere to Rule 
56(3) of GFR and to streamline its expenditure during FY 2026-27 to optimize the 
utilization of funds allocated to it and to avoid piling up of expenditure during the 
last quarter of the financial year. 
(para 2.12) 
 
3. The Committee observes that the Department had projected Rs. 98,331.90 crore to 
the Ministry of Finance for BE 2026-27, against which the actual allocation in BE 
2026-27 stands at Rs. 83,562.26 crore which is a shortfall of Rs. 14,769.64 crore i.e. 
15.02% compression. The Committee is of the view that the Department should 
project the shortfall, if required, at the time of Revised Estimates so that the scheme 
does not suffer due to shortage of funds. 
(para 2.13) 
 
4. The Committee is of the view that the capital expenditure, which stands at a 
negligible amount of Rs. 0.85 crore in BE 2026-27, should be substantially increased 
to support critical infrastructure requirements, particularly for schools in 
Aspirational Districts, LWE-affected areas, and tribal areas. 
(para 2.14) 
 
5. The Committee welcomes the steps taken by the DoSEL in pursuance of the 
recommendation given in 363rd Report and a MoU has been signed with the State of 
Kerala for implementation of PM SHRI Scheme. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation from 363rd Report to resolve the issue expeditiously 
and amicably with the States of Tamil Nadu and West Bengal. Further, the 
Committee is of the view that SNA-SPARSH, now being rolled out in States/UTs, 

53 
 
should be expanded to all States expeditiously to enable just-in-time release of 
funds, improved monitoring, and enhanced transparency in fund utilization. 
(para 2.15) 
 
6. The Committee is of the view that a dedicated Outcome Budget document be 
prepared for the DoSEL, linking every rupee of expenditure to measurable learning 
outcomes, enrolment targets, and quality indicators, aligned with the SDG 4 
framework. 
(para 2.16) 
 
7. The Committee is of the view that public expenditure on education, both Centre and 
States, as a percentage of GDP should be placed on a time-bound roadmap with 
clearly defined annual milestones to achieve the NEP 2020 target of 6% by 2030. 
(para 2.17) 
 
8. The Committee notes that the scheme was announced in 2019 but no actual 
expenditure has occurred under the Scheme till date. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that long-pending approval of the DHRUV scheme must be expedited 
and a timeline should be set for operationalization of the scheme. The Committee is 
also of the view that allocation of Rs. 50 crore in BE 2026-27 should be utilised 
productively and the Department should ensure that no carry-forward of unspent 
balances is taken into subsequent years. 
(para 3.5) 
 
9. The Committee is of the view that a transparent and scientific methodology for 
identification of gifted and talented children must be developed, ensuring 
representation from all States/UTs and socio-economic backgrounds, including 
SC/ST/OBC/Female and rural communities. A special outreach should be 
undertaken by the Department for girls children and children from disadvantaged 
communities to ensure equitable access to mentorship under DHRUV. 
(para 3.6) 
 
10. The Committee is of the view that the scheme should incorporate provisions for 
identifying gifted children in the domains of visual arts, performing arts, sports, and 
traditional knowledge in addition to STEM fields. In this regard, State 
Governments should be involved as implementation partners with the role of States 
in identification and nomination of candidates. 
(para 3.7) 
 

54 
 
11. The Committee is of the view that a digital platform should be created for the 
scheme to facilitate mentor-mentee interaction, tracking progress of the 
beneficiaries, and dissemination of knowledge resources in real time. The 
Committee is also of the view that annual performance reviews and independent 
evaluations of outcomes should be built into the scheme design from the inception so 
that proper monitoring could be done. 
(para 3.8) 
 
12. The Committee observes that the scholarship amount of Rs. 12,000 per annum has 
remained unchanged since the launch of scheme. The Committee is of the view that 
the scholarship amount should be revised to at least Rs. 24,000 per annum (Rs. 
2,000 per month), factoring in inflation and the actual cost of living for students in 
urban, semi-urban, and rural areas. The Committee also observes that for the year 
2024-25, a toal of 1,942,199 candidates appeared of which only 97,754 (5%) 
candidates were selected. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the total 
number of scholarships sanctioned (1,00,000 per year) should be substantially 
increased in line with the large number of eligible students appearing in the 
examination every year. 
(para 3.17) 
 
13. The Committee observes that AE under NMMSS in 2025-26, as on 13th February 
2026, stands at Rs. 27.36 crore against an allocation BE of Rs. 374 crore in BE stage 
which is only 7.31% utilisation with less than seven weeks remaining in the financial 
year. The Committee recommends the Department to identify the reasons for the 
exceptionally low utilisation of NMMSS funds in 2025-26, including (a) number of 
applications received, verified at L1 and L2 levels, and sanctioned as of 13th 
February 2026; (b) the number of applications pending at each stage of the NSP; 
and resolve the bottlenecks on priority so that eligible students are not deprived of 
scholarships they have already qualified for. 
(para 3.18) 
 
14. The Committee is of the view that States that do not conduct the NMMSS 
examination within the prescribed timeline should be subjected to a constant 
monitoring mechanism with corrective action protocols. The Committee is also of 
the view that the States which have historically shown low utilization rates should be 
provided dedicated capacity building support to ensure full utilization of their 
quota. 
(para 3.19) 
 

55 
 
15. The Committee recommends that the National Scholarship Portal (NSP) should be 
completely made multilingual and accessible to students in all regional languages to 
reduce barriers to application and encourage participation from remote areas. The 
Committee also recommends that the verification and disbursal process should be 
streamlined to ensure that renewals are processed within 30 days of the 
commencement of the academic year, preventing disruption to students' studies. 
(para 3.20) 
 
16. The Committee recommends that given the massive scale-up from Rs. 500 crore (RE 
2025-26) to Rs. 3,200 crore (BE 2026-27), a comprehensive national implementation 
framework, including clear norms for equipment procurement, teacher training, 
and school selection should be prepared before the funds are released to 
participating schools. The Committee also recommends that priority should be 
given to schools in aspirational districts, tribal areas, and educationally backward 
regions for establishment of ATLs to ensure equitable access to innovation 
infrastructure. In this regard, the scheme should include a structured maintenance 
and renewal budget to ensure sustainability of ATL operations beyond the initial 
setup phase. 
(para 3.26) 
 
17. The Committee recommends that a dedicated trained teacher/facilitator must be 
mandated for every ATL, with specialised training programmes conducted through 
respective SCERTs and DIETs. The State-wise targets for ATL establishment 
should be set with clear timelines, and progress should be tracked through 
PRABANDH portal or equivalent monitoring mechanism. 
(para 3.27) 
 
18. The Committee is of the view that the scheme’s convergence with CBSE's existing 
ATL network and NITI Aayog's Atal Innovation Mission framework should be 
ensured to avoid duplication of efforts and infrastructure. 
(para 3.28) 
 
19. The Committee recommends that annual ATL competitions and innovation fests 
should be organised at district, State, and national levels to showcase student talent 
and sustain engagement with special emphasis on female students. In this regard, 
gender-inclusive design principles be incorporated in ATL activities, with specific 
incentives for girl students to participate in innovation challenges. 
(para 3.29) 
 

56 
 
20. The Committee notes that there is persistent gap between the fund allocation and 
actual utilisation under Samagra Shiksha – for example 2025-26 BE of Rs. 41250 
crore vs AE of Rs. 22634 crore as of 13.02.2026. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department of School Education and Literacy should 
introduce a stricter release-linked-to-expenditure mechanism and review the fund 
utilisation pattern of States/UTs on monthly basis in order to make the scheme 
efficacious. 
(para 3.38) 
 
21. The Committee notes that the dropout rate for some States is persistently above the 
national average which is a matter of concern. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department should identify at least ten districts with the 
highest secondary dropout rates in each of the States where secondary dropout 
exceeds 15% and prepare a district-specific intervention plan in collaboration with 
the State government under Samagra Shiksha that address the locally-dominant 
factors of dropout.  
(para 3.39) 
 
22. The Committee is of the view that the target of universal school infrastructure 
(100% schools with toilets, drinking water, electricity, ramps, and libraries) should 
be achieved on a time-bound basis. In this regard, the Committee is of the view that 
special attention is needed for ramp availability which is currently 87.7% in 2024-25 
and playground access which is currently 79.9%. 
(para 3.40) 
 
23. The Committee notes that some States lag behind in closing the gender gap with 
respect to gross enrolment. In this regard, the Committee recommends that  gender 
gap in enrolment at secondary level must be addressed through targeted incentives, 
with special focus on States like Bihar, Jharkhand, and Madhya Pradesh where 
girls' dropout rates remain high. 
(para 3.41) 
 
24. The Committee notes that the NIPUN Bharat Mission has seen some successes but is 
set to be wound up this Financial Year. The Committee recommends that it be 
extended for another 5 years till 2032, with its ambit broadened to include children 
from Grades 3 to 5, with a focus on oral reading fluency in addition to basic literacy 
and numeracy. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry seek to increase 
the annual budgetary allocation from Rs. 2,500 crores to Rs. 6,000 crores to enable 
the Missions’s expanded focus and to enhance funding for Early Childhood Care 
and Education, teaching-learning materials, and capacity-building support for 

57 
 
teachers. This increase would expand reach from 2.5 crore to 6 crore children 
annually while maintaining the Rs. 1,000 per-child investment and keeping total 
expenditure under 1% national school education budgets. 
(para 3.42) 
 
25. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry consider a census assessment 
for all Grade 5 students (Government and private) to diagnose system health and 
enable early course correction post the completion of the expanded NIPUN Bharat 
Mission. The Ministry may also consider the use of Personalised Adaptive Learning 
(PAL) products, leveraging advances in technology to support education among 
children. 
(para 3.43) 
 
26. The Committee notes that the NEP calls for universal Early Childhood Care and 
Education. The Committee notes that it is particularly important for the Ministry 
and the WCD Ministry to work on education for 5-year–old children, whose health 
requirements for vaccinations, etc. have largely concluded and who are ready to 
learn. The Ministry should develop a focused package for 5-year-olds with special 
attention to their educational needs, and ensure that any such learning protocol is 
universalized across Bal Vatikas and Anganwadis. 
(para 3.44) 
 
27. The Committee observes that in 2022-23, AE under the scheme was Rs. 12,680.97 
crore which exceeded the BE of Rs. 10233.75 crore and came nearly to the RE of Rs. 
12800 crore. In 2023-24, AE had fallen to Rs. 8,457.72 crore against a BE of Rs. 
11,600 crore. Further, in 2024-25, AE was Rs. 9,903 crore against a BE of Rs. 
12,467.39 crore and in 2025-26, as on 13th February 2026, AE is Rs. 6,639.22 crore 
against a BE of Rs. 12,500 crore. The pattern shows year-on-year divergence 
between the allocations and the actual utilization by the schools. The Committee 
recommends that the Department should introduce a quarterly fund release 
schedule for PM POSHAN that is fixed at the beginning of the financial year to 
monitor the fund utilisation systematically. The Committee further recommends 
that the SNA-SPARSH model, currently being piloted under Samagra Shiksha, may 
be extended to PM POSHAN as a priority, so that funds flow in response to 
demonstrated expenditure rather than in bulk tranches that either arrive too late or 
too close to year-end for orderly utilisation. 
(para 3.51) 
 
28. The Committee notes that the cooking cost norms under PM POSHAN were 
increased by 9.5% with effect from 01.05.2025. In this regard, the Committee is of 

58 
 
the view that a comprehensive review of cooking cost norms should be conducted at 
least once every two years, factoring in CPI-linked inflation to ensure nutritional 
adequacy of meals. 
(para 3.52) 
 
29. The Committee notes persistent decline in the number of beneficiaries from 12.16 
crore in 2022-23 to 10.99 crore in 2024-25. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Department of School Education and Literacy should examine whether this 
reflects genuine reduction in eligible enrolment or gaps in scheme coverage, and 
take corrective measures accordingly. 
(para 3.53) 
 
30. The Committee notes that PM-POSHAN has not been implemented in the State of 
West Bengal in full spirit for last two years. The Committee recommends that the 
Union and State Governments work together to resolve all issues expeditiously.  
(para 3.54) 
 
31. The Committee is of the view that the role of Anganwadi Centres in complementing 
PM POSHAN for children aged 3-6 years should be formally integrated with clear 
responsibilities defined for School Education and WCD departments at State level. 
(para 3.55) 
 
32. The Committee is of the view that the learnings from the STARS project in the six 
participating States should be systematically documented and disseminated to all 
States/UTs to replicate successful models of pedagogical improvement and 
assessment reform. The Committee is also of the view that the Department should 
assess whether the STARS framework can be expanded to additional States as a 
domestic scheme (without external financing) given its demonstrable impact on 
learning outcomes and inform the Committee for its consideration. 
(para 3.60) 
 
33. The Committee appreciates that all six STARS States have established State 
Assessment Cells that have been an effective centre of learning. The Committee 
recommends that the State assessment systems strengthened under STARS should 
be integrated with the national PARAKH framework to ensure comparability and 
sustainability of assessment practices. 
(para 3.61) 
 
34. The Committee notes that the project is concluding its initial implementation phase 
in March, 2027. With regard to this, the Committee is of the view that the transition 

59 
 
plan for STARS-supported States after the project closure should be clearly defined, 
ensuring that gains made under the project are not lost. The Committee 
recommends that the teacher training activities supported under STARS should be 
linked to the DIET CoE programme under Samagra Shiksha for continuity. 
(para 3.62) 
 
35. The Committee is of the view that the project's outcomes on learning levels, teacher 
performance, and school governance should be independently evaluated by a third 
party before project closure. Further, the Department should explore a possible 
successor scheme or additional financing for scaling up evidence-based education 
interventions. 
(para 3.63) 
 
36. The Committee notes that despite the high BE allocations, allocations under PM 
SHRI has not been utilized consistently for last three FYs i.e 2023-24, 2024-25 and 
2025-26. The primary reasons cited are slow pace of expenditure by States, delay in 
fund transfer to SNA accounts, and non-implementation by the States of Tamil 
Nadu and West Bengal who are yet to sign the MoU. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation from its earlier 363rd Report and recommends the 
Department to take initiative to resolve the issue amicably with the State 
Governments concerned and release the pending funds on priority basis. 
(para 3.68) 
 
37. The Committee is of the view that the selection criteria for PM SHRI schools should 
be reviewed to ensure equitable geographical distribution, with adequate 
representation of schools in Aspirational Districts. The Committee is also of the view 
that all 21 components of PM SHRI saturation should be tracked school-wise and 
State-wise on a publicly accessible dashboard, with quarterly progress reports. 
Further, these schools should be monitored for learning outcome improvement 
through PARAKH assessments, with comparative pre and post data to demonstrate 
impact on educational ecosystem. 
(para 3.69) 
 
38. The Committee is of the view that community engagement and School Management 
Committee (SMC) should be actively prioritised as part of PM SHRI 
implementation to ensure local ownership. 
(para 3.70) 
39. The Committee is of the view that the teacher capacity building under PM SHRI 
should go beyond existing infrastructure and a robust in-service training 

60 
 
programme for teachers of these schools should be designed and implemented 
through the DIET CoE network. 
(para 3.71) 
 
40. The Committee appreciates the Joint Secretary-level field visits mandated by the 
Hon'ble Prime Minister's direction in the 50th PRAGATI meeting and recommends 
that the field visits should be continued and expanded to at least two visits per State 
per year. 
(para 3.72) 
 
41. The Committee observes that flat allocation of Rs. 160 crore for four consecutive 
years from 2024-25 to 2026-27 for ULLAS is inadequate given the scale of adult 
illiteracy in the country. The Committee is of the view that a significant 
enhancement in allocation is required to commensurate with the estimated 25+ 
crore functionally illiterate adult so that the target of making all adults above 15 
years of age literate by 2030 is achieved. 
(para 3.78) 
 
42. The Committee recommends that FLNAT (Foundational Literacy and Numeracy 
Assessment Test) should be conducted twice annually across all States, and results 
should be disaggregated by gender, social category, and age group. 
(para 3.79) 
 
43. The Committee observes that several large States such as Maharashtra, Gujarat, 
Haryana, Karnataka and Jharkhand have shown low or no release of funds under 
the scheme. The Committee is of the view that the Department should examine and 
address implementation bottlenecks in these States on priority. 
(para 3.80) 
 
44. The Committee is of the view that the volunteer teachers under ULLAS should be 
provided at least token compensation/incentives to sustain their motivation and 
engagement. Further, the scheme should leverage technology platforms such as 
mobile apps, community radio, and local language digital content to reach learners 
in remote areas for better output. 
(para 3.81) 
 
45. The Committee is of the view that the Community Learning Centres (CLCs) 
established under the scheme should be mapped and monitored for functionality, 
with linkages to NIOS for certification. 
(para 3.82) 

61 
 
 
46. The Committee appreciates that all utilization certificates in respect of KVS up to 
the FY 2024-25 have been timely submitted to the Ministry and there was no 
unspent balance as of 31.03.2025, except a nominal amount of Rs. 6.94 lakh, which 
has already been refunded to the Ministry. 
(para 4.7) 
 
47. The Committee observes that there is a significant shortage of staff in KVS both in 
the teaching and non-teaching positions (17% vacancy in teaching and 28% vacancy 
in non-teaching). For an organization like KVS which caters to a large proportion of 
population in providing quality school education, such a significant vacancy 
significantly hamper its smooth operations. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the vacancy positions in KVS, particularly for trained graduate teachers 
(TGTs) and post-graduate teachers (PGTs), should be filled on priority basis so that 
there is no compromise on the quality of education imparted in these schools. 
(para 4.8) 
 
48. The Committee is of the view that the 25 percent seat reservation for non-Central 
Government employees' children in KVs should be constantly monitored for 
equitable access by children from EWS and disadvantaged communities. 
(para 4.9) 
 
49. The Committee recommends that KVS should leverage its scale and infrastructure 
to serve as a mentor institution for nearby government schools under the NEP 2020 
framework and the learning outcomes in KVs benchmarked against national and 
international standards. 
(para 4.10) 
 
50. The Committee recommends that the Department should accord highest priority to 
construction of new KVs, particularly in North-Eastern States and underserved 
regions, with time-bound completion schedules. 
(para 4.11) 
 
51. The Committee appreciates the trend of utilization of funds by the Navodaya 
Vidyalaya Samiti with close to 100% utilization in the last three financial years. 
(para 4.17) 
 
52. The Committee observes that there is a significant shortage of staff in NVS both in 
the teaching and non-teaching positions (29.5% vacancy in teaching and 26% 
vacancy in non-teaching). The Committee in its previous 363rd and 368th reports 

62 
 
have emphasized on the need to fill up these vacancies in a time-bound manner. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendations from its 363rd and 368th 
reports regarding the persistence of vacancies in NVS. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the vacancy positions in NVS, both teaching and non-teaching, 
should be filled on priority basis. Further, the vacancy of specialist teachers for 
Music, Art, Physical Education and regional languages should be filled 
expeditiously through regular recruitment drives by NVS. 
(para 4.18) 
 
53. The Committee notes that the unique mental health challenges of the residential 
model, especially following the digital shifts post-NEP 2020. The Committee 
recommends the Department to move beyond the current practice of part-time or 
ad-hoc engagement, and should create permanent sanctioned posts for Psychological 
Counselors in every JNV which is critical as JNVs cater to rural talent who may 
face social isolation and academic pressure. Further, the budget for "Student 
Wellness" be carved out as a distinct sub-head under the NVS operational expenses 
in the DDG. 
(para 4.19) 
 
54. The Committee observes that NVS caters to a significant proportion of girl students 
in its network schools. The Committee, therefore, recommends that safety and 
security of students, particularly girl students, in JNV hostels should be accorded 
the highest priority, proper CCTV coverage must be maintained 24*7, and wardens 
must be trained adequately and sensitized in handling girl students and POCSO 
compliance. 
(para 4.20) 
 
55. The Committee is of the view that the lateral entry of students at Class IX and Class 
XI levels in JNVs should be continuously monitored to ensure that seats are not left 
vacant due to procedural delays. 
(para 4.21) 
 
56. The Committee observes that JNVs maintain a significant population of alumni 
network who work in successful positions in and out of the country. The Committee 
is, therefore, of the view that a dedicated alumni network of JNV should be 
leveraged for mentoring current students, career guidance, and institution building. 
The Department of School Education and Literacy may work towards establishing a 
dedicated portal for JNVs alumni for single place interaction with students. 
(para 4.22) 

63 
 
57. The Committee is of the view that NVS should conduct an outcome assessment to 
compare the learning levels of JNV students with national averages to document the 
impact and identify areas that require improvement. 
(para 4.23) 
 
58. The Committee appreciates enhanced allocation of Rs. 681.79 crores in BE 2026-27 
over the BE 2025-26 of Rs. 593.71 crore which is an increase of 14%. The 
Committee also appreciates the NCERT for maintaining a healthy funds utilization 
pattern over the past few years though there is room for some improvement as it is 
observed that the fund utilization dropped to 71.45% in the FY 2023-24 and 92.26% 
in the FY 2024-25.  
(para 4.29) 
 
59. The Committee notes of the vacancies in NCERT and observes that 130 posts of 
academic staffs are vacant against the sanctioned strength of 528. The Committee 
also notes that 133 posts of teaching staffs out of the total sanctioned strength of 271 
are vacant. Despite the recommendation of the Committee as contained in its 349th 
Report i.e. to "complete the process of filling up the vacancies with permanent posts 
in a time-bound manner and latest by the end of 2023, so that, NEP 2020 is 
implemented in letter and spirit” which was also reiterated in its 363rd Report, the 
vacancies are still lying vacant. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its 
recommendation as contained in its 349th and 363rd Report and directs the NCERT 
to fill up all the vacancies including backlog vacancies at the earliest in mission 
mode and latest by end of 2026. 
(para 4.30) 
 
60. The Committee recommends that the NCERT should accelerate the development 
and publication of new textbooks for Classes IX-XII in accordance with NCF-SE 
2023 on a priority basis. The NCERT should also publish textbooks in all 8th 
Schedule languages and major regional languages to support mother-tongue-based 
multilingual education as envisaged in NEP 2020. 
(para 4.31) 
 
61. The Committee welcomes the introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a basic 
universal skill. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to finalize 
the AI and Computational thinking curriculum for Grades 3 onwards by the second 
quarter of FY 2026-27. Further, these modules should be developed in 22 scheduled 
Indian languages to ensure inclusivity. Furthermore, NCERT must collaborate with 
the Indian Institute of Creative Technologies to establish content creator 
laboratories in schools, as proposed in the Budget speech 2026-27. 

64 
 
(para 4.32) 
 
62. The Committee recommends that NCERT expand PARAKH’s mandate to include a 
National Standard for School Board Equivalence. To ensure a level playing field for 
students from different State Boards in competitive exams, NCERT should also 
develop a "Common Assessment Blueprint" that focuses on competency-based 
evaluation rather than rote memorization, as envisioned in the NEP 2020. 
(para 4.33) 
 
63. The Committee recommends that the proposal for providing Deemed-to-be 
University status to NCERT should be expedited to enable NCERT to offer doctoral 
and post-doctoral programmes in education research. 
(para 4.34) 
 
64. The Committee is of the view that the NCERT should expand its network of 
Regional Institutes of Education (RIEs) with upgraded infrastructure and adequate 
in-position faculty to serve as centres of pedagogical excellence. Additionally, the 
Committee recommends that the Department increase the "Research and 
Innovation" grant for NCERT by 10% annually to support the study of Indological 
academic traditions and their integration into modern science and math curricula. 
(para 4.35) 
 
65. The Committee is of the view that the NCERT should develop a robust digital 
platform for open access to all of its textbooks, teaching-learning materials, and 
research publications. 
(para 4.36) 
 
66. The Committee is of the view that the NCERT should expand its engagement with 
international organisations such as UNESCO, IEA and PISA to benchmark Indian 
school education standards globally. 
(para 4.37) 
 
67. The Committee observes that out of the total sanctioned strength of 154 in all 
grades, only 48 are in-position and remaining 106 (68.83% of total strength) posts 
are lying vacant. Further, since the year 2021 the NBB has appointed a total of 222 
persons on contractual basis. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Department and NBB to fill up the vacancies by permanent appointments at the 
earliest on priority basis. 
(para 4.42) 
 

65 
 
68. The Committee is of the view that the allocation for NBB of Rs. 30.51 crore in BE 
2026-27 is significantly inadequate for an institution of its stature and mandate. The 
Committee therefore recommends that a substantial increase in fund allocation to 
NBB should be considered at the RE stage to enable it to scale up its activities. 
Further, partnerships with private sector CSR initiatives should be explored to 
supplement Government funding and enhance NBB's outreach. 
(para 4.43) 
 
69. The Committee in its 363rd Report had made its observations over geographic 
dispersion of across the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
NBB should establish regional Bal Bhawans in every State capital and UT 
headquarters to extend its reach to children across the country. Further, the NBB 
should develop a single digital platform for virtual participation in its activities, 
enabling children from remote areas to benefit from its programmes. Besides, the 
NBB should also develop special programmes for children with disabilities to ensure 
inclusive participation in creative activities. 
(para 4.44) 
 
70. The Committee recommends that the NBB should document and preserve 
traditional art forms and cultural practices through its children's programmes, 
serving as a cultural repository. 
(para 4.45) 
 
71. The Committee observes that out of the total 1471473 schools across the country 
only 951868 (64.69%) schools have access to computer facility while only 933987 
(63.47%) schools have access to internet facility. The Committee recommends that 
the target of ICT Labs access in all secondary schools should be placed on a firm 
time-bound roadmap, with State-wise targets and annual milestones. 
(para 5.4) 
 
72. The Committee welcomes the steps taken to introduce AI in the school curriculum. 
In this regard, the Committee is of the view that the introduction of AI in 
curriculum should be done through a well-designed, age-appropriate, and 
pedagogy-driven framework developed by NCERT in consultation with CBSE, IITs, 
and domain experts. The Committee is also of the view that while engaging children 
with use of AI in learning is slowly becoming essential part of education, steps must 
also be taken to ensure that the use of emerging technology for education does not 
become a reason for loss of childhood and innocence in the kids. 
(para 5.5) 

66 
 
73. The Committee recommends that the DIKSHA platform should be enhanced with 
AI-based adaptive learning capabilities and offline-first architecture for low-
connectivity areas along with periodic content updates aligned with new NCF-SE 
2023 textbooks. 
(para 5.6) 
74. The Committee recommends that the AVGC Content Creator Labs announced in 
the Budget Speech 2026-27 should be operationalized with clear implementation 
guidelines, teacher training programmes, and assessment frameworks. 
(para 5.7) 
 
75. The Committee notes that the broadband connectivity to all schools should be 
treated as an essential infrastructure. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the DoSEL should coordinate with the Department of Telecommunications and 
BharatNet for providing last-mile connectivity, especially to rural schools. Data 
security and privacy of students using digital platforms must be rigorously 
protected, with clear guidelines and accountability frameworks for digital service 
providers. 
(para 5.8) 
 
76. The Committee observes that the allocation for NER in BE 2026–27 has increased 
only marginally to Rs. 51,522.77 crore from Rs. 51,505.21 crore in BE 2025–26, 
which is inadequate considering the vast geographical expanse, difficult terrain and 
extensive school network in the region. When compared to RE 2025-26, the 
allocation shows an increase of about 18 per cent. The Committee is of the view that 
greater financial support is essential to address the unique developmental and 
educational challenges of the region. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Department should consider increasing allocations for NER at the RE stage and 
ensure targeted interventions to strengthen educational infrastructure, accessibility 
and quality of school education in the region. 
(para 5.12) 
 
77. The Committee recommends that the infrastructure gaps in NER schools, 
particularly in remote and border areas should be addressed under a special sub-
plan within Samagra Shiksha providing them with higher unit costs recognising the 
difficulty of terrain and transportation. Further, the teacher recruitment and their 
deployment challenges in NER should be addressed in collaboration with State 
Governments including incentivizing teachers who are transferred to remote and 
difficult areas. 
(para 5.13)

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Education, 
Women, Children, Youth and Sports, having been authorised by the Committee to present the 
Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Three Hundred and Seventy-Seventh Report of the 
Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No. 101) of the Ministry of Women and Child 
Development for the year 2026–27. 
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the estimated 
expenditure of the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India projected under various 
Demands for Grants for the ensuing financial year is required to be voted by Parliament. 
Consequently, the Demands for Grants of the relevant Ministries/Departments stand referred to the 
concerned Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee for detailed scrutiny under Rule 
270 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). 
While scrutinising the Demands for Grants, the Committee has made an appraisal of the 
performance, programmes, schemes and policies of the Ministry of Women and Child Development 
vis-à-vis the expenditure incurred out of the Consolidated Fund of India during the current financial 
year. 
 
3. In this Report, a scrutiny of the Budget allocations of the Ministry of Women and Child 
Development as sought under Demand No. 101 for the Financial Year 2026-27 has been made by 
the Committee. 
 
4. During the course of examination of the Demands, the Committee heard the views of the 
Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development, and other senior officers of the Ministry. 
Inputs from organisations/agencies, namely, the National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child 
Development (NIPCCD), Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA), National Commission for 
Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR), and National Commission for Women (NCW), were also 
made available to the Committee at its sitting held on 19thFebruary, 2026. 
 
5. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has mainly relied upon 
the following:- 
(i) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Women and child Development for the year 
2026-27; 
(ii) Expenditure Budget 2026-27 and Output Outcome Framework 2026-27; 
(iii) Annual Report 2025-26; 
(iv) Presentations made by the Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development and 
inputs provided by Senior Officers from National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child 
Development (NIPCCD), Central Adoption Resource Agency (CARA), National Commission for 
Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and National Commission for Women (NCW); 
(v) Written replies furnished by the Ministry of Women and Child Development to the 
Questionnaires (Issues and Schemes & Budgetary Allocations) prepared by the committee; and to 
the points/issues raised by Members during the meeting of the Committee. 
 
 
 

iii 
 
6. The Report is based on facts, figures and submissions (both oral and written) tendered by 
the Ministry of Women and Child Development to the Committee. 
7. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Secretary and officers of the Ministry of 
Women and Child Development, as well as the Heads/Officers of the organisations/bodies under 
the administrative control of the Ministry, for appearing before the Committee and furnishing the 
requisite information in connection with the examination of the Demands for Grants of the 
Ministry. 
8. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 23rd March, 2026 
and presented it to both Houses of Parliament on __March, 2026. 
9. For the facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the 
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

REPORT 
 
1.1  Overview of the Ministry  
Women and Children together constitute about 67.7% of the country's population as per the 
2011Census. Empowerment, protection and holistic development of women are central to the 
nation’s development, while the children are the future of the country. A major part of India’s 
population, around 158 million comprises children in the age group of 0-6 years. Ensuring their 
well being is a fundamental prerequisite for equitable development of a society. The Ministry of 
Women and Child Development (MWCD) is the apex body of the Government of India for 
formulation and administration of regulations and laws related to the welfare and development of 
women and children in the country. The Ministry came into existence as a separate Ministry with 
effect from 30th January 2006. It functioned as a Department under the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development since 1985. The Ministry was constituted with the prime objective of 
addressing the gaps in State action for women and children and for promoting inter-ministerial and 
inter-sectoral convergence to create gender equitable and child-centered legislations, policies, and 
programmes. 
 
1.2 Vision  
Empowered women living with dignity and contributing,  as equal partners in development 
in an environment free from violence and discrimination; and well-nurtured children with full 
opportunities for growth and development in a safe and protective environment. 
 
1.3 Mission  
1.3.1 Empowerment of Women  
Promoting social and economic empowerment of women through cross-cutting policies and 
programmes, mainstreaming gender concerns, creating awareness about their rights and facilitating 
institutional and legislative support for enabling them to realize their human rights and develop to 
their full potential. 
 
1.3.2 Safe and Secure Childhood  
Ensuring development, care and protection of children through cross-cutting policies and 
programmes, spreading awareness about their rights and facilitating access to learning, nutrition, 
institutional and legislative support for enabling them to grow and develop to their full potential. 
 
1.4 A brief note on the various Mission/ Schemes of the Ministry:   
To ensure better monitoring and efficient implementation, in the XVth Finance Commission 
Cycle, all the schemes being implemented by the Ministry of Women and Child Development have 
been clubbed into three verticals. All three missions are Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) 
implemented in partnership with State Governments and Union Territory Administrations. States 
and UTs are the primary implementing partners and the Central Government releases grants-in-aid 
to them on a cost-sharing basis. 
 
1.5 Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0:  
The Government of India approved Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 which is a 
strategic shift in Mission mode to develop practices that nurture health, wellness and immunity 
from malnutrition. The Scheme has been rolled-out across 36 States and UTs covering all the 
districts. During the 15th Finance Commission (FC) period, various components such as nutritional 
support for children from 6 months to the age of 6 years, pregnant women and lactating mothers 
and Adolescent Girls; Early Childhood Care and Education of children (3-6 years) and Anganwadi 
infrastructure including modern, upgraded Saksham Anganwadi have been subsumed under an 

2 
 
umbrella Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 (Mission Poshan 2.0). Package of the 
following six services is provided under the Mission Poshan 2.0 scheme through a network of 
Anganwadi centres across the country: 
(i) Supplementary Nutrition Programme (SNP) 
(ii) Pre-school Non-formal Education  
(iii) Nutrition & Health Education 
(iv) Immunization 
(v) Health Check-up  
(vi) Referral Services  
 
Three of the six services, viz., Immunization, Health Check-up and Referral Services are 
related to health and are provided through National Health Mission (NHM) & Public Health 
Infrastructure. 
 
 Poshan Abhiyan: Poshan Abhiyan was launched in March 2018 to achieve improvement in 
nutritional status of Children from 0-6 years, Adolescent Girls, Pregnant Women and Lactating 
Mothers, in a time bound manner and to achieve reduction in stunting, wasting  and underweight in 
children (0-6 years) as well as reduction in anemia in women, children and adolescent girls. In 
addition to addressing the challenge of malnutrition, the achievement of the Sustainable 
Development Goals (SDGs) lies at the fore-front of this programme design. Poshan 2.0 shall 
contribute to the SDGs, specifically, SDG 2 on Zero Hunger and SDG 4 on Quality Education.  
 
1.6 Mission Shakti: The erstwhile scheme of ‘Mission for Protection and Empowerment of 
Women’ has been revamped and brought under the Umbrella Scheme of Mission Shakti from the 
year 2021-22. Mission Shakti aims at strengthening interventions for women safety, security and 
empowerment. Mission Shakti comprises of two verticals ‘Sambal’ and ‘Samarthya’. It seeks to 
realise the Government’s commitment for ‘women-led development’ by addressing issues affecting 
women on a life-cycle continuum basis.   
 
1.6.1 SAMBAL: SAMBAL aims at safety and security of women and its sub-schemes includes 
components viz. Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, One Stop Centre, Nari Adalat and Women Helpline.  
 
1.6.2 SAMARTHYA: SAMARTHYA aims at empowerment of women and its sub-schemes 
include various components viz Shakti Sadan, Shakhi Niwas, Palna, Pradhan Mantri Matru 
VandanaYojana, National Hub for Women Empowerment, Gender Budgeting, Research/ Skilling/ 
Training/Media Advocacy etc. 
 
1.7  Mission Vatsalya: The scheme is being implemented with a view to support Children in 
Need of care and Protection (CNCP) and Children in Conflict with Law (CCL). The objective of 
Mission Vatsalya is to ensure that the best interests of children are always taken care of while 
designing the projects/ programmes. The objectives include establishing essential services, 
emergency outreach services for children and include strengthening of institutional and non-
institutional care services. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 
provisions and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 form the basic 
framework for implementation of the Mission. 
1.8 Bodies/Organisations under the administrative control of the Ministry:  
The following Institutions/Organizations/Bodies are under the administrative control of the 
Ministry and receive support from the Consolidated Fund of India: 
 
 Autonomous Organisations:

1.9 Savitribai Phule National Institute of Women and Child Development (SPNIWCD), 
erstwhile NIPCCD (renamed via Gazette Notification dated 30thJune, 2025): 
SPNIWCD is an Institute of global repute in women empowerment, child rights, child 
protection and child development. It acts as a think tank, catalyst, and facilitator of women 
empowerment, child rights, child protection, and child development programs by pursuing capacity 
building of functionaries, research and evaluation, networking, consultancy, and advisory services, 
as well as provision of specialized services through interdisciplinary teams. 
 
Statutory Bodies: 
1.10 Central Adoption Resource Agency (CARA):  
CARA is the nodal authority for regulating and promoting in-country and inter-country 
adoption of children. The Authority operates under the legal framework of the Juvenile Justice 
(Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (as amended in 2021), the JJ Model Rules, 2016 (as 
amended in 2022), and the Adoption Regulations, 2022. It also serves as India’s designated Central 
Authority under the Hague Convention on Inter-country Adoption, 1993, ratified by India in 2003. 
 
1.11 National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR):  
The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) is a statutory body 
established in March 2007 under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights (CPCR) Act, 
2005. Its vision and mission are centered on ensuring all laws, policies, and programs conform to a 
child-rights perspective as outlined in the Indian Constitution and the UN Convention on the Rights 
of the Child (UNCRC).  
 
1.12 National Commission for Women (NCW)  
The National Commission for Women (NCW) is a statutory body established in January 
1992 under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990. It functions as the apex national 
institution for protecting and promoting the rights and interests of women in India, operating under 
the aegis of the Ministry of Women and Child Development (MoWCD). NCW plays a critical role 
in strengthening the legislative framework through periodic reviews of laws and policies affecting 
women. These reviews are undertaken to assess the effectiveness of existing enactments, identify 
gaps in implementation, and recommend measures to ensure that the objectives of the legislations 
are fully realised. 
 
1.13 Rationalisation of Government Bodies 
The Government closed down the Central Social Welfare Board (CSWB), Food and 
Nutrition Board (FNB) and Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (RMK) as per recommendations in the Report 
on 'Rationalization of Government Bodies' prepared by the Principal Economic Advisor in 
November 2020. The process of merger and absorption of CSWB staff into SPNIWCD is 
underway.
