AN OVERVIEW 
The Ministry of Human Resource Development was set up in 1985 with the objective of 
integrating efforts towards the development of human potential in the areas of Education, 
Women & Child Development, Art, Culture, Youth Affairs & Sports. The Department of 
Education is an important constituent of this Ministry. During 1993-94 a budget provision of 
Rs. 2159.33 crores was made available for education in the Central Sector. This was increased to 
Rs. 2192 crores in the Revised Estimate 1993-94. 
2. There are a large number of subordinate offices and autonomous organisations under the 
Department which are engaged in carrying out the activities and programmes of the Department. 
They include, among others, the Directorate of Adult Education, National Council of 
Educational Research & Training (NCERT), National Institute of Educational Planning & 
Administration (NIEPA), University Grants Commission (UGC), Indian Council of Social 
Science Research (ICSSR), Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS), the Navodaya Vidyalaya 
Samiti (NVS), the Central Board of Secondary Education, the National Book Trust, Indian 
Institutes of Technology and Regional Engineering Colleges. 
3. The National Policy on Education, 1986 has been instrumental in laying down the 
priorities in education at the national level. Elementary Education has been getting the highest 
priority in the educational sector, to accelerate the pace for achieving Universal Elementary 
Education by the end of this Century. The Operation Black Board scheme, launched in 1987-88, 
aims at bringing about significant improvement in the provision of facilities in primary schools. 
This is expected to improve retention of children in primary schools. 
4. The programme of Non-Formal Education aims at bringing education to working children, 
girls and children living in habitations which are not covered by formal schools. NFE is envisaged 
as an alternative strategy for formal education and plays a complementary role in achieving 
Universal Elementary Education by covering drop-outs or those who have not enrolled for one 
reason or the another. 
5. The Adult Education programme provides basic functional educational skills for those who 
could not avail the opportunities for education through formal and non-formal schools. The 
Technology Mission for Literacy, set up in 1988 with the aim of covering the total area, has 
achieved success in the southern, eastern and western regions and the focus has now shifted to 
the Hindi speaking States which have a low percentage of literacy. 
6. The Department is giving serious attention to achieving Education for All, and its 
endeavours towards this end found mention during the "Education for All Summit" of 9 populous 
countries of the world, held in 'New Delhi' in December, 1993. As a result of these endeavours, 
the resource allocation to education is expected to be increased from the existing 3.2% to 6% of 
the GNP from the 9th Plan. 
7. In the school education field, there are 796 Kendriya Vidyalayas, including three 
Vidyalayas in foreign countries. These are opened in areas with a sizeable concentration of 
Central Government employees. 
8. The Navodaya Vidyalayas scheme, launched in 1985, provides good quality education to 
talented children predominantly from rural areas. There are 321 Schools which are residential and 
offer education free of charge for all students. 
9. In the area of Vocational Education, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme was started in 1988 
with the main objective of providing diversification of educational opportunities to enhance 
individual employability. Vocational courses, mainly in the areas of Agriculture, Business & 
Commerce, Engineering & Technology, Health and Para Medical, Humanities and Home 
Science, are introduced at the +2 level in schools selected by the State Governments. So far, 

Vocational Sections have been sanctioned in 5,588 schools creating a capacity for diversification 
of 7.96 lakh students. 
10. The scheme of pre-vocational education has also been launched at the lower secondary 
stage in 1993-94 with the objective of imparting simple marketable skills to students in classes IX 
and X. 
11. The Department of Education has been seeking bilateral and multilateral assistance from 
international agencies so that additional resources may be available for educational programmes. 
Some new projects have been started in the last few years such as Mahila Samakhya Project in 
four States with the assistance of Netherlands; Andhra Pradesh Primary School Project with UK 
assistance; Lok Jumbish Project in Rajasthan with the assistance of SIDA; Shiksha Karmi Project 
in Rajasthan with the assistance of SIDA and Bihar Education Project with UNICEF assistance. 
12. In the Higher Education Sector, the University Grants Commission is concerned with 
promotion and coordination of university education and determination and maintenance of 
standards of teaching, examination and research in universities. The total number of Universities 
in 1993-94 was 189 with 7938 Colleges and a student enrolment of 48.05 Jakhs. A new Central 
University is also being set up in Tezpur to increase the facilities for higher education in the 
North-Eastern Region. 
13. In the Technical Education field, 5 Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) have been 
established to provide instruction and research in some branches of Engineering and Technology, 
Science and Arts for advancement of learning. These Institutes are imparting education at the 
undergraduate, postgraduate and research level, in addition to sponsoring research and they are 
fully funded by the Central Government. One more liT is proposed to be set up in Assam. 
14. The Regional Engineering Colleges have been set up to enable the country to meet the 
growing requirement of trained technical manpower. There are 17 Regional Engineering Colleges 
which offer First Degree Programmes in Engineering and Technology, out of which 14 have 
facilities for postgraduate and Doctoral programmes and also conduct research. 
REPORT 
15. Human Resource Development is of paramount importance for the progress of the 
country and education is one of the most important components in this regard. Though we are 
committed to achieve the objective of Education for All (EFA) by 2000 but increasing population 
and limited resources at hand are the two obstacles in the way of achieving this goal. 
16. At present, Budget outlay for Education is 3.2% of the (Gross Domestic Product) GDP 
and the Department of Education has assured that from 9th Plan onwards the outlay will be 6% 
of the GDP. 
17. The Committee welcomes the decision of the Government that Education will get an 
allocation of 6% of GDP. The Committee also hopes that there would be reflection of this decision 
in the Budget Estimates of the year 1995-96 and of subsequent years. 
18. Revised Budget Estimates for 1993-94 of the Deptt. of Education is Rs. 2192 crores. There 
has been a 10% increase in the Budget Estimates for 1994-95 over the previous year at Rs. 2423.6 
crores, out of which Rs. 1548.3 crores have been provided for planned expenditure and the rest of 
Rs. 875.3 crores is earmarked for Non-Plan expenditure. 
19. Secondary and Physical Education have been allocated 24.3% of the Budget Estimates of 
Educationl Deptt. and 24.2% of the funds of the Deptt. have been provided for University and 
Higher Education. Elementary and Technical Education have been provided 21.6% and 18% 
respectively of the funds for 1994-95. 
20. The Secretary, Deptt. of Education, in his oral evidence before the Committee has stated 

that the major thrust of the budget is on Elementary Educatiofi) with the objective of achieving 
education for all by 2000, decentralisation of educational administration and review of all these 
programmes quarterly, by a group of Chief Ministers. 
Demands for Grants (1994-95) of the Department of Education 
21. Department of Education is running about a dozen schemes, but the Committee took up 
for consideration only some of the major ones, which have been stated in brief in the following 
paragraphs, alongwith the Committee's observations/recommendations thereon. 
I 
Elementary Education 
22. Article 45 of the Constitution of India provides for free and Compulsory Education for 
all children below the age of 14 years. It was expected that by the year 1995, India would achieve 
Universal Elementary Education. However, there is still 153 million children, as on March, 1991, 
in the age group of 6-14 who are yet to be covered under the scheme. They constitute 18 per 
cent of the total population of the country. The Committee hopes that by the end of this century 
this backlog will be covered and total universal Elementary Education will be achieved. 
23. The Revised Budget Estimate for 1993-94 for Elementary Education is Rs. 443.7 crores. 
In Budget Estimate for, 1994-95, has been given Rs. 523.86 crores for Elementary Education. 
24. While the Committee takes note of this increase in allocation for Elementary Education, it 
feels that in view of the rising prices, the increase in real terms, is not substantial. 
25. The Committee feels that the Deptt. may take steps to decentralise Elementary Education 
and take help of Panchayati Raj institutions for proper monitoring and implementation of the 
Scheme. 
Operation Blackboard 
26. In the Eighth Plan it has been provided that the Scheme would continue and a third 
teacher and a third room would be added to primary schools wherever enrollment exceeds 100 
students. Thirty per cent of such schools would be covered in the said plan. Besides these, 
Operation Blackboard would cover 10 per cent of upper primary schools during the last two years 
of the Plan.

28. The Committee also feels that monitoring machanism for regulation and implementation of

29. The Committee feels that the question of increase in the weight of primary school bags 
particularly in city schools should be seriously considered and appropriate measures be taken to 

lessen the weight. Mechanism for ensuring minimum standards in schools in regard to teachers as 
well as infrastructure, should be created and strengthened. 
30. The Committee is not satisfied with the efforts made on the basis of last year's committee 
report for reducing drop-outs from elementary schools especially of children belonging to 
Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe categories. 
31. The Committee feels that the scheme should first achieve the targets laid down earlier, 
that is they should fu-st cover all the single teacher schools before going in for three-teacher 
schools. 
32. The Committee feels that enrolment of girls in schools is not up to the expectations. More 
efforts are required in this direction.

Mahila Samakhya 
34. The Committee feels that increase in expenditure on National Resource Group and 
consultancy/meetings etc. under Mahila Samakhya, from Rs. 4.69 lakhs in 1992-93 to Rs. 80 Jakhs 
in 1993-94, was quite high. The Committee feels that this should be looked into . 
35. The Committee feels that a mechanism may be evolved to regulate and monitor the 
working of Voluntary Organisations who are implementing the Mahila Samakhya Scheme. 
Teachers' Education 
36. Rs. 69.1 crores have been provided in the Revised Budget Estimate for 1993-94 for 
Teachers' Education. For 1994-95, the allocation has been increased to Rs. 90 crores. 
37. The Committee feels that more emphasis should be laid on Teachers' Education by further 
increase in allocation and also take steps to evaluate, from time to time, the existing methodology 
of training programme. 
II 
Secondary and Physical Education 
38. In the year 1993-94 Revised Estimates, the Department of Education had provided 
Rs. 305.5 crores for plan and Rs. 256.7 crores for non-plan expenditure for Secondary and 
Physical Education. For 1994-95, the figures are Rs. 335 crores and Rs. 255.5 crores respectively. 
39. The Committee feels that secondary education in general is facing resource crunch 
therefore, suggests that sufficient funds may be allocated for its various schemes. 
Vocational Education 
40. Rs. 85 crores have been provided for the scheme in the Revised Estimates for 1993-94. For 
1994-95, the Budget Estimate has been increased to 88.46 crores. 
41. The National Policy on Education 1992 envisages well-planned programmes for 

Vocational Education for developing a healthy attitude among students. It is expected that about 
10% of higher secondary students would be directed to the vocational stream by 1995 and 25% 
by 2000 AD. 
42. The Committee feels that adequate funds be provided to implement the scheme and to 
achieve the fixed targets. 
Computer Education 
43. Computer education has been started in secondary schools keeping in view the recent 
chapges in the technology and its immense potentialities in day-to-day life. 
44. The Committee feels that the Budget allocation of Rs. 25 crores for 1994-95 is not 
sufficient as it is even less than that of last year's Revised Estimate (i.e. Rs. 26 crores). Therefore, 
more funds should be provided for computer education. 
45. The Committee also suggests that adequate infrastructural support for the upkeep and 
maintenance of computers should be provided and the scheme, should also be monitored 
effectively. 
Scholarships 
46. The Committee is unhappy over the curtailment of budget allocation under the head 
"Scholarships". Instead, the number of scholarships should have been increased to help the 
economically backward and meritorious students so that more and more students could complete 
secondary education and go for higher studies. 
47. The Committee feels that there should be more provision for loan scholarships for the 
benefit of needy students. 
Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan 
48. The Kendriya Vidyalaya Scheme was started in 1963-64 on the recommendation of the 
lind Pay Commission. Kendriya Vidyalayas are expected to be trend-setters in school educatiort, 
with the primary objectives of catering to the educational needs of children of transferable 
Central Govt. employees, including defence personnel, by providing a common stream of 
education.

63. The Committee feels that more attention should be paid to promote our composite and

65. The Committee feels that when there is need for greater emphasis on environmental

An Overview 
The Department of Youth Affairs & Sports is comparatively a new Depa ·tment which deals with 
the vital subject :>f youth and promotion of sports. Though both these subjects fall under the P!!rview 
of the States, yet Government of India has a very prominent role to play not only in terms of 
operating its own ~chemes but also for coordinating with State Governments and other agcnc1es. The 
Committee found that on youth side, though there are a large number of schemes, but bulk of the 
budget allocation is for the National Service Schemes (NSS) and Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan 
(NYt<S). National Scrvic.! Scheme (along ,.ith NCC) is the most important scheme fc; voiuntary 
participation by student community in a nation building. It is a low-cost scheme which aims at 
personality development of the students through their involvement in social service, literacy, health, 
and environment, etc. Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, on the other hand, mainly mobilises rural 
youth and focuses on the activities of the Youth Clubs. Amongst other impo;tant schemes there are 
the schemes for National lnteiration and Adventures. There is some scope for streamlining the 
remaining schemes also. Among the new initiatives, taken in the current year is the preparatior for 
the establishment of Rajiv Gandhi National Institute for Youth Development. 
2. On the Sports side, it is observed that the Department has to coordinate with the State 
Governments as well as sports federations, which are autonomous bodies working for 54 different 
disciplines. The important scheme being operated by the Department are the schemes of Grants to 
Sports Federations, and 'Assistance for creation of Sports Infrastructure. While the development of 
infrastructure is essential, it is felt that there is a tendency to set up large stadia in big towEs and 
cities and since the resources with the Centre, as well as State Governments are limited, creation of 
play-fields and other facilities at the Tchsil level do not get the required attention . The Sports 
Authority of India (SAl) is the executive part of the Department and is main.y concerned with the 
broad-based sports, as well as grooming of talented children It is also responsible for organisation of 
National Camps for participation in major international events. The performance of Indian 
sportspersons at the Olympic Games has been undistinguished and it is necessary that all efforts arc 
made oy various concerned agencies to raise the requisite/International standards. In this connectiOn , 
the Committee welcomes the reported consensus of the State Governments about the introduction of 
Sports and Physical Education as a compulsory subject from sehoul level onwards. 
3 It is observed that the Plan provision for 1993-94 was Rs. 98.10 crores including Rs. 37.19 
crores for Youth and Rs. 60.66 crores for Sports. Whereas. this year, Plan provision is Rs. 94 00 
crores only Rs. 4.10 crores less than the previous year Plan provision. The provision for 1993-94 
includes addition of Rs. 13.10 crores earmarked for preparation for the Asian Games . It is felt that 
Department consists of two important parts 1.e. Yout 1 and Sports, therefore, decrease in the 
allocation will go against thl!ir interest. Therefore, the Committee recommends that allocations may 
accordingly be increased.

GAMES AND SPORTS 
37. The Second major component of the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports is games and 
Sports and the Sports Authority of India is the Main organisation. In order to put the infrastructure 
created during ASIAD, 1982 and optimum utilisation and also to preserve and maintain the assets,

undertaken multifarious and wide ranging sports activities so much so that if has emerged as the 
premier body for sports at the national level. Its activities includes development of Sports, nurturing

creation of a central pool of sports equipment to be loaned to sports persons efforts to promote sports 
consciousness, promotion of women's sports, rural sports, conducting national coaching camps, etc. 
At present, the Sports Authority of India has six regional centres covering the whole country, two 
sub-centres and training centres and a high altitude Training Centre. 
38. However, the Committee expresses its concern over the deteriorating performance of the country 
in the field of sports and in this connection points out that the hopes generated at the time of setting up 
Sports Authority of India have been belied. This is mainly because of the fact that major share of 
allocation for the Sports Authority of India is spent on establishment, salaries and other miscellaneous 
heads and a modicum of amount is spent on sports promotion and development activities. A 
comparative analysis of the figures for the last three years including the current year, suggests that 
almost one-third of the total amount is spent on establishment and miscellaneous items and a little 
amount is spent on the development of sports:

45. This scheme aims at providing basic sports facilities to the rural children between the age of

47. Apart from the Sports Authority of India development and promotion of sports is undertaken by

(f) Corporate and Private Sector is doing commendabl e job in furthering the cause of sports by

behalf, do hereby present this Seventh Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants 1994-95 
(Demand No. 50) of the Department of Women and Child Development, Ministry of Human 
Resource Development.

REPORT 
Women and Children, who represent more than 50% of our population, constitute the two 
vulnerable segments of our society without whose upliftment real development cannot take place. 
Although total Budget Estimates for 1994-95 in the Central Plan outlay for women and child 
development show an increase of Rs. 96 crores as compared to Budget Estimates for 1993-94, the 
increase, as explained by Secretary (Women & Child Development), in her ora! evidence tendered 
before the Committee, is mainly on account of World Bank assistance of Rs. 38 crores to ICDS and 
an increase in sanction for Mahila Samridhi Yojna. On all other schemes increase in allocations for 
1994-95 is only marginal. It is a matter of concern for the Committee that in the SAARC Decade of 
Girl Child and condition of women, there has not been adequate increase in the Budget allocations.

3. The Committee feels that gender inequality is one of the problems all over the world. Actual 
development cannot take place unless the Govt. takes initiative to remove this bias and guarantees 
equal status to women as enshrined in our Constitution. Committee is of the view that all out efforts 
should be made for greater involvement of women in the national development process by raising their 
status - social, economic, legal and political - at par with that of man. The Department of Women 
and Child Development has started a number of schemes for the development and welfare of women 
and children The Committee has deliberated only on some of the points relating to Demands for Grants 
(1994-95) which are enumerated in the following paragraphs along with the Committee's observations 
and recommendations. 
Women Welfare and Development 
(i) Rashtriya Mahila Kosh 
4. Rashtriya Mahila Kosh was set up in March, 1993 under the Registration of Societies Act, 
1869. With the main aim to help the poorest of the poor and assist women who are unable to utilize 
formal banking facilities but are in need of credit. For the purpose, a Corpus of Rs. 31 crores was 
sanctioned, to be utilised in a phased manner. 
5. The Committee observes that as against Rs. 31 crores sanctioned last year for this scheme, only 
a token amount of Rs. one lakh has been earmarked this year. It feels that unless 

schemes for the utilisation of sanctioned money are formulated well in time, setting up of such 
funds becomes infructuous. Therefore, it recommends that Department should, ensure that schemes 
are framed for prop er utilisation of the funds without delay. 
(ii) National Commission for Women and Commissioner for Women's Rights 
6. The Nation al Commission for Women was set up as a nodal agency to monitor the 
enforcement of lega l status of women, to review the existing legislation and suggest amendments 
and to liaise with the concerned Ministries, State Governments and NGOs, in order to create 
awareness and spread literacy. For this purpose, an amount of Rs. 1.75 crores in RE was 
provided in 1993-94, which has been increased to Rs. 2 crores in the Budget Estimates for 1994-
95. 
7. The Committee notes that there is substantial increase in the Budget provisions for the 
National Commission for Women for 1994-95, as compared to 1993-94. Govt. should ensur e full 
utilisation of the budg et of Rs. 2 crores by the Commission. 
8. The Committee recommends that Govt. should fulfil the assurance given to th e Parliament 
by creat ing the post of Commissioner for Women 's Rights and all consultations and other 
formalities be completed as early as possible. 
(iii) Hostels for working Women 
9. To protect young working women in urban areas from exposure to undesirable and anti­
social elements, financial assistance to the extent of 50% of the cost of land and 70% of the 
cost of building construct ion is provided to Voluntary Organisations. In 1993-94 Rs. 7.00 crores 
were provided which has bee n increased to Rs. 7.75 crores in the Budget for 1994-95. This 
year's target is to provide assistance to 60 hostles which would benefit about 3000 working 
women.

11. The Committe e is of the view that though there is acute shortage of working Women' s 
Hostels in the country, the Department could not achieve the physical targets during 1993-94, but 
ambit ious targets have been flXed for 1994-95. The Committee desires that effective steps should 
be taken by the Depar tment to achieve the targets set for 1994-95. 
12. As frequent complaints are received about mismanagement of the hostels rece1vmg grants 
and assistance from the Government the Committee is of the view that there is need for evolving 
some system of monitoring so as to control any sort of irregularities in these hostels. For this 
purpose, the Committee recommends that a Government representative be included on the Board 
of Management of each of such hostels. 
13. The Committee eA.presses its concern over the inadequacy of hostels for working women 
and recommends that , taking into consideration the importance of these hostels, Government 
should encourage construction of more such hostels not only through grants but also by allotment 
of land where ever necessary. 

(iv) Education for prevention of atrocities against Women 
14. The programme was sta rted in 1982 with the aim of creating public opinion against exploita tion 
of women and atrocities against them. This objective is sought to be achieved mainly through 
programmes, publicity and research work , as well as holdin g meetings, conferences, seminars , 
exhibitions, etc. 
15. Financial assistance extended in 1993-94 for this purpose was Rs. 35.00 lakhs and the same 
amount has been allocated during 1994-95. 
16. The Committee expresses its concern over the increasing numbers of cases of atrocities against 
women an d recommends that Govt. should conduct some review of these publicity programmes to find 
out whet her these are sufficient to create a significant impact on the public mind. 
17. The Committee recommends that the amount sanctioned for the year 1993-94 for legal aid in 
cases of atrocities against women should be increased. 
18. The Committee was informed of training and other awareness generation programmes 
undertaken by the Department. Production of legal literacy manuals in regi ona l languages and gender 
sensitization are part of this programmes. The Committee feels that such programmes should be 
extended to the grass root level also. 
(v) Indira Mahila Y ojna 
19. Indira Mahila Yojna, as originally conceived in 1991 and included in the President's Address of 
the year, has four basic components: (i) Awareness generation (ii) Income generat ion (iii) Convergence 
of inter-sectoral services; and (iv) Integration of field cadres of all related departments in the country. 
20. The Committee expresses its deep concern over the fact that though the scheme was announced 
in the President's Address in 1991, till this date it has not been operationalised. 
21. The Committee was informed by the Department that the original draft scheme for Indira 
Mahila Yojna contained components of awareness generation, income generation, integr ated system of 
delivery, inter-sectoral services and integration of field cadres of concerned Departm en ts, with an 
allotment of Rs. 1785 crorcs for the Eighth Plan. The concerned Departments could not, however, 
come to a consensus on integration of cadres and transfer of schemes from one Ministry to the other. 
Subsequently, there was a revised scheme to cover 200 blocks, with income generation and awareness 
generation components (Rs. 78 crores for the remainder of the 8th Plan.) But this also is yet to be 
approved by the Planning Commission. The Provision of Rs. 8 crores in the 1994-95 Budget may go into 
the World Bank-aided ICDS project, if the approval does not come in time. 
The Committee feels that such a big scheme should be implemented only when proper assessment of 
financial and infrastructural implications is made. Duplication of efforts should be avoided. whether a 
single-window delivery system would benefit women, in immensely varied circumstances, has also to be 
assessed. 
(vi) Mahila Samridhi Yojna 
22. This is a new scheme launched on 2nd October, 1993 to promote thrift, self-relia nce and certain 
amount of economic independence among rural women. It is implemented by the Depar t· of Posts 
through the network of 1.32 lakh post offices in rural areas. An amount of Rs. 10.5 cror cs \',as initially 
sanctioned for the scheme which has been increased to Rs. 19.89 crores in the Budgetar y orovis ions for 
1994-95. 
23. The Committee notes that significant increase in allocations for Mahila Samridhi Yojna has been 
made this year. The Comm.ittee, however, recommends that there should be proper monitoring to see 
that these funds are properly utilised. 
24. The Committee is of the view that various programmes under the Mahila Samridhi Yojna are 
implemented keeping in view the welfare of rural women, whereas poor women in urban areas , who are 
also in need of assistance, are not covered under it. The Committee recommends that requiremen ts of 
needy urban women belonging to the weaker sections of society should also be kept in mind while framing 
and implementing schemes for women's welfare. 

25. Committee also feels that there is not sufficient awareness among the rural people regarding 
the benefits of Mahila Samridhi Yojna. Secondly, the postmasters in the villages are not fully info.-med 
and trained about the scheme, and there is also dearth of forms. The need is, therefore, to train 
postmasters about the functioning of the scheme and to make the forms available so as to avoid 
inconvenience to the needy. 
26. There should also be a monthly review of the progress made under the scheme so as to take 
corrective measures wherever necessary. 
Nutrition and Child Development 
27. The Committee expresses its concern over the sharp decli~e in the Plan Budget estimates 
under the Head 2235 for Child Welfare. As against. Rs. 43.35 crores in 1993-94, it has gone down to 
Rs. 20.17 crores in 1994-95 and recommends restoration of the last year allocations. 
(i) Integrated Child Development Services (/CDS) 
28. The main thrust of ICDS programme is on the provision of Anganwadis in every village and 
urban slum areas. Generally, there is one Anganwadi for a population of 1000 in rural areas and 
urban slum areas and of about 700 in tribal area~, which is run by an Anganwadi worker, a female 
voluntary worker and a helper. By the end of 1993, 3120 ICDS projects were sanctioned which 
benefited about 1.94 crorc children and women. For the year 1994-95 an outlay of Rs. 426.00 crores 
has been approved for the ICDS and 200 new projects are likely to start. 
The Committee feels that a large portion of the increased outlay is likely to be absorbed in the 
increased honorarium to Anganwadi workers. Therefore, the Committee feels that the amount available 
for the projected expansion of the scheme to cover new areas seems to be insufficient. Of 5239 blocks, 
2119 block remains to be covered. At the rate of 200 projects per year, it will take another 10 years for 
all blocks to be covered. Thus is too slow. To expedite the process, any shortfall in the projected 
expansion by the end of the 8th Plan should be properly estimated and additional allocations made. 
29. The relative success of the ICDS scheme in improving child health and lowering IMR is due 
to its decentralized and popular structure. probably because of this, ICDS is being increasingly seen 
as an umberlla organisation within which other schemes could be incorporated. Thus, early childhood 
education is now a part of ICDS_. There is a new scheme for adolescent girls, creches and day care 
centres arc sought to be made a part of ICDS. Indira Mahila Yojana, in its revised form, will become 
a component of ICDS. Separate allocations have been proposed for these schemes, but the National 
Creche Fund has only been notified. Allocation of Rs. 8 crores for Indira Mahila Yojna has not yet 
been approved. Therefore, the Committee recommends that until and unless spearate additional 
allocations are obtained for these additional components, ICDS should concentrate on strengthening 
and expansion of its own structure with whatever allocations it has. The proposal to entrust a 
percentage of !CDS schemes to NGOs should be properly assessed before it is implemented, because in 
the absence of community-based monitoring arrangements, it would be difficult to ensure accountability 
of these NGOs. 
30. With the usc of ICDS infrastructure, a special scheme for adolescent girls has been 
formulated, mainly for those who have been out of schools, to meet their nutritional, educational and 
recreational needs. 
31. Regarding education of adolescent girls, the Committee recommends that there should be a 
scheme to help meritorious girls enabling them to pursue their studies further. 
32. In order to meet the requirement of trained personnel for implementing the programmes for 
pre-school children, the Bal Scvika training programme was started in 1961-62. There are 25 Bal 
Scvika training Centres and each centre is provided with a sum of Rs. 1,74,750/- to train 50 Bal 
Sevikas each year. 
33. The Committee observes that out of the three components of ICDS, namely executive, workers 
and recipients, two do not appear to be happy with the service. Therefore, monitoring system should be 
strengthened to ensure proper functioning of the ICDS Scheme to the satisfaclion of all its components. 

of the population through ICDS, as well as nutritional education. In this context, the Committee 
recommends revival of the scheme of supply of milk to the under-nourished school Children. 
44. The Committee also feels that, year after year, the focus of attention of the Deptt. keeps on 
changing from one scheme to another and there seems to be no long-term perspective. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that instead of framing new schemes every year and letting the earlier ones to 
just continue, the Department should concentrate on some major schemes and work to achieve the 
targets fixed through suitable action plans. The Department was set up in 1985 but its strerigth has 
remained the same although many new schemes have been introduced during this period. The 
Committee feels that strengthening of Departmental infrastructure is necessary inorder to ensure the 
effectiveness of the schemes.

AN OVERVIEW 
There are two main components of the Department i.e. Cult:ur~ and Arts. A . separate 
department, called the Department of Arts, was constitu ted in August, 1985 with the aim .,of setting 
up the Indira Gandhi National Centre for Arts (IGNCA)-a major centre for Arts, Humanities and 
Cultural heritage . The vast treasure of our culture is being preserved, promoted and propagated 
jointly by the Central and Srate Governments and Union Territory Administrations through out the 
country . The Archaeological survey of India is the largest and most important part of the Department 
of Culture engaged in conservation and excavation of old historical sites and about 25 per cent of the 
total budget provisions of the Department of Culture goes to this institution. Awareness generation 
and dissemination of information about our glorious past is done through exhibition of antiquities and 
artefacts preserved in museums spread throughout the country. Different Academies, National School 
of Drama, Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Zonal Cultura l Centres ,' Libraries, Memorials 
like Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti, Kalaksherra, Madras etc., functioning under the Department 
of Culture, cater to the artistic and literary needs of the people . The Anthmpological Survey of India, 
a subordinate office of the Department, has been carrying out researches on cultural aspects of Indian 
population. · 
2. The total outlay on culture during the Eighth Five Year Plan (as initially approved for the 
Department of Culture) amounts to Rs. 727 crores (including both Centra l as well as State sectors) . 
The Central sector share is Rs. 385.00 crores, supplemented by an additional allocation of Rs. 75.00 
crores, making it a total of Rs. 460.00 crores.

National ~ultural Fund be set up for the preservation and protection of ancient monuments. It needed, 
money from this fund may also be appropriated to other schemes starved of funds. ~

The Committee takes strong exception to the failure of the Department and recommends that 
henceforth budget allocations given to the Department should be fully utillsed and appropriated. The 
Committee also notes that the distribution of available funds is also not need-based. While on the one 
hand, funds are being blocked by allocaling them to such scheme where appropriation is less and are 
being surrendered on the other, some schemes where appropriation is cent percent and more grant is 
required, suffer from Jack of resources. Therefore, the Committee recommends that instead of 
surrendering the untilised funds the Deptt. should reallocate them for the needy schemes in time. 
7. The Secretary, Deptt. of Culture, during the course of his oral cvidehce tendered bef6re the 
Committee stated that this year the major thrust of the Deptt. are on the Scheme of setting up of 
rural libraries assistance to private museums, documentation and promotion of folk and tribal arts, 
attracting private sector in the field of arts and culture by according them tax exemptions etc., 
encouraging people's initiative and participation in the process of cultural development and organising 
festivals of India abroad. 
8. In order to give fillip to the culture and to restore and refurbish its dying facets, Govt. has 
drafted an Approach Paper on National Policy on Culture. Views/comments received from Members 
of Parliament, eminent person in the field of literature, arts and culture, critics and administrators, 
etc. on the Policy Paper have been discussed in the meetings of the Consultative Committee of the 
Department. Presently, by the Draft Approach Paper on National Policy on Culture is under 
consideration of this Standing Committee and it proposes to submit its report to the Parliament soon. 
REPORT 
9. The Committee, taking note of the revolutionary changes taking place in communications and 
mass media and threat to the Indian culture from outside, emphasises that culture should be seen in 
right perspective and stresses the need of countering cultural invasion from outside. The Secretary, 
during the course of his oral evidence before the Committee, while taking note of the concern of the 
Committee stated that efforts are being made to have parleys with the Secretaries of Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting and Department of Tourism in order to ensure better coordination 
between them in this regard. The Commmittee urges upon the Government to make all-out efforts to 
contain cultural invasion and to restore our cullural ethos, ideals and values. 
10. The Committee expresses its concern over the neglect of the rural areas due to the· 
centralisation of programmes in the urban areas by the Department of Culture. More and more 
programmes of the department are concentrated in the major cities and the rural areas are being 
neglected in the process. It was admitted by the department that in our cultural programmes priority 
is being given to the urban areas due to reason that major cultural institutions are located in the cities 
and there are better transport and other facilities available in cities for the foreign delegates and 
dignatrics visiting these centres. The situation can improve only when more and more such facilities 
are provided in the rural areas to facilitate the establishment of cultural centre s in villages or semi­
urban areas. 
The Comm ittee was also informed that there is a provision with the Department to extend 
building grant of Rs. 10 lakhs to any organisation for setting up of auditorium at any place including 
the rural areas. if it has a piece of land and is ready to spend matching amount. During the year 1993-
94, fifty nine such institutions/organisations were given building grants to the tunc of Rs. 1.38 crores. 
But the logic of the Department does not appear to be sound enough in the sense that if the semi­
urban , under-developed and rural areas are neglected and rejected on this pretext, how the cultural 
needs of the vast majority of people living in these areas would be met. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the programmes and resources of the Department be considerably decentralised and 

taken to the backward, rural and und erdeveloped urban areas where ancient cultural heritage still 
holds· appeal and r equire s to be galvanised by the centre.

excavation of ancient sites, study of inscriptions, research and training in different areas of 
archaeology, etc. Povisions made for this head during the last two years are given in the table.

12. There has been an increase of Rs. 1.90 crores this year, as against the revised estimates of the 
last year, which, in view of price esclation, is negligible. Therefore, the Committee feels that allocation 
for ASI should be adequately increased because a large number of monuments are in dilapidated 
condit ions and need urgent repairs and a great number of monuments and sites remain unidentified 
an d unprotected. Out of around 8,000 monuments, about 3,500 are centrally prot ected . The Committee 
expresses its concern over the fact that even the centrally protected monum ents do not have proper 
maintenance and foolpr oof protectioq. Cases of larceny of artefacts, idols etc. have been occuring from 
time to tim e. During the course of evidence the Committee came to know that the number of staff 
engaged in preservations and maintenance of monuments is so small that the ratio works out to 1lfz 
staff per monument. Therefore, the Committee recommend s that staff strength of the ASI engaged for 
protection and preservation of monumenrs be adequately increa sed and all other necessary mea sure s be 
taken to check the increasing menace of pilferage. Some amount from the propo sed National Cultural 
Fund may also be utilised for the purp ose. 
The Committee is also of the view that , as envisaged in the Eighth Plan document related to the 
Department of Culture, voluntary organi sations should be attracted and encouraged to take up the task 
of preservation atid prot ection of monu'mcnt s. 
13. Even after one hundred and twenty five years of its existence, ASI has not been able to cover 
all parts of the country as far as excavation and exploration of ancient historical sites are concerned. 
Nor it has been able to deciphe r all the inscriptions. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
network of ASI should have been exten sively expanded and enlarged. It should also be well equipped. 
The scheme of village to village survev should also be undertaken and expanded. 
Anthropological Survey of India 
14. Researches in anthropology and allied disciplines and study of customs and traditions are 
some of the major functions undertaken by the Anthropological Survey of India. In the Eighth Five 
Year Plan document it was proposed to salvage and document those specimens of the tribal and folk 
art which face the threat of extincti on. It was also proposed to study inherent socio-religious 
disabilities of the tri bals, nature of tran sforma tion and mobilisation of their specia l skills in arts, dance 
and tnusic an d mastery over musical instruments. But , no follow-up action on these lines is found in 
the Annual Plans of the Departme nt. Therefore, the Committee urges upon the Government to pursue 
vigorously those objectives. Reasons for decrease in the plan allocation of Rs. 140.00 lakhs from Rs. 
150.00 lakhs (Plan Expenditure Revised) of the year 1993;94 are not tenable. Hence the Committ ee 
recommends that the provision should be increased. Study and research in the field of conservation of 
environment, welfare of women and children, nutritional status of Indian population, etc. have also 
been added to its activities, recently. 

15. In keeping with its aims and objectives, the Anthropologi cal Survey of India took up a 
national project called 'People of India' to analyse Indian population on the bas is of bio-cultural 
variables and socio-cultural determinents like marriage , kinship , region, language etc. Out of the 
proposed 43 volumes of the prestigious National Project 'People of India'- three under national and 
two under State series have so far been published. The remaining work should be expedited. 
Museums 
16. Museums play a vital role in the preservation of documents and objects of cultur al antiquity. 
In this field, at present, there are ten premier institutions under Govt. of India , includin g the 
National Reserach Laboratory for Conservation of Cultural proper ty located at Lucknow. Out of the 
ten institutions, three each are located at New D elhi and Calcutta and one each at Lucknow , 
Allahabad, Hydcrabad and Bombay, all situated in major cities. To provide representation to cultural 
aspects of othe r states of Indian Union, a new scheme for Promotion and Stre ngthening of Reg ional 
and Local Museums has been mooted and is env isaged to be ope rationlised during the Eighth Five 
Year Plan period. Govt. is also providi ng assistance for open ing private museums. Govt. proposes to 
intensify this scheme through a Committee which will look after them. But for this well conce ived 
scheme a meagre amount of Rs. 10 lakhs has been provided for the year 1994-95. There has been no 
change in the allocations for the last three years. In such a situation the Committee wonders how the 
scheme contemplated for the Eighth Plan could be implemented within the time-frame with this 
insignificant budget allocation. As the Eighth Five Year Plan is left with only two financial years, the 
Committee strongly recommends enhancement of financial allocation to speed up the implementation of 
the scheme. 
National Council of Science Museums (NCSM), Calcutta 
17. It is an autonomous organisation engaged primarily in the task of popularising science and 
technology among the studen ts in particular and the masses in general thr ough a variety of interactive 
and innovative programmes and activities like science exhib itions, schoo l centre s, portable 
planetarium and national science seminars etc. and setting up of a Science City in Calcutt a, is the 
highlight of the activities of the National Cou ncil of Science Museums. In the Eighth Plan docume nt it 
was proposed to create 1000 science centres to reach the common man, five new regional centres, 20 
district science centres and 203 school science centres in the under privileged rural schoo ls, 20 new 
mobile science exhibition buses, a science train, etc. The total outlay for the 8th Plan period of Rs. 
4500.00 lakhs for these ambitious proposals is too littfe. Slight increase in the allocatio n for this year, 
as against the last year's Budget Estimates, of around Rs. 161 lakhs and of Rs. 111 lakh s in Revised 
Estimates may not be said to be adequate in view of the rising prices. The implementation of the 
scheme has made very little progress and should be speeded up. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
_that additional grant be given for this scheme to increase scientific temper among the people. 
National Museum, New Delhi 
18. During 1994-95, the National Museum , New Delhi, proposes to organise exhibitions of 
Persian manuscripts in Teheran, an exhibition of Indian Art at Singapore and of miniature paintings 
at Tashkent. Apart from this, it is also proposed to introduce such new programmes as developing 
software for physically handicapped persons, lending consultancy services to the State and other 
museums, introduction of disc system for documentation of its huge collect ion , microfilming of 
manuscripts and computerisation of its library, etc. 
19. The provisions made for this year, as against last year, remain more or less the same. Plan 
provision has fallen from Rs. 200.00 lakhs to Rs. 190.00 lakhs and Non-P lan provisions has increa sed 
by only Rs. 7 lakhs in compariso n to the Revised Estimat es of the last year. Thus, there has been a 
decrease of Rs. 3 lakhs this year. The Committee is surprised to know as to how with this small 
allocation. It would be possible to ach ieve the targets set for this year. The Committee therefore, 
recommends that the allocation for National Museum be increased appropriately. 
Indian Museum , Calcutta 
20. The total provisions made this year for Indian Museum, Calcutta, arc less by 1.45 lakhs as 
agianst the Revised Estimates (both Plan and Non-Plan) of the last year. In this situat ion, apart from 

carrying out on-going functions the proposal to construct a new building for display of valuable 
artefacts may find itself in rough weather. It was also envisaged in the Eighth Plan document to set 
up new galleries on textiles, folk arts, gems and jewelleries. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
that sufficient grant should . be provided to the Museum so that these schemes are completed. 
Institutes and Organisations of Tibetan and Buddhist studies 
21. There are. four autonomous institutes, namely, the Central Institute of Higher Tibetan 
Studies, VaranasC the Central Institute of Buddhist Studies, Leh; the Sikkim Research Institute of 
Tibetology and the Library of Tibetan Works & Archives, Dharamsala, which are engaged in 
preservation and propagations of Tibetan culture and tradition, restoration of ancient Indian literature 
preserved in Tibetan language, imparting higher education in Buddhist philosophy and literature, etc. 
The Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, Varanasi, enjoys the status of a 'Deemed 
University'. The Committee while expressing its satisfaction over the encouragement given to these 
institutes feels that they should be allowed to pursue their academic interest without any extraneous 
influences. 
22. The Committee feels that due attention is not being paid in these institutes to promotion and 
development of Pali, one of ancient language of India and, therefore, recommends suitable steps in this 
regard. 
Libraries 
23. The Committee feels that the reading habi!S of the general masses are on the wane, partly 
owing to revolutionary changes in electronic media, partly due to the shift in social values titled more 
to materialism, and partly because of high prices of books. In this situation, libraries have to be 
opened on a large scale with even distribution in urban and rural areas. 
24. There are six major libraries under the Department of Culture. The total budgetary provision 
(lOth Plan and Non-Plan) for the year 1994-95 under this _head is Rs. 13.36 crores a tot"al increase of 
Rs. 2.38 crores in comparison to the Revised Estimates (Both Plan & Non Plan) of the last year. In 
view of the rising prices of books and other allied items, maintenance cost of buildings etc. this 
increase of Rs. 2.38 crores in not enough. 
25. The tendency of centralisation is perceptible in the scheme of libraries also. The Committee 
feels that suitable scheme be devised to spread the network of libraries to District Headquarters and 
small towns. There is also a need to interlink the major libraries with computer network. It will 
facilitate the research scholars and other persons desiring any information sitting in one library to 
gather additional information from all the connected libraries. 
26. The Delhi Public Library, established in 1951 with the assistance of UNESCO to provide free 
library service to the citizens of Delhi, has also now developed into a Metropolitan Public Library. A 
major portion of its activities is located in the affluent localities of Delhi and the rural and 
underdeveloped areas are being neglected. Therefore, ·the Committee, recommends that Govt. should 
take adequate steps to spread it~ network of libraries and reading rooms In the slum and 
underdeveloped areas of the National Capital. More and more mobile library vans should also be made 
available. In view of all these, the Committee recommends that the budget allocation for Delhi Public 
Library be enhanced appropriately. 
Raja Ram Mohan Roy Library Foundation, Calcutta 
27. Established in 1972-, it is an autonomous organisation fully funded by the Deptt: of Culture. 
The · main aim of the library is to support and promote library services. in the country. 
28. Increase in its budget provision this year is welcome. However, some irregularities in the 
fuqctioning of the library have come to the notice of the Committee. Guideliues on book purchasing are 
not being adhered to and books are allegedly being purchased at higher rl}tes than the market rates. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that these matters be looked into. 

Rural Library Scheme 
29. The Committee is happy to note that the Department of Culture has decided to focus its 
attention on the rural populace by deciding to set up rural libraries in villages. A teacher from the 
local school is proposed to be made in-charge of the library which will, in the incipient,have around 
300 books. The Committee is of the view that these libraries should also ~ave such books which may be 
used by neo-Iiterates in the post-literacy stage. It is, undoubtedly a well conceived scheme and generous 
funds should be provided for it. The Committee recommends that this scheme be made a pilot project 
so that about five and half lakh villages could be covered within a stipulated time-frame. The 
Committee also recommends that separate allocation be made for individual states. In consultation with 
the Ministry of Rural Development, the assistance of Panchayats may be sought to ensure speedy and 
effective implementation of this scheme. The Committee also recommends that the modalities for the 
implementation of this scheme be worked out as early as possible so that the scheme implemented in 
right earnest.

/. Sahitya Akademi

1956 with the objective of working actively for development of literature and to foster- and coordinate 
literary activities in all the Indian languages and to promote through them the cultural unity of the· 
country. To achieve these objectives, the Akademi is running programmes such as granting literary 
awards, translation and publication of books in different languages, etc. The Akademi also provides 
assistance to State Akademies. 
31. The Committee is not happy with the budgetary allocation made for the Akademi this year, 
which is only Rs. 57 lakhs more than the Revised Estimates of the last year :-

II. Sangeet Natak Akademi 
33. The Sangeet Natak Akademi, which come into being in 1953, is a national institution engaged

Ill. Lalit Kala Akademi 
34. The Lalit Kala Akademi an apex institution in the field of art was established in 1954 for the 
promotion and development of paintings, graphics, sculpture, ceramics, etc. in the country. The major

bringing out art publications, and implementing cultural exchange programmes. 
35. The allocation for the Akademi this year has come down from Rs. 2.85 crores (Revised 
estimates) of the year 1993-94 to Rs. 2.40 crores. The Committee urges upon the Govt. to increase the

National School of Drama 
36. The National School of Drama, established in 1959, is a premier institution devoted to 
imparting training in the field of theatre and to propagate dramatics in the country. Increase in this 
year's budgetary provisions for the institution from Rs. 266.65 lakhs to Rs. 285.00 lakhs is welcome. 
The National School of Drama proposes to set up regional centres, ~hich is a welcome step, and the 
Committee desires that these regional centres should enjoy due autonomy in their functioning and not 
made mere branches of the National School of Drama, New Delhi. 
Promotion of Art & Culture 
37. A number of organisations and institutions are active in promoting and disseminating 
different types of art and cultural activities in various regions and zones of the country. A brief sketch 
of their activities, objective 's vis-a-vis provisions thereof is given below:-
/. Centre for Cultural Resources & Training 
38. The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training , set up in 1979 with its headquarter in New 
Delhi, is doing a commendable job in the propagation of culture, especially among college and school 
students. One of the major activities of the Centre is to train inservice school teachers in the area of 
linkage between education and culture and to provide a cultural component in the curricula. The 
Centre also prepares audio-visuals and printed materials to be used in schools for cultural education. 
The centre also took over the scheme 'Cultural Talent Search Scholarship' from the Deptt. of Culture 
in 1982 under which 300 children in the age group of 10-14 years are awarded scholarships each year 
in various fields. 
39. The Centre has been entrusted with the task of interlinking culture with education, mass 
media and the scheme of the Deptt., bearing an identical nomenclature, has since been merged with 
the centre 's scheme. 
40. The Committee is of the view that it is not practically feasible to cover whole country by the 
one and only Centre in New Delhi and hence feels the need to decentralise the activities of the Centre 
by opening sub-centres in various zones and regions. 
41. The provisions made for the Centre are not in consonance with the multifarious activities of the 
Centre. A comparative analysis of the allocation suggests that there has been a meagre increase of 
Rs. 20 lakhs in Plan and 0.65 lakhs in Non-Plan expenditure, as against the revised estimates of the last 
year. Since this is the only institution which is taking culture down to the general masses, students and 
teachers, the Committee recommends that more resources should be allocated to the Centre, 
particularly keeping in view the Committee's recommendation for opening sub-Centres at various 
places. 
Zonal Cultural Centres 
42. At present, there are seven Zonal Cultural Centres which cover the entire country. The niain 
functions of the Zonal Cultural Centres are to provide facilities for the creative development in the 
entire spectrum of culture, particularly in that of folk and tribal art. These centres are also 
implementing National Cultural Exchange Programmes, Republic Day folk dance festival and setting 
up Shilpgrams etc. For the year 1994-95 a sum of Rs. 200 lakhs has been earmarked for zonal cultural 
centres. During the year 1992-93 there was an under-utilisation of the approved outlay to the tune of 
about Rs. 175 lakhs, mainly because of the delay in allotment of land by State Government for setting 
up of Shilpgrams. The Committee, however, feels that such delays should be &voided so that funds are 
utilised in time. The Committee recommends that speedy progress be made in setting up Shilpgrams at 
the remaining six zonal cultural centres, particularly the one being set up at Thanjavur. The 
Committee also feels that centrewise allocation should also be reflected in the documents of the 
Department. 
43. Documentation and propagation of folk art constitute one of the main functions of Zonal 
Cultural Centres and as stated by the Secretary, Department of Culture, it is also one of the major 
thrust areas during this year. But the work being done in this regard cannot be said to be satisfactory. 
There is no indication as to how much money each Zonal Cultural Centre spends on the propagation of 
the living folk art forms at the grassroot level in villages where they are actually performed. Therefore, 

'he Committee is of the view that due emphasis of the Zonal .Cultural Centres should be on folk arts 
and necessary financial assistance should also be provided for the same. 
44. The Committee is constrained to note tha t the hopes generated at the time of establishment of 
Zonal Cultural Centres have not been fulfilled and realised. Because these centres are not pursuing the 
programmes and schemes for. which they were set up, therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
.time has come for a high-powered Review Committee to be constituted to look into the working of the 
Zonal Cultural Centres. 
Dissemination of Tribal Folk Art & Culture 
45. Under this scheme, financial support is given to voluntary cultural organisations, institutions 
and individuals-both tribal and non-tribal for undertaking small duration projects of around one year 
for preservation and development of tribal folk art and culture, conduct of tribal cultural activities, 
including their festivals and festivities. This year, there has been an increase of Rs. 10 lakhs for this 
scheme. But the Committee is not happy with the working of the voluntary organisations/institutions 
in this field because it is found that the assistance does not percolate down to the folk artistes, 
although the Secretary, Department of Culture, has submitted before the Committee that Gqvern­
ment is taking necessary steps to ensure that the artistes get the desired benefit. The Committee 
recommends the pro,gressive establishment of a network of organisations to ensure that folk artistes in 
villages are enabled to derive full advantage of the scheme meant for them. Assistance should also be 
given for opening performance centres or auditoria at the village and block level so that artistes could 
perform and interact with each other to improve their particular art forms. 
Multipurpose cultural complexes at States & National Cultural Complex in Delhi 
46. Under this scheme, financial assistance is proposed to be extendep....to autonomous bodies for 
settmg up art complexes in the States to improve the quality of life among youth and students and to 
sensitize them to what is aesthetically and morally good in our society and also to expose them to the 
finest forms of creative expressions. 
47. The Committee is not happy with the progress made in the scheme and expresses its serious 
concern over the fact that almost two financial years have elapsed and the projects have not been 
finalised yet. The Committee is also not happy with the idea of creating more and more cultural 
infrastructure in big cities and towns at the cost of rural areas. However, the Committee is satisfied to 
note that multi-purpose complexes, are being set up in smaller towns, rural and backward areas and 
recommends that other schemes being formulated by the Deptt. should also be located in sucn areas. 
The Committee also recommends that the National Cultural Complex (Parisar), proposed to be set up 
in Delhi, be established in the trans -Yamuna or outer Delhi areas. 
48. The Committee is also of the view that instead of concentrating only on huge cultural 
complexes, Govt. should set up smaller units where the deprived, under .privileged and unprivileged 
may have access to all forms of culture as well as to practice and promote their arts. The Committee 
also holds that the Department may construct multi-purpose stadia in smaller towns and cities which 
could be utilised for sports during the day and for cultural purposes in the evening and night. 
Asiatic Societ~, Calcutta 
49. The A~iatic Society, Calcutta, is an institution of national importance involved mainly in 
oriental studies and research, research in humanities and science, publication of periodicals, books 
and other literature. At present, there are around 12 senior fellows and 30 junior research scholars 
attached to the Society. 
SO. The Committee is surprised to note that a drastic cut has been resorted to in this year's budget 
allocation for the society. The plan provision has been reduced from Rs. 341.00 lakhs (Revised 
Estimates) during the year 1993-94 to Rs. 200.00 lakhs for the year 1994-95. The provision is 
understood to have been reduced in view of the opening of the Asiatic Society, Bombay. The Committee 
desires that the activities of the Asiatic Society, Calcutta should not suffer pending opening of Asiatic 
Society, Bombay. 

51. No financial assistance has been provided to the Asiatic Society, Bombay, during the Eighth 
Five Year plan. The reason behind this Is stated to be that the Planning Commission has earmarked a 
provision of Rs. 200.00 lakhs to be given to the Society as corpus fund. But this fund also has not 
reached the Society so far as it is pending approval from the Ministry of Finance. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that government sho11ld expedite the matter and release the amount without 
any further delay. 
Assistance to Cultural Organisations 
52. For promotion and dissemination of Culture the Department extends financial assistance to 
voluntary organisations under various schemes such as Scheme for Building grants to voluntary 
organisations, Scheme for financial Assistance to Dance, Drama and Theatre Ensembles, Financial 
Assistance for Research Support to voluntary organisations · engaged in Cultural Activities, Grants to 
Institutions I Individuals engaged in literary Activities. 
There· has been only marginal increase in allocations for these schemes and the Committee 
recommends that they should be enhanced adequately. 
Maulana Abu! Kalam Azad Centre for Asian Studies 
53. This centre, proposed to be set up in the wake of the centenary celebrations of Maulana Abul 
Kalam Azad, is still not complete. The Committee is surprised to note that this ·year budget provision 
for the Centre has been reduced by Rs. S lakhs, for the reasons not acceptable to the Committee. The 
Committee recommends that there should be no further delay in the setting up of this Centre. 
Indira Gandhi National Centn: for Arts 
54. The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts was estaolished in 1985 as an autonomous 
Trust. The Government had contributed to its Corpus Fund Rs. 46.75 crores between 1987-88 and 
1993-94. The balance of Rs. 3.25 crores of the Committed amount has been provided in this year's 
Budget. For the building fund, the Government has so far allocated Rs. 32.35 crores and in this year 
Rs. 16.75 crores have been provided. The Committee regrets to note that even after eight years of 
establishment of the Centre, its main projects including the building are yet to be completed, though 
requisite allocations. are being made by the Government. The Committee has been told that work on 
the construction of the building has started In the real sense only in March, 1994. The other activities 
of the Centre like microfilming of unpublished manuscripts and creation and updating of data base are, 
however, in progress. The Committee feels that steps should be taken to utilise the funds fully and 
speedily so as to achieve the desired objectives. 
Memorials and Centenaries 
55. The Department of Culture proposes to commemorate this year the 125th birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi through Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti. But the allocation earmarked for the 
purpose is most inadequate. Also, in 'this year, the country will observe the 75th Anniversary of the 
Jallianwala Bagh Massacre but no budgetary provision has been made for this purpose. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that the budget provision for celebration of the 12Sth birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi be increased and adequate funds be allocated for the observance of the 75.th 
Anniversary of Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.
