VII.      CENTRAL INSTITUTE OF PSYCHIATRY, RANCHI
7.1       The Plan allocation for this Institute in BE 1999-2000 was Rs. 3.80 crores, which was reduced to Rs. 2.71 crores
in the RE.  For 2000-2001, the Plan allocation is Rs. 3.00 crores.
7.2       Last year, the Committee was informed that the allocation of Rs. 2.80 crores in 1998-99 for the Institute was
enhanced to Rs. 3.80 crores in 1999-2000 for filling up 260 vacant posts.  However, the Committee finds that  posts
could not be created on account of ban orders issued by the Department of Expenditure.  This issue has been continuing
for a considerable time as  an IWSU study conducted for the Institute had recommended creation of 260 posts on
16.1.97, i.e. about three years ago.  The Committee is of the view that given the nature of the ailment, the patients of this
Institute need special treatment.  Doctors and para-medicals with specialized skills should be appointed to treat the
patients more efficiently.  It is an undesirable situation specially in view of that CIP, Ranchi is a teaching institute of a
national level.  The Committee is,  therefore, of the view that creation of additional posts is a necessity which cannot be
avoided.
7.3       To a query as to  the latest position in respect of the Draft Cabinet Note conferring autonomous status to the CIP,
Ranchi , the Department replied that  the Note  was circulated to the concerned Ministries and their comments received
are being examined. The Department of Expenditure vide their O.M.  dated 5.3.99 desired to clearly bring out the
financial implications on the upgradation and to come up with a proposal for rationalization of the manpower in the
Institute.  Some information has been received from the Institute which is being examined.  The Committee is of the
view that the issue of granting autonomous status to CIP, Ranchi has been unduly delayed.  The response of the
concerned Ministries/Departments has also not been quick and encouraging.  The Committee recommends that a
decision may be taken without any further delay.
VIII.     ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS)
8.1       The All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi is a premier medical institution of the country.  The Plan
allocation for the Institute in BE 1999-2000 was Rs. 81 crores, which was reduced to Rs. 70 crores in RE.  The plan
allocation for 2000-2001 is Rs. 91.30 crores.  Asked about the reasons for reduction in RE, the Department stated that
the EFC memo relating to the setting up of an Organ Bank, procurement of PET Scan, and setting up of Trauma Centre
at AIIMS could not be cleared during 1999-2000 and hence the reduction in RE.
8.2       The Committee is worried to note that despite its earlier recommendation, no progress seems to have been made
in respect of setting up a Trauma Centre.  The workshop on Trauma Centre was held in the Institute on 9-10 July, 1999. 
The Committee, however, finds that recommendations made at the workshop are still in the process of examination. 
The Committee recommends that the Department should make concerted efforts for completion of all the procedural
formalities prior to setting up the Trauma Centre.  It should be ensured that allocation made for this purpose should not
be left under utilised in 2000-2001 like the previous year.
8.3       It came to the notice of the Committee that Dr. R.C. Anand, Medical   Superintendent of the Institute who had
earlier been suspended on corruption charges was reinstated pending inquiry.  The Committee has come to know that
the reinstatement of Dr. Anand has not been approved by the Governing Body of the Institute.  The Committee fails to
understand as to why Dr. Anand was reinstated before the outcome of the inquiry instituted against him.  The
Committee feels that an institute of repute like AIIMS should avoid such controversy.

X.        NATIONAL MALARIA ERADICATION PROGRAMME
10.1     In the case of National Malaria Eradication Programme, the plan provision of Rs.240.00 crores in BE 1999-2000

States of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Gujarat, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura, Uttar
Pradesh, Chnadigarh and Daman & Diu.  168.04 million population were targetted to be covered by residual insecticidal
spray in 1998-99, but only 79.26 million population could be covered.  The Committee is of the view that corrective
measures need to be taken in this regard.
10.3     The Committee has been informed that the major constraints affecting the effective implementation of the
National Malaria Eradication Programme, such as vacancies in key positions, inadequacy of vehicles, frequent transfer

Rajasthan and Maharashtra have initiated action for recruitment of Multi-Purpose Workers/Surveillance Workers. 
Other States are also being advised to remove the constraints. The Committee is of the view that besides a regular
channel of interaction with the State Governments for removal of constraints, the Department should also closely
monitor the implementation of the National Malaria Eradication Programme.

Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and West Bengal have been considered to be endemic as reports of more
than 10 cases of Dengue Fever and Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever have been received from these States in the past.  The
Directorate of National Anti Malaria Programme propose to intensify the Dengue Control measures in these endemic
States in the first phase although the Programme would ultimately cover all the States/UTs.
10.5     The Department further informed that the endemic States were requested to convey their formal concurrence for
implementation of the programme on 50.50 cost sharing basis.   However, response have been received only from the
States of Haryana, Rajasthan, U.P. and Chandigarh and the remaining States have been  reminded to expedite their
views/comments.  The Committee recommends that the Department should pursue this matter with the remaining States.

between 2000 and 2005. Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaign, which was implemented in 21 States/UTs. till June,

XII.      NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR CONTROL OF BLINDNESS
12.1     The aim of the National Programme for Control of Blindness launched  in 1976 is to reduce the blindness rate
from 1.49% to 0.3% by 2000 A.D. Besides, a World Bank Assisted Cataract Blindness Control Project is being
implemented since April, 1994 in  seven States i.e. Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Rajasthan,
Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu,  where prevalence rate is very high.  Physical achievements have been – Cataract
Surgery – 100%, training – 80%, OTs – 70%, IOL – 133%.
12.2     The Committee is  constrained to note that in the States of Goa, J&K, M.P., Nagaland, Orissa, Rajasthan and
Chandigarh, the prevalence rate of blindness is much more than the national average.  The Committee, therefore, feels
that special efforts should be made for the above mentioned States.
12.3     The Committee notes that  Epidemiological Blindness Survey has been conducted on a pilot basis  in the two
districts i.e. Bharatpur in Rajasthan and Sivaganga in Tamil Nadu in 1998-99 to assess the prevalence of blindness. 
Prevalence of blindness in illiterates is as high as 14.90% in Bharatpur District of Rajasthan.  Major cause of blindness
is cataract with 57.3% and 53.4% rate of prevalence in the two districts. The Committee feels that given the vastness of
the country such surveys should be conducted in more districts.
12.4     The Committee is constrained to note that  under the National Trachoma and Blindness Control Programme as
against a provision of Rs. 700 lakhs as grant-in-aid to State Governments during 1997-98, actual expenditure amounted
to only Rs. 110.48 lakhs due to the poor performance of the States in developing the service units.  During 1998-99 
also, the position was somewhat similar. States of MP, Orissa, UP, Assam, Delhi, Gujarat, Haryana, HP,  J&K,
Karnataka, Kerala, Meghalaya, Punjab were having unspent  balances lying with them.  The main reason for unspent
balances is the reluctance on the part of the State Govts. to create the posts due to the liability at the end of the plan
period.  Situation is more worrying in the case of Orissa as funds  were not released by the Finance Department of the
State Govt. to the executing Agencies.  The Committee recommends that the implementation of the Programme in the
States should be closely monitored  and in the event of any problem, the matter should be taken up with the concerned
State Government.

public awareness and community support are the two most vital objectives, which if implemented as per the strategy

patients who receive  free treatment at Government hospitals.   As you are aware, Civil Courts are already for

private hospitals.  The Committee finds that notwithstanding the fact that certain modifications have been made in the
procedure for referral to recognised hospitals and reimbursement of expenditure of medical treatment, patients are still
facing considerable difficulties.  The Committee is of the view that the Department should enter into arrangements with

the bill (restricted to package rates) should be raised directly to the parent department/office/CGHS directorate as the
case may be.  The Committee feels that the Hospitals would have no objection if their bills are settled within a
reasonable period of time.  The Committee also feels that there should be periodical review at least once in three years
of the approved package rates, keeping in view the increase in the cost of medicines and other facilities.

services rendered by doctors of Government Hospitals/CGHS Dispensaries.  Suggestion of the Department of Consumer

OVERVIEW 
1. The National Health Policy (1983) has reiterated India's commitment to attain "Health for 
All (H.F .A.) by 2000 A.D.". The Eighth Plan envisages that health facilities must reach the 
entire population by the end of the Plan period. The B.F.A. paradigm, according to the 8th 
Plan, must take into account not only the high risk vulnerable groups i.e. mothers and children, 
but must also focus sharply on the underprivileged segments within the vulnerable groups. Health 
for under privileged will be the key strategy for the HFA, by the year 2000 A.D., a declaration 
to which India is a signatory. This can only be achieved by associating the pre-defined segments 
of population with not only the health planning process but also with the method for the 
, evaluation of programmes. 
2. India is facing highly complex and challenging health problems. There are health hazards 
of communicable diseases like leprosy, T.B. and malaria, besides challenges of post-transitional 
diseases like cardio-vascular and cancer. Above all these, we are also faced with horrendous 
threat of AIDS. These health problems are further aggravated by wide spread poverty, which 
leads to malnutrition, unhygienic sanitation, illiteracy and ignorance. Population growth is playing 
further havoc on the availability and quality of health services. 
3. Department of Health deals with the health administration of the country, including drugs 
control and prevention of food adulteration . 
4. The main functions of the Deparment of Health are to undertake national programmes of 
health for the prevention and eradication of communicable diseases; to promote education 
research and training in various medical disciplines; to prevent adulteration of food as well as 
drugs; to promote research and treatment on scientific lines in Indian Systems of Medicine; to 
provide primary health care at the doorsteps of the people; to implement better health care 
programme for tribals, and to collaborate with WHO and other international agencies. 
5. For the financial year 1994-95, Budgetary allocation of the Department of Health is Rs. 
1255 crores, this is 18.34 per cent more than the previous year's allocation. This increase, as 
stated by the Department, is due to steep escalation in the prices of consumable items, machinery 
and equipments, publications, raiVair traffic fares, etc. Grant s of additional instalment of D.A., 
Interim Relief, increased number of patients in Government hospitals and increase in cost of 
insecticides, anti-leprosy and anti-T.B. drugs, etc. 
6. According to the Ministry's documents, the major thrust of Budg~t provisions in 1994-95 is 
on National Leprosy Eradication Programme, National Programme for Control of Blindness, 
National Tuberculosis Control Programme and National AIDS Control Programme. It also 
emphasised on setting up of a separate Directorate of Indian System of Medicine and 
Homoeopathy. 
7. The public expenditure in the health sector, both at the Centre and the States put 
together, has been a little over 1.5 per cent of G.D.P. The WHO had recommended that public 
health care expenditure should cross at least 5 per cent of GDP, if equity and universal coverage 
are to be realised. The Committee hopes that concerted efforts will be made to increase health 
expenditure upto 5 per cent of GDP in the next year's budget. 
8. However, the Budget for 1994-95 does not reflect that the Department is heading towards 
Health for All by 2000 A.D. It is noted that more funds are allocated for curative functions 
rather than for prevention of diseases. Programmes of health are uneven in States which may be 
corrected by the efforts of the Department. State should also participate actively in achieving the 
goal of Health for All. However, Department should also provide help to States by releasing 
money on time.

34. The Secretary, Department of Health, in his oral evidence considered before the Committee

35. The Committee feels that disorders in mental health is one of the major problems that the

II 
HOMOEOPATHY AND INDIAN SYSTEM OF MEDICINE 
36. Under the Eighth Plan a provision of Rs. 83 crores has been made for ISM and 
Homoeopathy. In the Budget Estimates of 1993-94, Rs. 20.9 crore was allocated for ISM & 
Homoeopathy. However, it was reduced toRs. 17.25 crores in the Revised Estimates. For 1994-95 
there is a provision of Rs. 25.9 crores. 
Homoeopathy 
37. The Committee notes that ISM & Homoeopathy as a whole were not able to spend the 
money allocated to them last year. It feels that before providing more money to them they should 
ensure that the same will be spent fully and properly. 
38. The Department proposed to equate facilities of Homoeopathy with other Indian systems of 
medic.:i.ne. The Committee feels that the Department is not taking it seriously. Homoeopathy has 
been provided less funds in comparison to the other systems of medicines and no steps have been 
taken to ensure full utilisation of funds allocated and release of funds on time. 
39. The Secretary, Department of Health in his oral evidence had explained that reduction in 
total allocation to Homoeopathy is due to two factors-the provision for CCH (Central Council of 
Homoeopathy) in 1993-94 included additional funds for printing of Central Register (bilingual) of 
registered practitioners of Homoeopathy; and provision for NIH (National Institute of 
Homoeopathy) included grant for capital works . The Committee is not statisfied with the 
explanation and recommends that more allocations to Homoeopathy be provided. 
40. There is a decrease in funds for Central Council of Homoeopathy, and National Institute of 

Homoeopathy Calcutta. In case of NIH, allocations are reduced from 120 lakh s in 1993-94 to 40 
lakhs in 1994-95. For the 8th plan it has been allocated Rs. 6 crores. 
41. The Secretary Deptt. of Health in his oral eviden ce, before the committee had explained 
that reduction in Plan allocations to NIH is due to the fact that grant for 1993-94 included Rs. 47 
lakhs for capital works. The Committee is not satisfied with this explanation as even if Rs. 47 
lakhs is excluded from 1993-94 allocation of Rs. 120 lakh s, still there remains a gap of Rs . 33 
lakhs in the 1994-95 budget provision, in comparison to last year's allocat ions. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends restoration of the grants at the level of previous year. 
Indian Systems of Medicine 
42. On the que stion of setting up of a separate Dire ctorate of Indian Systems of Medicines 
and Homoeopathy, the Department of Health informed the Committee that it has prepared a 
proposal for setting up a separate Directorate of Indian Systems of Medicines and Homoeopathy 
for strengthening these systems, including non-drug therapi es like Yoga and Naturopahty. 
43. The basic objectives of the proposal is to strengthen the organistional set-up for ISM & 
H so as to effectively initiate organised measures to enable each of the systems of Indian 
Medicines , i.e., Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani, to devel op, in accordance with its genius and 
enable each of these systems to play its due role in the overall health care delivery system, to 
achieve the goal of "Health for All" by 2000 A.D. In addition, Yoga and Naturopathy, which are 
time-tes ted drugless therapies and Homoeopathy should also be promoted and strengthened to 
realise their potential in promot ing the public heal th. The Committee recommends that this 
Directorate should be set up expeditiously. 
44. On the question of increase in allocation from Rs. 20 lakhs in 1993-94 (RE) to Rs. 100 
lakhs for National Institute of Siddha, the Department explained that the proposal for setting up 
NIS in Tamil Nadu had been pend ing fl want of concrete proposal from the Government of 
Tamil Nadu. This year Tamil Nadu Government is in the process of getting land for the institute 
of Siddha. The Committee was also informed that the state Government is also willing to 
participate financially in the institute. Therefore, the Department is hopeful of starting the work 
on the institute during 1994-95. 
45. In the Eighth Plan Rs. 500 lakhs has been kept as assistance for upgrading ISM, PG 
Departments. However, in 1993-94 Rs. 25 lakhs was allocated anu in the Revised Estimates it 
was reduced to Rs. 20 lakhs. For 1994-95 also Budget allocatio n is Rs. 20 lakhs. 
Ayurveda 
46. Budgetary allocation for many of the institutes of Ayurveda for 1994-95 has been reduced 
in -:omparison to last year 's. For example, funds for Central Council for Research in Ayurveda 
and Siddha, New Delhi, have been red~ced from Rs. 346 lakhs to Rs. 330 lakhs. In the case of 
National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur, it has been reduced from Rs. 190 lakhs to Rs. 180 lakhs 
and for Gujarat Ayurveda University, Jamnagar, funds have been reduced from Rs. 130 lakhs to 
Rs. 127 lakhs. In case of Pharmacopoeil Labo ra tory for Indian Medicin e, Ghaziabad, there is a 
drastic reduction from Rs. 195 lakhs to Rs. 35 lakhs. 
47. The Committee expresses its displeasure over this decrease and recommends that 
increased funds should be provided to the institutions of Ayurveda. 
48. The Committee has also taken a serious note of the fact that there is not sufficient 
infrastructure to check and regulate the quality of Ayurvedic medicines. The Committee, in the 
discussions, also named some of the famous products of Ayurveda which have been found 
1m pure. 
49. The Committee recommends that standards for Ayurved ic med icine should be fixed and 

nonitored. The Secretary Deptt. of Health had stated in its oral evidence, had stated that 
;tandard of Ayurvedic medicines can be checked only at the stage of manufacturing and after 
:hat it is very difficult. The Committee recommends to take appropriate measures for this. 
50. The Committee also notes that the Department had proposed to establish a National 
Institute of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani Medicine, Homoeopathy and Naturopathy on the lines 
of All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi. But, till now all these institutes are in 
very bad condition and they are nowhere near to the standards of AIIMS, in any sense. 
The Committee feels that scientific research in Indian Systems of Medicines is not done 
properly. It shows sleekness on the part of the Department. 
Unani Medicine 
51. The Central Council for Research in Unan i Medicine (CCRUM) was established in 
1979 to initiate, aid, develop and co-ordinate scientific research in different aspects, fundam en­
tal and applied, of Unani Medicine and to promote and assist institutions of research for the 
disease, their prevention, caution and remedies. 
52. In 1993-94, CCRUM was provided Rs. 371 lakhs (Revised Estimates). For 1994-95, it 
is further increased to Rs. 507 lakhs. 
53. The Committee, while satisfied with the allocatiOn made for the development of 
Unani Medicine, however, recommends that the Department should ensure that the funds are 
utilised properly and achievements are evaluat~d regularly and effectively. 
Development & Cultivation of Medicinal PJants 
54. To meet the shortage of plants for manufacture of quality ISM & H drugs, a scheme 
for central assistance for development and cultivation of medicinal plants in the ISM & H hBs 
been initiated. Under the scheme, financial assistance is provided to eligible Government/ 
semi-government or~anisations, including the ISM & H institutions and pharmacies for non­
recuning expenditure i.e., fencing. land shaping, irrigation, equipments and construction of 
sheds etc. for cultivation and development of identified species of medicinal plants: 
55. The Department has taken steps for production of medicinal plants. This will save 
some of the im~,...,rtant medicinal plants from extinction, and also ensure the availability of 
these plants iu the market. However, the Committee feels that these efforts should be 
continued. 
Excise Duty 
56. The union Budget for 1994-95 has propo sed 10 per cent E;"cise Duty on •he 
Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani medicines, alongwith Homeopathic medicines and the med icines 
of alternative sy:.tems. 
57 The Cou.rnittee feels that i.1 the cootempo,.ary scenerio of globalisation of the science 
of Ayurveda, the proposed levy of 10 per cent Excise Duty adversely affects the exc-,lft of 
Ayurveda Siddha and Unani Medicines. which is sti11 in the ptimitive stage of growth. 
58. The Committee also feels that at home , where Aymvedic medicines have always been 
a common man \ alternate remedy, the proposed levy would lead tc price enhancem ent in 
Ayurveda , Siddhc.. and Unani medicines. 
59. The Committee recommends that the Depar tment should take necessary steps to 
remove Excise Duty. 

Yoga 
60. Budgetary allocation for Central Council for Research in Yoga and Naturopathy has 
been increased by Rs. 10 lakhs from Rs. 30 lakhs in 1993-94 to Rs. 40 lakhs in 1994-95. For 
Central Research Institute for Yoga, .New Delhi (CRIY) also, budgetary allocation for 1994-95 
is Rs. 20 lakhs which is 10 lakhs more than previous year's allocation. 
61. The Committee is satisfied that allocation for Yoga has been increased during this 
year's budget, but feels that more attention should be paid for popularisation of Yoga in 
schools and colleges as well as residential areas. Media should also be used effectively. Proper 
monitoring of the utilisation of funds should also be done. 
III 
HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES 
Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) 
62. The Committee takes serious note of the continuous decrease in the budget provision 
of CGHS. In 1993-94 a provision of Rs. 95.72 crores (BE) was made for CGHS. However, in 
the Revised Estimates it was enhanced to Rs. 117.72 crores . In 1994-95 Budget Estimates it 
has been provided Rs. 104 crores. In the 8th Plan CGHS has been allocated Rs. 15 crores for 
planned expenditure. 
63. The Secretary, Department of Health, explained to the Committee that there is no 
large-scale reduction in outlays for hospitals and CGHS Dispensaries. In some hospitals, 
where larger outlays were provided in 1993-94 for procurement of specific machinery and 
equipment, corresponding reduction has been made in the budget provision for 1994-95. 
However, provision for essential services, which is covered under non-plan expenditure, has 
been raised in all cases. 
64. He further stated that in CGHS due to rise in the cost of drugs it is expected that 
higher outlay will be necessary during the current year. Additional funds will have to be 
provided at the R.E. stage to meet these liabilities. 
65. The Committee is not satisfied with the reasons <tdduced by the Department for 
decrease in the allocations. It feels that Central Government Employees are not served well 
by CGHS. There are complaints from C.G.H.S. beneficiaries in regard to non availability of 
required medicines, delay in supply, insistence for pre-payment by private recognised hospitals 
etc. The Committee recommends that the Department should look into this matter and take 
remedial measures. The Committee also recommends for increase in funds of C.G.H.S. and 
the Department should see that quality of services improves to the satisfaction of be­
neficiaries. 
Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi 
66. In 1993-94 this institute was allocated Rs. 4.16 crores but it spent Rs. 4 crores. For 
1994-95 it is again allocated Rs. 4.51 crores. 
67. The Committee is concerned at the bad state of Central Institute of Psychiatry , (CIP) 
Ranchi. The Committee feels that a review of the functioning of this institute is made. 
All India Institute of Medical Sciences 
68. The Secretary, Department of Health , in his oral evidence had stated that the Vlllth 
Plan outlay for AIIMS is Rs. 100.00 crores. In the B.E. 1993-94 a sum of Rs. 73.48 crores 
(Rs. 26.23 crores Plan+Rs. 47.25 crores in Non Plan) had been provided which was enhanced 

to Rs. 82.63 crores (Rs. 32.23 crores in Plan + Rs. 50.40 crores in Non-Plan) in the Revised 
Estimates, 1993-94. Though the provisions of Rs. 82.05 crores (Rs. 29.05 crores in Plan+ Rs. 
53.00 crores in Non- Plan) in B.E. 1994-95 is marginally low with reference to R.E. 1993-94, it is 
substantially more with reference to B.E. 1993-94. 
69. The Committee feels that there is no increase in the allocations for AIIMS in real terms. 
The Committee recommends that it should be provided with sufficient funds to carry out its 
increasing responsibilities. It is one of the premier institutions in the field of medical education, 
research and treatment. The Committee feels that it should maintain its supremacy and speciality 
with up-to-date equipments and highly qualified doctors. The Committee also recommends that 
functioning and achievments of AIIMS may be reviewed periodically by an experts Committee. 
Para Medical Personnel 
70. The Department informed the Committee that shortage of para medical personnel of 
certain categories is there. In order to overcome this problem the Ministry of Human Resource 
Development, in cooperation with the Ministry of Health, have started vocational courses in 
various para-medical disciplines in a number of institutions. 
71. There is also a proposal for establishing a National Institute of Nursing Education and 
Research in Kerala which was examined in this Deptt. It is felt that the objectives of the 
proposed Institute are being largely fulfilled by the Nursing Council of India and the Deptt. of 
Health. Thus, the proposed institute may duplicate the functions of professional bodies like the 
Nursing Council. However, upgradation of nursing services, both qualitatively and quantitatively 
have been engaging the attention of the Department, and the different possibilities for achieving 
this have been under active consideration. It is, however, premature to make an allocation for 
the proposed National Institute. 
72. The Deptt. is also promoting various Health Related Vocational Courses (HRVC) for 
which the nodal department is the Department of Education in the Ministry of Human Resource 
Developm ent. The courses ident ified so far relate s to Medical Laboratory Technology, X-R ay 
technician , Ophthalmic techniques and A.N.M.'s training. 
73. The Committee notes that the Department has accepted the fact that there is a serious 
shortage of para-medical personnel. The Committee is concerned to note that the num ber of 
nurses is less thaa the number of doctors in many cases. The Committee hopes that this shortage 
is a short-term iJhenomenon and very soon it will be overcome. It recommends open ing of more 
institutions for tra ining of para-medical personnel, creation of additional p::>sts and strP.amlining of 
the recruitment process to achieve these goals. It also recommends for increase in the allocat ion 
for para-medical training institution·s.

Indian Council of Medical Research 
75. The non-plan Budget Estimate of ICMR, for 1994-95 is Rs. 2238 lakhs, consisting of 
grants in aid of Rs. 1860 lakhs and Mi,scellaneous Receipts of the Council of Rs. 378 lakhs. The 
plan Budget Estimate for 1994-95 is Rs. 28 crores. This amount is to be utilised for intra-mural 
. projects (Rs. 190 lakhs) as well as extra-mural projects (Rs. 880 lakhs). 
76. The Committee recommends that proper system of evaluation of research activities 
should be developed~ to assess the working of the Council. 
Serologist and Chemical Examiner. 
77. In 1993-94, Serologist and Chemical Examiner (SCE) spent Rs. 54 lakhs (Re.vised 
Estimate) and it is allocated the same amount of Rs. 54 lakhs in 1994-95 (Budget Estimate). 
78. On the question of abolition of posts in SCE, the Department informed the Committee 
that the abolition would take place not through retrenchment, but by not filling up the posts as 
and when they fall vacant/placement in the surplus cell. The decision to abolish the posts is on 
account of the fact that most of the States have established their own Forensic Science Institute 
Laboratories. 
79. The Committee feels that the reason given for abolition of technical posts is not 
plausible. As per the report of the Department number of medico-legal cases in forensic serology 
coming form the states has not gone down, showing that the demand for such services continues 
to be there. Also, this is not the only work done by the Department. The Department is the only 
indigenous producer of VDRL antigen and different antisera of internationally recognized 
standard; they are earning revenue and saving foreign exchange. Before the decision is 
implemented the Committee feels that assessment of the work done by the Department must be 
undertaken to see whether a massive curtailment of posts would not hamper this work. 
North Eastern Indira Gandhi Regional Institute of Health and Medical Sciences, Shillong 
80. A sum of Rs. 100.00 lakhs was provided in BE 93-94. During the year 1993-94, the 
institute made a demand for sanction of funds to meet the cost of land acquisition and fencing 
work, to be reimbursed to the Govt. of Meghalaya. Accordingly, a sum of Rs. 110.00 lakhs was 
released to NEIGRI towards the grant-in-aid for the year 1993-94. However, a sum of Rs. 500.00 
lakhs was sought in BE 94-95 as provision to meet the cost of civil works etc. 
81. On the question of low grants, the Department had stated that the preparation of site 
plan, detailed plans and estimates of building, statutory clearance, invitation of tender etc. Take 
substantial ~e ~nd it cannot be said with certainty that substantial expenditure on actual 
construction ca~ achieved during the year 1994-95. Therefore, a small provision is made. 
However, if the progress can be speeded up, the additional requirements can be attended to at 
the R.E stage. 
82. The Committee is not satisfied with the progress of NEIGRI, as it is behind schedule. 
Therefore, the Committee reco'iltmena that, a time schedule should be fixed for the completi o11 
of the work and the Department should make every efforts to complete it on time. 

IV 
MISCELLANEOUS 
I 
83. The Committee is disappointed to know that there is no scheme for starting and running 
mobile dispensaries/clinics, particularly in rural areas. It recommends start of such schemes to 
cover rural and for off-places in hills and tribal areas so that people in these areas could get 
urgently needed medical facilities at their doorstep, instead of running to hospitals in towns and 
cities. 
84. The Committee also feels that D.G.H.S. Scholarship Scheme is providing very small 
amount for scholarships in the context of the present price situation. The Committee recommends 
that stipends/scholarships should be raised keeping in view the present rate of inflation and rising 
costs. 
85. The Committee is happy to note that Health Education has been started in about 50,000 
schools. However , it recommends that this should be made compulsory in schools and necessary 
steps be taken in this direction.

PREFACE
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this
Ninetieth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.44) of the Department of Family Welfare, 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the year 2000-2001.
 
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of Family
Welfare and also heard the Secretary and other Officials of that Department   on the said Demands for Grants in its
meeting held on 27
th   March, 2000.
 
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 15th  April, 2000.

REPORT
 
I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1       India with just 2.4% of the world landmass constitutes 16% of the present world population.  The census of 1991
had indicated the population of India as 846.3 million.  In the decade of 1981-91, 163 million persons were added to the
population of India.  On 11th May, 2000, India is projected to have 1 billion (100 crore) population.  If the present rate
of annual growth of population  of 1.74% continues, India may overtake China in 2045 to become the most populous
country in the world.
1.2      With a view to check the growth of population, the Family Welfare Programme was taken up with the
introduction of Planning in the country.  The objective of the Family Welfare Programme for the country has been to
stabilise population at a level consistent with the needs of national development.  To achieve this goal the Department
continues to implement the three-pronged strategy of :
(i)         improvement in the health status of women and children;
(ii)        fulfillment of the unmet needs of contraception with a special focus on widening the range of choice
available to the people; and
(iii)       professionalising and broad-basing the Information, Education    and Communication Campaign on
Family Welfare, by not only using the mass media, but also involving the community, NGOs, women’s
organisations in the local specific IEC work at the district, sub-district and village level.

The Committee feels that there is a need for improvement in Family Welfare measures in such states if the current high
population growth rate of the country is to be effectively checked.
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The Committee notes that the allocation for the Department has been substantially enhanced from Rs. 2940.60
crores in  BE 1999-2000 to Rs. 3541.47 crores in 2000-2001.  Out of  Rs. 3541.47 crores, Rs. 3520.00 crores form the
Plan component and Rs. 21.47 crores is the non-Plan component.
Commenting on the allocation made to the Department, the Secretary stated that in the Annual Plan proposal for the
year 2000-2001 sent to the Planning Commission, a requirement of Rs. 6056.78 crores was projected.   However, an
outlay of only Rs. 3520 crores  for 2000-2001 has been fixed by the Planning Commission, which is grossly insufficient
and is far below of even the Department’s minimum requirement. 
2.2       The Committee was further informed that the annual plan allocations, though increasing each year, have not
been adequate to meet the existing cost of maintenance of infrastructure.  There has been no increase in the
infrastructure since 1980s.  Besides that, huge arrears on account of committed expenditure of salary etc. have been
building up over the years.  During 1999-2000, additional funds by re-appropriation and supplementary grants of the
order of Rs.400 crore had to be provided to clear the arrears certified on the basis of audit till 1996-97 and 1997-98 in
most of the cases.  The statements of 1998-99 are yet to be received.  Projected requirement for this specific purpose is
Rs.900 crores for 2000-2001.
2.3       Adverse impact of non-settlement of arrear claims of state govts. on the Family Welfare Programme, which is a
100 per cent centrally funded programme has been engaging the attention of the Committee for considerable period. 
Last year, the Committee had recommended that the Planning Commission may be approached for one time grant.   In
response, the Department has informed that a Committee has been set up to solve this problem.   As per the latest
information, recommendations of the aforesaid Committee are yet to be finalised in consultation with the States.   The
Committee feels that setting  up a Committee and then awaiting its recommendations is indirectly an effort to evade the
issue.   Settlement of arrear claims of State Governments  is a long-standing problem which needs a  solution at the
earliest. The Committee reiterates that the Planning Commission should be approached for one-time grant.
2.5       The Committee is not in agreement with the proposal placed by the Department before the XI Finance
Commission in September, 1998 for transfer of liability of maintaining the health infrastructure set up in the States over 
the earlier Plan periods to the State Governments’ budget.  The Committee  fails to understand as to how majority of the
states, being already in a very bad shape so far as mobilisation of resources is concerned, would be able to bear this

enormous liability.
2.6       Performance Budget should clearly reflect both the financial provision and corresponding physical achievements
of different schemes/programmes during the financial year. The Committee, however, observes that Performance
Budgets of almost all the Departments are prepared in such a manner that one does not get a clear idea in this regard. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take corrective steps in this regard, if the
Performance Budgeting is to have any meaning.
III.       RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
3.1
              There are at present 5435 Rural Family Welfare Centres functioning in the country which were established at all
the block level PHCs sanctioned upto 1.4.80.  These centres are entrusted with the responsibility for implementing the
Family Welfare Programme, i.e. planning, mobilisation, monitoring, administration and supervision in their areas.  
Block level PHCs have either removed a PHC or got strengthened as CHC.   Besides that, to provide basic health and
family welfare services to the rural population, 1,37,027 Sub-centres are functioning as on 30.11.99 out of which 97,757
Sub centres are funded by Govt. of India and the rest are funded under the State Minimum Needs/Basic Minimum
Services Programme.
3.2
              Sub-Centres and PHCs provide basic health and family welfare services  and implement the Family Welfare
Programme in all respects.  The Committee observes that all India achievement level of targets set for 1998-99 by the
Planning Commission in respect of Sub-Centres /PHCs / CHCs is as follows :-

IV.       URBAN FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
4.1       For providing Family Welfare and MCH services in the urban areas there are 1083 Urban Family Welfare
centres and 871 Health Posts functioning in the country.   A provision of Rs. 58.50 crores has been made for these
services during 2000-2001.  
4.2  Last year, the Committee was informed that in order to improve out-reach service delivery system in urban slums,
Urban Revamping Scheme has been introduced which envisages re-organisation of existing Urban Family Welfare
Centres.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the progress made under this scheme. The Committee notes
that the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) has approved the extension of the VIII India Population
Project to 94 additional cities/towns in West Bengal, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh for providing Family welfare
services to the urban slums population as well as to UP and Tamil Nadu for taking up logistic projects.   The Committee
hopes that the Project  will be completed within the prescribed time  limit i.e. 30.6.2001.
V.        REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH PROGRAMME
5.1       The concept of RCH Programme is to provide need-based, client-oriented, demand-driven, high quality and
integrated RCH services to the beneficiaries.  The RCH programme is a composite programme incorporating the  inputs

8.1       The Information, Education and Communication (IEC) component of  National Family Welfare Programme is
mainly to create an effective communication strategy to inform the masses about the  means and measures of Family
Welfare programme, educate them about the perils of over population and motivate and persuade them to adopt small
family norm, using all possible channels of media.  A multi-pronged strategy to carry out IEC activities is being
implemented by the Department through respective Mass Education and media set ups created in the states and media
units of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.   The activities listed  are –
i)          RCH-IEC activities through Zila Saksharata Samitis
ii)         Mahila Swasthya Sanghs
iii)         Sensitisation of Opinion Leaders Scheme.
iv)        Preparation of IEC Print material
v)         Production of Audio-Visual Software
vi)        Intensification of IEC activities in 135 demographically weak districts etc.
 
Allocation of Rs. 30.00 crores is proposed in BE 2000-2001 for this scheme.   This is in addition to the provision made
in RCH of Rs. 130.00 crores for IEC activities.
8.2       The Committee  finds that a number of activities are being carried out for awareness generation in the masses
about Family Welfare measures. Local agencies are also being actively involved and 135 demographically weak
districts have also been specifically focussed  in this regard. There is no dearth of funds also for this purpose.   The
Committee however, fails to understand that inspite of so many measures, effect of IEC activities is still not reaching the
targetted sector.   The  Committee is of the view  that  in states where level of health and population indicators is much
below the average level, there is a need of having  area specific IEC activities.   In weak pockets and remote,
inaccessible and tribal areas of such states, intensive  campaigns in local dialect and based on local perspectives in
active cooperation with local agencies should be taken.  Mere initiation/launching of such activities would not be
sufficient. Follow up action with modifications and corrective measures as and when necessary would also be required. 
The Committee feels that in states where there is lack of initiative on the part of administration at whatever level,
Department can take steps to associate the local MPs/MLAs in the family welfare measures.   Another effective measure
can be convergence of IEC activities of all the concerned Departments at the Centre.   The Committee feels that in states
also, this kind of exercise would lead to better achievements in family welfare measures.  The Committee recommends
that the Department should take necessary measures in this regard.

XII.      NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY
12.1     The Committee notes that after many years of deliberation and consultation, the National Population Policy,
recently approved by the Cabinet, has been presented to Parliament.   The Committee has been informed that the
immediate objective of the National Population Policy is to address the unmet needs of contraception, health
infrastructure,  health personnel and to provide  integrated service delivery for basic reproductive and child health care.  
The medium term objective  is to bring the total fertility rates to replacement level by 2010 through vigorous
implementation of intersectoral operational strategies.  The long term objective is to achieve a stable population by
2045, at a level consistent with the requirement of sustainable economic growth, social development and environmental
protection.
12.2     The Committee notes that a number of new structures, i.e. National Commission on Population, State/UT
Commissions on Population, Coordination Cell within the   Planning Commission  and a Technology Mission are
proposed.   The Committee is of the view that although objectives behind these proposed structures are laudable,  states
lagging behind in the implementation of Family Welfare Programme need special focussing.  Only with the active
participation of dedicated personnel both Govt./NGOs at state and central levels,  desired goals can be achieved. Since
programme implementation vests with the state govts., considerable efforts are required to monitor and guide the
planning and implementation of the comprehensive, multi-sectoral national population policy.  The Committee would
also like to  point out that the issue of Family Planning should be given top priority as various development projects
would have no meaning in view of high rate of population growth.  The Committee strongly feels that a meeting of all
political parties should be convened by the Prime Minister to discuss this problem threadbare and arrive at a consensus.

XIV.    COMMITTED LIABILITY
14.1     The issue of committed liability has been engaging the attention of the Committee since 1997-98.  At the end of
the 8
th Five Year Plan, the Planning Commission had issued very detailed guidelines to carry forward the committed
expenditure from Plan to the non-plan side .   A lump sum provision of Rs. 500 crores in the Ministry of Finance Budget
for 1997-98 was provided for this purpose.   As a result of this exercise,  however, only a sum of Rs. 150 crores was
transferred from Plan to non-Plan for the various Ministries as committed expenditure during 1997-98.   Rest of the
amount was surrendered as the proposals were not found acceptable.   Secretary (Expenditure) while deposing before
the Committee on 27
th March, 1999 had informed that the Tenth Finance Commission had given a breathing time till
1999-2000 for this transition.
14.2     The Department has now informed that the issue of transfer of committed liabilities to non-plan was taken up
with the Ministry of Finance in 1997-98 but it was decided that no provision could be made for committed liability of
the scheme under non-plan as it was not permissible under the Planning Commission guidelines on the subject which
reads as follows :-
“The committed expenditure liability is to be borne by the Central Govt. in respect of Central Plan schemes and by the
State govts. in respect of state Plan schemes.   As regards all centrally sponsored schemes, the state govts. will provide
for the committed expenditure liability”
14.3     The Committee notes with serious concern that while grants for Plan Schemes are getting reduced, non-Plan
allocation and expenditure are steadily  increasing.   What is happening is that the committed expenditure which should
appropriately be charged to the Pool, is being passed on to the respective Departments which is totally against the
guidelines of Tenth Finance Commission/Planning Commission.  If the committed expenditure is charged to the Pool, it
will not have any burden on the specific schemes of the Department.  Secretary (Expenditure), who appeared before the
Committee last year was in full agreement with the stand taken by the Committee.   The Committee  is, however,
constrained to observe that in spite of Committee’s repeated efforts/directives to assist the Departments, no progress has
been made in the matter.   It seems that breathing time till 1999-2000 given by  the Tenth Finance Commission has not
been availed of by any Department.    There is total lack of initiative on the part of the Departments.  The Committee
again emphasises  that the Department should get this matter resolved without any further delay.   The way the 
Department including Ministry of Finance is trying to escape their responsibility is against the expressed wishes of the
Finance Commission and the recommendations made by the Committee.  This tendency, the Committee is constrained
to observe, is not in consonance with the principles which are well-established.   The Committee again reiterates that the
Department should pursue the matter and report to the Committee about the outcome thereof.

1996-97 pointed out by the Central Internal Audit increased to approximately Rs. 4255 lakhs in 1997-98.  Irregularities
were noticed under the same heads for both these years and states are also the same.   The Committee wonders how in
view of there being irregularities of such high amount, funds continued to be released in subsequent years to the states.  
Doubling of the objectionable amount is an indication that no corrective measure whatsoever was initiated.  
Irregularities like misappropriation of funds and mis-classifications of central receipts to the state heads, transfer of
amount to personal ledger account without  incurring actual expenditure and diversion of fund and staff of family
welfare programme to other state programmes are very serious and deserve drastic measures. (Para 13.2)
.           The Committee, is therefore, constrained to observe that the communications sent to the Ministries or the
Departments by the Secretariat on behalf of the Committee should be given due attention and all efforts should be made
to furnish the requisite information/ paper in Hindi version thereof to the Committee expeditiously and within the time
limit. (Para 13.3)
COMMITTED LIABILITY
            The Committee notes with serious concern that while grants for Plan Schemes are getting reduced, non-Plan
allocation and expenditure is steadily increasing.   What is happening is that the committed expenditure which should
appropriately be charged to the Pool, is being passed on to the respective Departments which is totally against the
guidelines of Tenth Finance Commission/Planning Commission.  If the committed expenditure is charged to the Pool, it
will not have any burden on the specific schemes of the Department.  Secretary (Expenditure), who appeared before the
Committee last year was in full agreement with the stand taken by the Committee.   The Committee  is, however,
constrained to observe that in spite of Committee’s repeated efforts/directives to assist the Departments, no progress has
been made in the matter.   It seems that breathing time till 1999-2000 given by  the Tenth Finance Commission has not
been availed of by any Department.    There is total lack of initiative on the part of the Departments.  The Committee
again emphasises  that the Department should get this matter resolved without any further delay.   The way the 
Department including Ministry of Finance is trying to escape their responsibility is against the expressed wishes of the
Finance Commission and the recommendations made by the Committee.  This tendency, the Committee is constrained
to observe, is not in consonance with the principles which are well-established.   The Committee again reiterates that the
Department should pursue the matter and report to the Committee about the outcome thereof. (Para 14. 3)

Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.43) of the Department of Indian Systems of Medicine
& Homoeopathy,  Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the year 2000-2001.

Systems of Medicine & Homoeopathy, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and also heard the Secretary and other
Officials of that Department  on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held on 28

REPORT
 
I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1.      The National Health Policy  of  1983 visualised the importance of Indian Systems of Medicine and
Homoeopathy and its role in the national health care system. India has  a  large resource  of ISM&H practitioners whose
services need to be fully utilised in the national health care delivery   system. The main objective of the Department   of 
Indian Systems of Medicine and  Homoeopathy (ISM&H) is to develop and promote  the  indigenous systems of
Medicine (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani,  Yoga  and  Naturopathy) and Homoeopathy  in an organised and scientific manner
in the country.
1.2       While deposing before the Committee, the Secretary stated that inspite of there being  quite a number of
hospitals and colleges of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, funding for this indigenous sector has been
extremely low.   Level of acceptance has also been very low.   The Secretary   emphasised that the main thrust of the
Department would be strengthening of educational institutions.    Another thrust area was to increase the availability  of
medicinal plants.    Other areas which need special attention are prevention of patenting of Indian Medicinal
Plants/Herbs drug standardisation, modernisation of State Pharmacies, preservation of extinct plants.  
1.3       The Committee has been informed that clinical trial of a contraceptive – Pippalyadi Yoga comprising of four
plant-based drugs conducted on 2000 women during the last three years has proved successful in  ninety per cent cases.  
At present, final trial of this contraceptive  is going on.  The Committee has been given to understand that research work
under ISMH has to undergo clinical trial which is a very cumbersome and time-consuming procedure.    There is no
other alternative as clinical material is available on a large scale only in allopathic hospitals.   The Committee is of the
opinion, that due to the prejudiced approach of allopathic doctors towards ISMH, a separate body having eminent
persons from ISMH should be set up for trying the efficacy of drugs.
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The total allocation both Plan and Non-Plan taken together, provided to the Department for the year 1999-2000
was Rs. 97.96 crores which was reduced to Rs. 93.03 crores at the RE stage.  While there was only marginal decrease in
the Non-Plan allocation at RE stage from Rs. 41.83 crores to Rs. 41.03 crores, Plan allocation was reduced to Rs. 52
crores from Rs. 56.13 crores.   The Committee notes that out of the total Plan allocation in BE 1999-2000, Rs. 49.01
crores were meant for ongoing schemes, Rs. 7.11 crores were provided for new schemes.   The Committee is perturbed
to observe, that as against a marginal reduction in the RE allocation for old schemes, provision meant for  new schemes
was drastically reduced to Rs. 3.47 crores.  What is a cause for more concern is that as per the expenditure figures
booked upto January, 2000, under-utilisation is again reflected in the provision made for new schemes.  Expenditure
reported is only Rs. 1.17 crores, less than half the reduced allocation of Rs. 3.47 crores at the RE stage.   The Committee
finds that this trend has been evident in 1997-98 and 1998-99 also.  Details of new schemes which are yet to be finalised

2.2       For the year 2000-2001, the Department has been provided Rs. 143.50 crores.  Significant increase has been
made on plan side by almost doubling the allocation of last year.  The Department has stated that   out of the Plan
Allocation of Rs. 100.00 crores for BE 2000-2001, Rs. 65.00 crores has been allocated for on-going schemes and Rs.
35.00 crores for new initiatives for quality control and standardization, for medicinal plants, and preparation of ISM&H
Drugs.  The new initiatives inter-alia  include setting up of National Board for Medicinal Plants, Innovative Scheme for
Development of Medicinal Plants and State Drug Testing Laboratory and Pharmacies etc. Welcoming  this increase, the
Committee would like to emphasise   that concerted efforts are required to be made for optimum and judicious
expenditure of allocation made for new schemes. Finalisation of new schemes which have been under formulation stage
since 1997-98/1998-99 should not be delayed any further.
2.3       Performance Budget should clearly reflect both the financial provision and corresponding physical achievements
of different schemes/programmes during the financial year.  The Committee, however, observes that Performance
Budgets of almost all the Departments are prepared in such a manner that one does not get a clear   idea in this regard. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take corrective steps in this regard, if the
Performance Budgeting is to have any meaning.
III.       AYURVEDA
3.1       The allocation for Ayurveda under Plan in BE 1999-2000 was Rs. 12.09 crores which was enhanced to Rs. 12.54
crores at RE stage.  For 2000-2001, Rs. 13.20 crores have been provided under Plan.  On a specific query as to in what
manner, the enhanced allocation was proposed to be utilised,   the Department submitted that the increase in plan
provision in BE 2000-2001 for Ayurveda is mainly to meet increased liability of salary, NPA and capital expenditure for
construction.
3.2       The Committee was informed that there were 13 posts lying vacant in the National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur
for which advertisements have been given in the newspapers. The Committee notes that out of 79 teaching posts in the
Institute, 66 have been filled.   Although considerable improvement has taken place when compared to the situation few

91st Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/91streport.htm[01-07-2016 15:12:10]
years ago, the Committee is of the view that sustained efforts should be made to expedite the filling up of these 13
teaching posts.
3.3       Last year, the Committee had recommended that an action plan should be drawn for popularising the Ayurvedic
system of treatment in and outside India.  The Department has informed that an International Exchange Programme to
propagate ISMH abroad has been launched under which financial assistance is given for the exchange of
delegations/experts with other countries, setting up the Ayurveda & Siddha or Yoga Therapy centres for demonstration
purpose in foreign countries and organising International Conferences/National   Conferences and Seminars. The
Committee would like to emphasise that only established professionals of ISM&H should be covered under this
programme.  The Department has signed MOU with the Govt. of Russia for collaboration in the field of traditional
medicine.   MOUs with other countries are also planned. The Committee hopes  that the Department would continue
making efforts in this direction.  The Committee was also informed that the Department was  exploring the possibility of
setting up   Health Resorts in conjunction with ITDC to attract foreign tourists.  Govt. of Himachal Pradesh has shown
some interest in a  project for using existing built-up capacity in their hotels for arranging  Panchkarma treatment for
foreign tourists. The Committee hopes that there  would be more initiatives of this kind. 
3.4       The Committee notes that a number of measures have been taken by the Department for preventing misleading
advertisements regarding Ayurvedic medicines.  There is a proposal to amend the Drugs & Magic Remedies
(Objectionable Advertisement) Act to make it more effective and a Committee appointed for the purpose has submitted
its recommendations which are at present under the examination of  the Department of Health. While appreciating the
move, the Committee is of the view that the Department of ISMH should be fully  involved in the process of amending
the Act.
3.5       The Department has informed that   160 misleading advertisments have  been forwarded to various State
Governments.  6 Advertisements were forwarded to ‘Arogya Dham’ and 7 to ‘Nav Bharat Times’ as these appeared in
these magazines/ newspaper. However, no feedback from the States has so far been received. The Committee finds that
out of 160 misleading advertisements, maximum number  of advertisements are reported to be from Uttar Pradesh ,
Madhya Pradesh and Delhi.   The Committee recommends that the Department should  intensify its efforts and if
necessary, intervention at the higher level in the State Govt. be made.  The Committee is of the view that in the event of
any misleading advertisement appearing in a magazine/newspaper, contradiction by the Department should invariably
follow.
3.6       The Committee is perturbed   to note that due support to individual practitioners   is not there as, at present,
financial assistance  is being provided by the Department to Govt. Organisations and NGOs only due to limited
resources. The Committee, however, feels that  there is a genuine need for providing support to individual practitioners
doing good work for  the growth of Ayurveda or  ISM, as a whole. Department should make all efforts  to convince the
Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance to get the funds allocated for the purpose.
3.7       The Committee observes that    there   was a nominal provision  of Rs. 1 lakh as Grant-in-aid for Advanced
Ayurveda Centre for Mental Health in  NIMHANS in BE 1997-98.   However, allocation was increased to Rs. 25 lakhs
at the RE stage which was fully utilised.  In 1998-99 also, allocation of Rs. 20 lakhs was fully utilised.   However, the
Committee is surprised to note that provision of Rs. 20 lakhs in 1999-2000 had to be reduced to Rs. 1 lakh as the issue
of sharing of project cost between the Department of Health and the Department of ISMH is pending, hence, no further
grants were required to be released.    The Committee is not convinced by the explanation given by the Department and
expresses its serious concern over such an element of uncertainty in starting a new Scheme.    The Committee, therefore,
is of the view that decision in the matter  should be taken at the earliest.
3.8       The Committee observes that the Siddha System is not getting proper attention by the Department.    The
Committee notes that there has been inordinate delay in the construction of building for the  National Institute of
Siddha, Chennai.  Funds are being allocated since 1997-98 for construction.  During the year 1999-2000, construction of
boundary wall was proposed and draft project report for construction of the building   is still under consideration.    The
Committee desires that the construction of the building be initiated at the earliest.           The Committee observes that so
far Siddha System has not gained popularity specially in northern part of the country.   The Committee desires that
suitable steps  for propagation of Siddha System be taken.    Measures taken in this regard may include inter-alia
strengthening of the existing units of the Siddha system in northern parts of the country.  
IV.       UNANI

4.1       Allocation for ‘Unani’ under Plan for 2000-2001 is Rs. 10.50 crores as compared to Rs. 8.55 crores provided in
BE 1999-2000.  According to the Department, the increase is mainly due to increase in plan allocation for the  National
Institute of Unani Medicine, Bangalore from Rs. 1.21 crores in 1999-2000 to Rs. 3.50 crores in 2000-2001 for
construction of the first phase of the building for hospital, administrative block and hostel accommodation etc. of the
Institute.
4.2       Last year, the Committee had observed that the procedural requirements should be expedited so that construction
work of the main building of National Institute of Unani Medicine, Bangalore is started without any further delay.    The
Department has informed that the project has been approved by EFC on 28.6.99 and  efforts were being made to
accelerate the construction work of NIUM, Bangalore.    The Committee, however, is perturbed to note that against an
allocation of Rs. 1.21 crores for the purpose in 1999-2000, no expenditure has been reported upto January, 2000.   The
only progress made in 1999-2000 is that the Hospital  Services Consultancy Corporation   has been awarded contract for
construction of the building complex of the Institute.   The Committee hopes that the construction work would be started
in 2000-2001.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the latest position.
4.3       It has been informed that although estimate for construction of RRIUM, Srinagar has been approved by the
Executive Board of CCRUM, another place in Nasimbagh for construction of RRIUM, Srinagar has been suggested by
the University of Kashmir.  In the case of RRIUM, Karimganj, the land has been taken over from the Government of
Assam and required estimates for construction have been called for.  With regard to CRIUM, Hyderabad, modifications
recommended by the SFC of the Council are under active consideration.
4.4       The Committee is not happy with the situation.   Since several years, the Committee has noted, that the work of
these institutions is being delayed on one or another plea/suggestion/modification.  It seems that no corrective measure
has been taken so far. The Committee would like to impress upon the Department that requisite formalities should be
completed expeditiously so that work relating to construction of buildings for  all these Institutes is started at the
earliest.     
V.        HOMOEOPATHY
5.1       For Homoeopathy, the plan provision was Rs. 6.27 crores in BE 1999-2000 which was increased to  Rs. 6.95
crores at RE stage.  It has been substantially increased to the level of Rs. 8.20 crores in BE 2000-2001. The Department
has informed that the enhanced allocation in BE 2000-2001 is proposed to be used for salary, NPA, stipend for students,
maintenance of institutes and capital expenditure in the National Institute of Homoeopathy.
5.2       The Committee is happy to note that the Postgraduate Course in Homoeopathy has been introduced in the 
National Institute of Homoeopathy, Calcutta during the academic year 1998-99 in three subjects.  Last year, the
Committee was given to understand that the increase in the bed capacity for in-patient department of NIH, Calcutta was
linked  up wth the  introduction of the post-graduate course in Homeopathy.   The Committee hopes that necessary 
action in this regard would also be taken  during 2000-2001.  The Committee would like to be apprised in this regard.
VI.       YOGA AND NATUROPATHY
6.1       For Yoga and Naturopathy, the BE for 1999-2000 on the plan side was Rs. 6.20 crores, which was reduced to
Rs. 5.83 crores at the RE stage.  Allocation for the year 2000-2001 has been brought back to the level of BE of last year
i.e. Rs. 6.20 crores.   According to the Department, the allocation of Rs. 6.20 crores would be adequate for the Central
Council for Research in Yoga and Naturopathy (CCRYN), Morarji Desai National Institute of Yoga and the National
Institute of Naturopathy (NIN).
6.2       The Committee has been informed that the Planning Commission has not supported the establishment of a
separate campus comprising of a Degree College of Yoga with an attached hospital to MDNIY, New Delhi and NIN,
Pune.   The Committee   notes that the main reason given by the Planning Commission for not supporting these
proposals is that the Central Government should not set up its own Degree or PG Courses or hospitals.  If the demand
for such courses emerge, institutions should be set up by the State Government within the State Plan as Health is
basically a State Subject.   Central Government's role should only be to provide guidance, create standards undertake
research and form linkages.  The  Committee is of the view that this matter should again be taken up with the Planning
Commission.
VII.      MEDICAL EDUCATION
7.1       At present, there are 311 Undergraduate and 47 Postgraduate ISM&H colleges in the country.  However,

91st Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/91streport.htm[01-07-2016 15:12:10]
standard of education in some of the institutions is far from satisfactory and they are nowhere near the norms fixed by
Statutory Bodies. According to the Department, during the year 1998-99, 126 Ayurveda, 29 Unani and 2 Siddha
Colleges/institutions were visited   for assessing the standard of education in conformity with the minimum standards
and requirements prescribed /laid down by  the Central Council of Indian Medicine (CCIM). During 1999-2000, 125
Ayurveda and 27 Unani colleges have been visited upto 30.10.99.   81 Homoeopathic colleges were visited by the
Central Council of Homoeopathy (CCH) upto Nov.,99 during 1999-2000.  Shortcomings pointed by the
visitors/committee have been communicated to the authorities of the Colleges, Universities and State Governments for
their removal.
7.2       The Committee has  been informed that the  norms for starting new ISM College and to prescribe phase-wise
requirement in term of infrastructure, staff, hospital requirement etc. drafted by CCIM were examined by the Ministry. 
The Council has been advised to reconcile the ambiguities   and a  revised draft is awaited from them.  In regard to the
Homoeopathic education, the Minimum Standards Education Regulation, 1983 is in the process of being amended.   The
Committee notes that ten new colleges have been permitted for Ayurvedacharya and one for the Kamil-e-lib-o-Jarahat
course of Unani respectively during 1999-2000.  Similarly, ten new colleges  have been allowed to start admission in
First BHMS Direct Degree Course subject to certain conditions during 1999-2000.
7.3       Regarding para-medical education in pharmacy and Nursing, the Department informed the Committee that they
have incorporated the pharmacy education as an add-on component.   However, the component of nursing education as
an add-on component could not be approved.  The matter relating to the establishment of Pharmacy Council of India
and Nursing Council of India were still under consideration in the Department.   When asked for the reason for not
approving nursing as an add-on component, the Department submitted that the nursing is not a statutory function and the
nurses trained in the modern nursing could also be deployed for working as nurse in ISM&H health care
institutions/units.  However, pharmacists are very essential category required also to discharge statutory functions and
dispensing of drugs.  Therefore, pharmacy was included as an add-on component.
7.4       Last year the Committee was informed that setting up of a regulatory body for education in Yoga and
Naturopathy was under the active examination of the Department.   The Committee finds that it has not been possible as
yet to give practical shape to this proposal.  The All India Council for Technical Education  (AICTE) has been requested
to take up the work relating to regulation of Yoga and Naturopathy   Education.   Besides, guidelines have also been
issued to  all States/UTs for regulating education in Yoga and Naturopathy.   States have been advised  to set up their
own Board of Accreditation/Body for regulating education in Yoga and Naturopathy.  Once the States set  up their own
bodies, the Central Government will set up a suitable apex body at the central level to regulate education  in Yoga and
Naturopathy at Central level, it has been informed.    The Committee is constrained to observe that response from
AICTE is still awaited.  The Committee feels that while emphasizing for establishment of suitable   body at States level,
the Department should not wait for completion of this work and it should initiate action to set up a regulatory body at
central level. 
7.5       Regarding need to check huge amounts of donation/capitation fee being taken by some colleges under ISM&H,
it was informed the draft regulations in the matter prepared by CCIM were under consideration of the Department.    In
the case of Homoeopathy colleges, a draft regulation has already been circulated to the State Govts.   However, only a
few states have so far responded.   The Committee is of the view that finalisation of fee structure for ISMH should be
expedited so that exploitation of students by private colleges is put to an end.
VIII.     QUALITY CONTROL OF DRUGS
8.1       The Committee was informed that laying down the pharmacopoeial standards and quality control of ISM&H
drugs, is one of the priority areas of the Department. The proposal to strengthen the two national level laboratories,
namely, Pharmacopeial Laboratory for Indian Medicine (PLIM) and Homoeopathic Pharmacopeial Laboratory   (HPL),
Ghaziabad, has been approved by the EFC recently and the necessary follow up action has been initiated.   Besides this,
32 laboratories have been given financial assistance to develop pharmaceutical standards. State Governments of A.P.,
Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, U.P. Orissa, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan have also shown interest in setting
up State Drug Testing laboratories for ISM&H.   An initiative   to frame a scheme for setting up of State Drug Testing
laboratories for ISM&H as a centrally sponsored scheme has also been taken. The Committee feels, despite afore-
mentioned measures  taken by the Department, there is still need for improvement in this sensitive area.
8.2       The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Department to the functioning of PLIM and HPL.  The
main objectives of   both these Labs are to lay down the pharmacopoeial standards for single drugs and compound

            The efficacy of  most of the ISMH drugs is dependent upon the use of pure and genuine raw material obtained
from medicinal plants.  However, due to over exploitation, unscrupulous collection and denuding of forests, supplies
have been dwindling.   The Department informed the Committee that it has initiated various steps to enhance the supply

results.  The Department further informed that it has taken initiative to set up a National Board on Medicinal Plants as a
statutory body.  The Committee would like to impress upon that the proposal be actively pursued and the Board be set
up during the current year. The Committee has also noted that the Planning Commission has set up a Task force on
conservation, cultivation, sustainable use and legal protection of medicinal plants.  The Task Force has set up a ‘Core
Group’ to conduct a study of demand and supply position of medicinal plants in the country and  export.  The
Committee was informed that there is no authentic data on the demand, consumption and availability of medicinal
plants material and for this purpose the Department propose to undertake a separate study at national level .  The
Committee feels that this kind of study can be entrusted to the proposed National Board of Medicinal Plants. 
X.        INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS
10.1     The Department informed the Committee that a major area of concern is the keen interest being taken by  foreign
countries in the development of herbal products and intellectual property rights.  Some of the well known medicinal
plants of India have been patented abroad and heritage of Ayurveda needs to be protected. In order to put a check on
these attempts, a Patent Cell was  set up in the Department.   The Task Force of the Planning Commission decided to set
up a `Core Group’ for consolidation of information on the botanical and the medicinal use of plants referred to in the
Ancient Texts.  The objective is to place this in the public domain- a  pre-requisite to prevent patenting of plant based
medicinal plants.   The Committee has also noted that necessary steps on creating Traditional Knowledge Digital
Library (TKDL)  to prevent the patenting of documented knowledge of ISM has been initiated. The Department has
already taken up the matter in conjunction with the Department of Industry, NIC, CSIR, ICAR and a core group has
been set up for this purpose.  
10.2     The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the Patent Cell is still functioning with inadequate
manpower and many posts are lying vacant.    The Committee has been informed that the Department’s efforts to create

It has been informed that the Department has evolved an Information, Education and Communication (IEC)
Scheme with the objective to create awareness about the efficiency of various pathies under ISM&H, their cost
effectiveness, treatment of common ailments etc. by using various media channels.  For this purpose, the Department
organises seminars and workshops, training programme at various levels for involving various health functionaries and
also uses Doordarshan and All India Radio to spread information. The Committee hopes that various IEC activities
undertaken by the Department would result in giving wider publicity to ISM&H.
XII.      COMMITTED LIABILITY
12.1     The issue of Committed Liability has been engaging the attention of the Committee since 1997-98.  At the end
of the Eight Five Year Plan, the Planning Commission had issued very detailed guidelines to carry forward the
Committed Expenditure from Plan to the Non-Plan side.  A lump sum provision of Rs. 500 crores in the Ministry of
Finance Budget for 1997-98 was provided for this purpose.  As a result of this exercise, however, only a sum of Rs.150
crores was transferred from Plan to Non-Plan for the various Ministries as committed expenditure during 1997-98.  Rest
of the amount was surrendered as the proposals were not found acceptable.  The Secretary (Expenditure) while deposing
before the Committee on 27
th March, 1999 had informed that the Tenth Finance Commission had given a breathing time
till 1999-2000 for this transition.
12.2     The Department has  informed that the Planning Commission had mentioned that the outlay for the Department
had been increased from Rs.108 cores in the Eighth Plan to Rs.266.35 crores in the Ninth Plan and the outlay for Annual
Plan 1997-98 was Rs.35.30 crores which was increased to Rs. 50.00 crores in 1998-99 and Rs.59.13 crores in 1999-
2000. According to the Planning Commission the Ninth Plan outlay included provision for such incremental liabilities.
12.3     The Committee notes with serious concern that while grants for Plan Schemes are getting reduced, Non-Plan
allocation and expenditure is steadily increasing.  What is happening is that the committed expenditure which should
appropriately be charged to the Pool, is being passed on to the respective departments which is totally against the
guidelines of Tenth Finance Commission/Planning Commission.  If the committed expenditure is charged to the Pool, it
will not have any burden on the specific schemes of the Department. Secretary (Expenditure), who appeared before the
Committee last year was in full agreement   with the stand taken by the Committee.   The Committee is, however,
constrained to observe that in spite of Committee’s repeated efforts/directives to assist the Departments, no progress has
been made in the matter.   It seems that breathing time till 1999-2000 given by the Tenth Finance Commission has not
been availed of by any Department.   There is total lack of initiative on the part of the Departments.   The Committee
again  emphasises that the Department should get this matter resolved without any further delay.   The way the
Department including Ministry of Finance is trying to escape their responsibility is against the expressed wishes of the
Finance Commission and the recommendations made by the Committee.   This tendency, the Committee is constrained
to observe, is not in consonance with the principles which are well-established.   The Committee again reiterates that the
Department should pursue the matter and report to the Committee about the outcome thereof.
