GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
III.            Maintenance of Enrolment,  Progression and Retention Registers.
Observation of the Committee
3.1        The Committee during its visits noticed that except the schools being run by the Shiksha Karmi and Lok Jumbish
Projects in Rajasthan, and in some parts of Assam no other schools of the State Governments are maintaining the Enrolment,
Retention and Progression Registers to monitor the drop-outs rates in the primary and upper primary schools.   The Committee
finds that no corrective action has been taken by the concerned State Governments.   The Committee expresses its serious
concern over this state of affairs.
Comments of the Department

107th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/107threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:18]
All the States and UTs, whose response has been received, endorse the recommendation of the Committee regarding
maintenance of Enrolment, Retention and Progression Registers by the Village Education Committees.
 Observation of the Committee
3.2        The Committee has noticed that in the past the emphasis has been only on enrolment due to which large number of
fictitious enrolment figures in Class I were noticed.   These fictitious figures of enrolment not only affect the policy making but
also make it extremely difficult to estimate the correct drop-out rates.   The Committee has seen that the data available in the
official documents appears to have been given only as estimated data because whatever data procured during the field level
visits was found contrary to the data available in the official documents.
Comments of the Department
            States, mostly agree with the assessment of the Parliamentary Standing Committee.
Observation of the Committee
            The Committee feels that there is a need to convince the administrators and teachers about the need for correct enrolment
figures.   Guidelines  should be issued for regular monitoring of absent students and planned efforts should be made to ensure
continued participation of every child in the schools to prevent drop-out.   The Committee recommends that the task of
monitoring the Enrolment, Retention and Progression Registers should be assigned to the Village Level Education Committee
Comments of the Department
3.3        All States/UTs which have responded agree with the recommendation of the Parliamentary Standing Committee.  In
DPEP, an Educational  Management Information System (EMIS) to computerize educational data has been developed.   The
need for improved data quality and cross checking has been stressed.
On a specific query by the Committee about steps taken by the Department for improving the quality of data, the
Department informed that a Committee on Educational Statistics has been constituted.   Provision for establishment of
Education MIS is part of the proposals for preparatory  activities under the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan.   Besides that, 219 DPEP
districts have established effective EMIS and the data is regularly analysed.   For example, in Tamil Nadu, previous year’s data
is being maintained school wise by the Block Education Officer and the data contained in the Data Capture  Format (DCF) is
duly certified/authenticated by him.   Similarly, in Orissa, Karnataka and Kerala, the data is crosschecked by Cluster Resource
Centre Co-ordinator  (RCC).
Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee takes note of the various measures initiated by the Department for improving the quality  of data with
respect to maintenance of Enrolment, Progression and Retention Registers for monitoring the drop-out rate in primary and upper
primary schools.   The Committee hopes that all these measures would result in increased enrolment and retention of students.   
The Committee, however, is of the view that alongwith computerized data, field level visits both at regular intervals and without
prior notice should also continue.   The Committee notes that its recommendation regarding maintenance  of Enrolment,
Retention and Progress Registers by the Village Education Committees has been endorsed by all the States and UTs.  and hopes
that the same will be implemented at the earliest.
IV.            Opening of More Primary and Upper Primary Schools
Observation of the Committee
4.1        The scheme of `Operation Blackboard’ was launched in 1987 with the objective to bring about both qualitative and
quantitative improvement in primary education.   Central Government has extended financial assistance to the extent of Rs.
1551.68 crores from  1987-88 till 31st March, 1995.   However, till 31st March, 1995 only 81%  of the total Central funds i.e. Rs.
1253.09 crores  could be utilized by the States.
Comments of the Department
            Some States have reported higher utilization.   Others have mentioned that funds released in the last financial year would
be utilized  shortly.
            When specifically asked to clarify  the present position of utilisation of funds by the States,  the Department informed
that under the scheme of Operation Blackboard (OB), Central Govt. has extended financial assistance to the extent of Rs.
2617.26 crores from 1987-88 till 31 st March, 2000.  The utilization percentage of the funds sanctioned for teaching learning
equipment and salaries of teachers appointed under OB is 86.29%.   Thus, there is an improvement of over 5%.  Most of the
unutilized funds are for procurement of TLE which involves various procedures such as identifying material, advertising,

107th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/107threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:18]
inviting and processing tender, executing agreement etc.  In order to further accelerate the pace of utilization, the State Govts.
have been asked to decentralize procurement of TLE.
Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee expresses its grave concern over non-utilisation of around 14% of the financial assistance under
Operation Blackboard given to the States by the Centre.  Basic infrastructure in most of the schools in the country is still lacking
and there is  greater demand for quantitative as well as qualitative improvements in elementary education.   In this context, a
mere request to States to decentralize procurement of Teaching Learning Equipment may not be enough.   The Committee,
therefore,  recommends that Ministry may thoroughly look into this issue and take suitable remedial measures for full and
proper utilisation of Central funds.
Observation of the Committee
4.2        Even after a decade of the launching of Operation Blackboard, the Committee finds that so far as basic infrastructure is
concerned, it cannot be said that all the primary schools all over the country are fully provided for.   The Schools visited by the
Committee during its study tours were selected in advance by the State Governments.   So, they cannot be said to be true
reflection of the physical state of primary schools.  Even then the Committee is constrained to state that these  pre-arranged
schools were also lacking in basic facilities.   No doubt, by and large, school buildings were there and in some cases extensions
were also being carried on.   But these were insufficient to the needs of school-going children.   Drinking water and toilet
facilities were also inadequate.   In some of the schools, which the Committee visited, the students were being made to sit on
bare floor.   The Committee also observed that in majority of primary schools, two or three classes were being held in one room
under the supervision of only one teacher.   The Committee feels that this state of affairs is responsible, to some extent, for  non-
retention of children in schools.  Urgent steps, therefore, need to be taken for creating facilities so that every class has its
separate room.   The Committee during its visits noticed that due to non-availability of infrastructure and lack of schools, very
large number of children, perhaps 20%, do not have access to school.   The problem is particularly more grave at the upper
primary stage from class VI to VIII specially in the case of girls.   On ascertaining the reasons for not opening new schools, the
Committee was informed that the rigid norms for opening new schools  and increase in the population of the State are the main
barrier, resulting in more out-of- school children.
Comments of the Department
            While there has been progress in provision of school facilities under Operation Blackboard, the assessment of the
Parliamentary Standing Committee is very correct that much more needs to be done in order to provide basic infrastructure for
all children.   The States and UTs  have indicated the efforts being made by them.   Govt. of Maharashtra has pointed out that
inspite of maximum allocation of funds for construction of classrooms, there is still a need to construct about 52000 classrooms
in that State.   It has suggested that Govt. of India sanction 100% grants for construction of school rooms under JRY under the
revised guidelines for Jawahar Gram Samriddhi Yojana.   From the saving under the Yojana, school buildings can be
constructed on 75-25 sharing (Centre-State).  Besides funds under Ministry of Rural Development, construction of classrooms is
also taking place under the District Primary Education Programme and Lok Jumbish Project.  Govt. of Gujarat has liberalized
the norms for upgrading lower primary schools to upper primary schools and 4200 lower  primary schools are being upgraded
this year.   Andman and Nicobar has no rigid norm for opening schools.  The statement showing the funds released since
inception uptill 1999-2000 under Jawahar Rozgar Yojana/ Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana, for construction of school buildings
under Operation Black Board (OB) is at Annexure-I.   As per the information available, 1,82,381 classrooms have been
constructed under the scheme by 31.3.2000.
            It was clarified by the Department that funds are released for construction of school buildings under Operation
Blackboard (OB) out of saving, if any, from Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana/JRY.   Rural Development Department of the State
Govt. co-ordinates with the State Education Department for submission of proposal under OB.   The funding pattern under the
scheme is 75:25 between the Centre and the State Rural Development Departments.   The Funds under the scheme are to be
released directly to the DRDAS/ZPs.
Recommendations of the Committee
The Committee notes that an amount of Rs. 35,366.53 lakhs has been released to various States during the period 1990-
2000 and 1,82,381 classrooms have been constructed upto 31.3.2000.  States like Orissa, A.P., Assam, Karnataka and  M.P.
have been the major beneficiaries.   However, no release could be made under GSY/JRY to Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, U.P. West
Bengal after 1992-93, in case of Goa only once in 1992-93, only in 1991-92 in respect of Meghalaya and in respect of
Pondicherry  only in 1990-91.   The Committee also notes that Bihar could not take the benefit of the scheme as apparently there
was no saving under JRY/GSY.   The Committee feels that some alternative source of funding has to be provided keeping in
view the financial position of the States.

Observation of the Committee
6.4        The Committee is of the considered view that the working environment and workload of teachers,  particularly those
working in rural primary schools, are far from satisfactory and contribute, to a large extent, to lack of motivation on their part.   
Following factors can be cited as responsible for this situation:-
(a)            Schools without adequate buildings and devoid of essential facilities;
(b)            Lack of teaching aids and libraries;
(c)            Heavy curriculum and workload, particularly for rural primary teachers;
(d)
               Multi grade teaching responsibilities without adequate supervisory support;
(e)            Commuting from long distances;
(f)            Lack of proper housing facilities;
(g)                Non-instructuctional and administrative duties such as supervising elections, participating in census operations,
conducting family planning activities etc., producing adverse impact on the main task of teaching.
Comments of the Department
            The States are in agreement with the findings of the Committee.   They are making all efforts to improve the motivation
of teachers.   Motivational training is also imparted to teachers in DPEP in some States.   In addition, through the 24% allocation
of funds for civil works in DPEP, provision of school infrastructure has considerably improved.
Observation of the Committee
6.5        The Committee feels that State Governments should initiate immediate action so as to bring about overall improvement
in the working conditions of teachers.
Comments of the Department
            States are making efforts in this direction.   The Central Government has also issued instructions to states regarding
allowing teachers to carry out their primary task.   Govt. of Gujarat has issued instructions to review non-teaching load of
primary school teachers.
Recommendation of  the Committee
            The Committee has been informed that State Governments are making all efforts to improve the motivation of teachers
and the Central Government has also issued necessary instructions to the State Governments in this regard.   The Committee is
not able to understand as to how the State Governments are going to improve the motivation of teachers and also lessen their
(Teachers’) extra workload to enable them to concentrate on their primary duty of teaching.    It has also been stated that
motivational training is imparted to teachers in DPEP in some States.  The Committee does not feel convinced with this as it is
aware that coverage of DPEP is still very less as a large part of the country still  remains uncovered.   The Committee is
therefore, of the view that the Department needs to address this issue with all seriousness as motivation of teachers is very
important. 
VII.           Change in Examination System
Observation of the Committee
7.1      The Committee finds that in many States students even in primary classes are promoted to the next class only on the
result of the annual examination.   This indirectly acts as a demotivating factor so far as retention of children in schools is
concerned.  There are  a couple of States viz.   Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal where there is no examination system upto the
level of Classes V and VI.   Students are being promoted only on the basis of attendance.
7.2      The Committee, however, recommends that annual examination system as the criteria for promotion to the next class
should continue.
Comments of the Department
           Many states hold annual examination, though promotion to the next class does not necessarily depend on it.   Promotion
is both on the basis of attendance and examination. Regarding annual examination for promoting students to the higher class 
and on the policy of detention, different States follow different criteria and policy. 
Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee has been informed that different States follow different criteria for promotion to higher class and
detention of the students.   The  Committee feels that it would be better if a uniform policy of promotion and detention is
followed by all the States, taking into consideration all related aspects.   The Committee hopes that the Department would take

initiative in this regard.
IX       Non-Formal Education Programme/Prehar Pathshala as a Backup Method
Observation of the Committee
9.1      Out of school children are being taken care of under the Non-Formal Education Scheme since 1979.   Almost all the
States are running NFE centres.   NGOs are also contributing a lot in this field.   However, even after two decades, the NFE
scheme could not achieve the desired target to bring back the non-formal students to the mainstream education.   There are a
varied number of factors responsible for it.    Poor infrastructure, lack of motivated and trained instructors, very low
honorarium for instructor, lack of community participation, no linkage between Formal and Non-Formal System of education,
NFE being treated as second grade education can be cited as the major reasons for NFE Scheme’s failure.
9.2      The Committee is of the considered view that revamping of entire NFE Scheme with special emphasis on the following
points is urgently required:-
a)
         Creation of Basic facilities at NFE Centres.
b)         Increase in honorarium for instructors.
c)         Involvement of community and  PRIs.
d)         Training of Instructors.
e)         Mechanism for effective supervision and monitoring of NFE Scheme.
Comments of the Department
            The revised scheme of NFE called Alternative and Innovative Education, is in the process of approval.   It has taken into
account the issues suggested by the Parliamentary Standing Committee.   The new scheme is based on different existing,
successful, replicable NFE models in the country.
            Under the revised scheme,
(i)         NFE and the formal system are to be dovetailed into one at the district level where a detailed school mapping
exercise will be undertaken to locate precisely the un served habitations and educationally less privileged areas.
(ii)        Both the community and the PRIs will be actively involved in sharing responsibilities.   They will create the
demand, identify teachers where necessary and provide learning space where required;
(iii)       Honoraria for instructors have been increased five fold.  All costing patterns have been made more realistic;
(iv)       Adequate training and supervision are built in.  The states are free to choose from a set of options.   Non-
academic monitoring and supervision can even be given to the PRIs (as has been done with the Education
Guarantee Scheme in Madhya Pradesh).  Regular training will be organized through the CRCs, BRCs and
DIETs.
             The Department was requested to clarify as to whether NFE under the revised scheme of Alternative and Innovative
Education will be able to provide recognition to non-formal education at  par with the formal education.  The Department
informed that the revised scheme aimed to provide education of a quality comparable /equivalent to the formal schools.   Several
inputs have been included in the scheme that would ensure quality including a minimum duration of 4 hours for the central
school, at least 30 days training for the volunteer teacher before the opening of the centre, regular academic support, 2 days
monthly review and planning meeting etc.
  Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee notes that the Alternative and Innovative Education Scheme has received Cabinet approval and
modalities  for its  implementation are being finalized in consultation with the State Governments.   The Committee is of the
view that   a consensus on operationalisation of the scheme in various states should  be arrived at without further loss of time,  
so that the scheme is implemented, as considerable time has already been taken in clearance  of the scheme.
XI.            Establishment of Residential Primary Schools for children of Construction Workers and Migratory
Population.
Observation of the Committee
11.1      The Committee during the visits has observed that in many states large number of Nomadic Tribe, construction and
agricultural workers move from one place to another due to the very nature of their profession and also in search of work.  
Because of their frequent mobilization, their children suffer a lot in the field of education due to which they are either not
admitted in school or if in case, children are admitted in school, the drop-out rates are very high amongst such children.

107th Report

11.2      The Committee understands that  a scheme for Residential Upper primary/Secondary Schools in Rural Areas already
exists.   Government should take effective steps to implement the same without further delay.   Besides that, NGOs can be
effectively involved in the task of motivating migratory labour  in sending their children to the nearby schools.
Comments of the Department
            There was a proposal to set up Residential Primary/Upper Primary Schools.   Planning Commission was of the view that
the primary school going age is a tender age where residential schools should be avoided as children need to be with their
parents.   In the light of these comments, the proposal was not pursued.
Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee still holds the view that the children of the nomadic tribes, shifting cultivators and construction workers
are the most vulnerable groups of school drop-outs.   Therefore, there should be sufficient motivation for these target groups.  
XVI.            Continuation of Plan Projects
Observation of the Committee
            The  Committee was given to understand by Secretaries of the State Governments during the discussions that many
schemes which were introduced during the Plan period were not continued in the next Plan due to which the State Governments
had to face a lot of problems to continue that project because of non-availability of funds.   The State Governments were of the
opinion that before discontinuing any scheme in the next Plan period the viability of the existing schemes should be reviewed
and they should be carried forward on merit basis.   The Committee recommends that view-point of the State Governments may
be examined by the Centre.
Comments  of the Department
            This  has been taken up with the Planning Commission in the specific context of support for teachers’ salaries under the
Operation Blackboard.  The Committee was given to understand that the Planning Commission, however, did not support the
proposal for providing support to the payment of teachers’ salaries irrespective  of the plan proposal on the ground that State
Govt. should appoint teachers at the beginning of the Plan so that they may fully avail the provisions of salary payments for five
years.  The Department has requested the Planning Commission to reconsider its decision.  In the light of the problem faced by
States , the SSA has proposed a long term financial partnership with States.
Recommendation of the Committee
            The Committee notes that a long term financial partnership with States has been envisaged under Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan.   The Committee hopes that this provision would prove to be of much assistance to State Governments in
implementing the various components of  Sarva Shiksha  Abhiyan thereby resulting in maximum coverage of children under
elementary education.
XVII.            Community Involvement
Observation  of the Committee
17.2      The Committee feels that there is a need for formation of Village Core Teams to mobilize the people which will
ultimately form the Village Education Committee.   The Committee understands that Panchayati Raj  Institutions have been
given sufficient powers by 73 rd and 74 th Constitutional Amendments to have an effective say in the functioning of schools in
their area.   But, so far, this has been only on paper.   State Governments have still to show their willingness to implement these
Constitutional amendments by handing over all the powers and required funds as envisaged.  In West Bengal and Andhra
Pradesh, the Committee during its visit noticed that these Panchayati Raj Institutions are discharging a pivotal role in the rural
economy and also in spreading education.  The Committee hopes that in  the very near future, scenario in the field of elementary
education would definitely change in the light of all the Constitutional amendments made.   The Committee, however, urges
upon the Department of Education to call a meeting of the Education Ministries of all the State Governments to work out
modalities to provide a legal Status to the Panchayati Raj Institutions in the regard.
Comments of the Department
-        V.E.Cs have been constituted in all DPEP districts and have been involved in several aspects of DPEP interventions
such as:
-                VEC school improvement grant;
-                Mircoplanning
-                School Mapping
-                Advocacy and environment building for enrolment.

            On a specific query about the suggestion of the Committee for calling a  meeting of State Ministers, the Department
replied that no meeting of Education Ministers has been held since the receipt of the Report of the Committee.  The matter will
be discussed in the next meeting.  However, the issue relating to transfer of Management of Elementary Education to PRIs has
been discussed by the National Committee of State Education Ministers set up under the Chairmanship of HRM to develop
structure and outlines for implementing universal elementary education in a mission mode.  The Committee held two meetings
on 11.2.99 and 6.3.99 and submitted its report in October 1999.
            The Committee, inter-alia, recommended that within the framework of Panchayati Raj as recommended by the CABE
Committee on Decentralised Management of Education, efforts should be made to  strengthen the trend towards transfer of
elementary educational institutions to the control of PRIs.  The district elementary education plan should be derived from the
village plans drawn up jointly by the VECs, PTAs and teachers.
Based on the report of this Committee, this Ministry has formulated the Programme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan with a
holistic and convergent approach.  This Programme also incorporates the recommendation of the CABE Committee on
Decentralised Management of Education, it was clarified.
 All State Governments  were urged by the Department to implement the recommendation of the CABE Committee. 
Fifteen States and four UTs have taken action to decentralise management of education as per the  recommendations of the
CABE Committee on Decentralised Management of Education.
Recommendation of the Committee
            In the 71 st Report of the Committee on the Problem of Drops outs, the Committee had suggested for a meeting of the
Education Ministers of all State Governments to work out modalities to provide legal status to the Panchayati Raj Institutions.  
However, no such meeting in this regard has taken place till now.   The Committee in this respect again reiterates that a meeting
of the Education Ministers of all States should be convened to discuss this issue.
 
CHAPTER-IV
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH
FINAL REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT ARE STILL AWAITED.
NIL
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
MAINTENANCE OF ENROLMENT,  PROGRESSION AND RETENTION REGISTERS
            The Committee takes note of the various measures initiated by the Department for improving the quality  of data with
respect to maintenance of Enrolment, Progression and Retention Registers for monitoring the drop-out rate in primary and upper
primary schools.   The Committee hopes that all these measures would result in increased enrolment and retention of students.   
The Committee, however, is of the view that alongwith computerized data, field level visits both at regular intervals and without
prior notice should also continue.   The Committee notes that its recommendation regarding maintenance  of Enrolment,
Retention and Progress Registers by the Village Education Committees has been endorsed by all the States and UTs.  and hopes
that the same will be implemented at the earliest.
OPENING OF MORE PRIMARY AND UPPER PRIMARY SCHOOLS
            The Committee expresses its grave concern over non-utilisation of around 14% of the financial assistance under
Operation Blackboard given to the States by the Centre.  Basic infrastructure in most of the schools in the country is still lacking
and there is  greater demand for quantitative as well as qualitative improvements in elementary education.   In this context, a
mere request to States to decentralize procurement of Teaching Learning Equipment may not be enough.   The Committee,
therefore,  recommends that Ministry may thoroughly look into this issue and take suitable remedial measures for full and
proper utilisation of Central funds. (Para 4.1)
The Committee notes that an amount of Rs. 35,366.53 lakhs has been released to various States during the period 1990-
2000 and 1,82,381 classrooms have been constructed upto 31.3.2000.  States like Orissa, A.P., Assam, Karnataka and  M.P.
have been the major beneficiaries.   However, no release could be made under GSY/JRY to Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, U.P. West

Bengal after 1992-93, in case of Goa only once in 1992-93, only in 1991-92 in respect of Meghalaya and in respect of
Pondicherry  only in 1990-91.   The Committee also notes that Bihar could not take the benefit of the scheme as apparently there
was no saving under JRY/GSY.   The Committee feels that some alternative source of funding has to be provided keeping in
view the financial position of the States. (Para 4.2)
            The Committee has been informed that State Governments are making all efforts to improve the motivation of teachers
and the Central Government has also issued necessary instructions to the State Governments in this regard.   The Committee is
not able to understand as to how the State Governments are going to improve the motivation of teachers and also lessen their
(Teachers’) extra workload to enable them to concentrate on their primary duty of teaching.    It has also been stated that
motivational training is imparted to teachers in DPEP in some States.  The Committee does not feel convinced with this as it is
aware that coverage of DPEP is still very less as a large part of the country still  remains uncovered.   The Committee is
therefore, of the view that the Department needs to address this issue with all seriousness as motivation of teachers is very
important. (Para 6.5)
CHANGE IN EXAMINATION SYSTEM
            The Committee has been informed that different States follow different criteria for promotion to higher class and
detention of the students.   The  Committee feels that it would be better if a uniform policy of promotion and detention is
followed by all the States, taking into consideration all related aspects.   The Committee hopes that the Department would take
initiative in this regard. (Para 7.2)
 
NON-FORMAL EDUCATION PROGRAMME/PREHAR PATHSHALA AS A BACKUP METHOD
            The Committee notes that the Alternative and Innovative Education Scheme has received Cabinet approval and
modalities  for its  implementation are being finalized in consultation with the State Governments.   The Committee is of the
view that   a consensus on operationalisation of the scheme in various states should  be arrived at without further loss of time,  
so that the scheme is implemented, as considerable time has already been taken in clearance  of the scheme. (Para 9.2)
ESTABLISHMENT OF RESIDENTIAL PRIMARY SCHOOLS FOR CHILDREN OF CONSTRUCTION WORKERS
AND MIGRATORY POPULATION
            The Committee still holds the view that the children of the nomadic tribes, shifting cultivators and construction workers
are the most vulnerable groups of school drop-outs.   Therefore, there should be sufficient motivation for these target groups.  
(Para 11.2)
CONTINUATION OF PLAN PROJECTS
            The Committee notes that a long term financial partnership with States has been envisaged under Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan.   The Committee hopes that this provision would prove to be of much assistance to State Governments in
implementing the various components of  Sarva Shiksha  Abhiyan thereby resulting in maximum coverage of children under
elementary education. (Para14)
COMMUNITY INVOLVEMENT
            In the 71 st Report of the Committee on the Problem of Drops outs, the Committee had suggested for a meeting of the
Education Ministers of all State Governments to work out modalities to provide legal status to the Panchayati Raj Institutions.  
However, no such meeting in this regard has taken place till now.   The Committee in this respect again reiterates that a meeting
of the Education Ministers of all States should be convened to discuss this issue. (Para 17.2)

PREFACE
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this
Hundred and Ninth Report on Action Taken by Government on the Recommendations contained in the 72
nd  Report on

2.         The Seventy-second Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 8 th December, 1998.  Replies of the
Government on the recommendations contained in the Report, received from the Department of Elementary Education
and Literacy, Ministry of Human Resource Development were considered by the Committee.  Clarifications were also
sought by the Committee from the representatives of the Department.  .
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 8th June, 2001.

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the recommendations contained
in its Seventy-second Report on the Adult Education which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok
Sabha on 8
th December,1998. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the
recommendations contained in the Report.  They have been categorized as follows:-
(i)                  Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government: Para  15, 16 and 18.2
(Chapter-I)
(ii)                Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the
Government’s replies: para-10,11, 12.1, 13.2, 17.2, 19  and 21.2 (Chapter-II)
(iii)               Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government have not been accepted by
the Committee : Para-8.1, 8.2, 9.1, 9.2,14,17.1, 20.1 and  20.2 (Chapter-III)
(iv)              Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government have not been
received- Para –Nil, (Chapter-IV)
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
Recommendation
15.       Keeping in view the social background of women, there should be exclusive centres being run by women

109th Report

volunteers (Preraks) and during the timings convenient to women at large.
Action Taken
            The Adult Education centres are chosen mutually by the volunteers and the learners identified in a particular
area.  Care is taken to keep the centre as close to the habitation as possible.  Wherever possible/feasible, women
volunteers are appointed to run the centres for women exclusively.
Recommendation
16.       The Committee feels that the village education committee/local community should be involved in the selection
of volunteers for running of Adult Education Centres in order to ensure the acceptability of Preraks in the community.
Local students from higher classes may also be involved in this task
Action Taken
            The selection of volunteers is done with the active involvement of the Village Education Committee/local
community.  The interested local unemployed youth and students  are also involved in this task
Recommendation
18.2
          The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should plan its media campaign keeping in view the
region-specific demands of areas where Adult Education Programme is yet to take its roots.  Advertisements/Posters in
the language of the area and according to the specific social background would result in higher participation in this
programme.
Action Taken
            With regard to the recommendation of the Committee for making media campaign region-specific and release
advertisements/posters in the language of the area and specific to social background, so as to attract higher participation,
it is submitted that the suggestion has already been included in the Media Policy prepared for the 9
th  Five Year Plan.
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE
IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES
Recommendation
10.  The Committee finds that districts identified are those which had taken up the campaign programme  without
adequate preparation, the project had dragged behind for two to three years and are stagnating  after an initially
successful total literacy phase.  However, mere identification of districts and allocation of funds would not achieve the
desired results.  Concerted efforts by the Central Government are required so that the State Governments are impressed
upon to take corrective measures. 
Action Taken
As regards restoration of the campaigns stagnating for various unavoidable reasons, it may be stated that the
component of operation restoration had been approved by the Cabinet under the Scheme of Special Projects for
Eradication of Illiteracy. 
The Districts to be taken under operation restoration are not merely identified but a concerted effort is made to
revamp and revitalize these stagnating campaigns by sending special teams to such districts.   The concerned Zilla 
Saksharata Samities  have also been advised to prepare action plans with specific strategies so that the campaigns could
be implemented more effectively.  Based on the reports of the Consultants , the revised action plans are examined
closely by the National Literacy Mission Authority and wherever necessary additional funds are sanctioned for such
campaigns. 
Further Comments
On a query as to which are the districts where special teams have been sent and the outcome/feedback state-wise,
the Department stated that National Literacy Mission (NLM)  set up a Sub-Committee in 1996 to coordinate the literacy
activities of 25 districts identified in six States where Operation Restoration of TLCs had been initiated.  Special teams

109th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/109threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:20]
of consultants were sent to all 25 districts and the teams submitted their reports indicating the reasons for slow progress
of the Campaign, present status, weaknesses and strengths prevailing for taking up Operation Restoration etc.  On the
basis of the assessment of the ground realities, special action plans were formulated to revamp and revitalise the
campaigns.  Owing to the concerted efforts of the National Literacy Mission, the literacy campaigns in a majority of the
identified districts have been revived.  Out of the 25 districts identified for Operation Restoration, 16 districts have
completed Total Literacy Campaigns and entered Post Literacy, while 2 districts after having completed Post Literacy
have entered the Continuing Education phase.
Recommendation
11.       The Committee also recommends that steps should be taken for introducing some vocational courses based on
local  needs which have become source of income for the participants.
Action Taken
            During the second phase of the campaign approach, i.e. the post literacy phase, various vocational courses under
the skill development programme are introduced by Zilla Saksharata Samities for which adequate grant are released by
the National Literacy Mission. 
Further Comments
The Department has further replied that  Zila Saksharatas Samities (ZSSs) have been advised to form women
groups and other self-help groups/cooperatives whereby women beneficiaries are taught appropriate techniques relating
to market economy so that they can sell their products for their economic betterment.
            In reply to a query whether any feedback regarding forming of such groups has been received from the states,
the Department has informed that Women’s groups and other Self-help Groups have been formed in almost all the
districts where Continuing Education programme has been launched and many post literacy districts.  For example,
information regarding formation of Self-help Groups has been received from Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh,
Karnataka and Kerala.  In Dumka district of Bihar this was taken up quite some time back and called ‘Didi Bank’.
Recommendation
12.1 The Committee is of the view that successful implementation of Adult Education Programme would also indirectly
result in a positive impact on various Government Run Family Welfare Programmes. 
Action Taken
            As per the reports received from various districts , it has been established  that women constitute more than
2/3
rd  of the total beneficiaries under Adult Education Schemes. The skills such as rural art/vocations are organized  for
women beneficiaries at Adult Education Centres.  Under the Scheme of Literacy Campaigns , Zilla Saksharata Samities
have been advised to form woman groups and other self-help groups/cooperatives whereby women beneficiaries are
taught appropriate technique relating to market economy so that they can sell their products for their economic
betterment.  
Recommendation
13.2     The Committee is of the firm view that Adult Education Programme should strictly adhere to the age-group of
15-35 years . 
Action Taken
            With regard to the clientele under the Scheme of Literacy Campaigns, it may be stated that the NLM’s target
age-group is 15-35 years.  However, children from 9-14 age-group are covered only when the Scheme of Non-Formal
Education is either not in operation or its coverage is  inadequate.  This is done to avoid any future accretion to the
NLMs target of 15-35 years age-group. 
Recommendation
17.2  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should impress upon the State Governments to take
steps to involve the VAs having a good track-record in reaching out to illiterate population in tribal areas.
Action Taken

In this regard the Voluntary Agencies are funded for literacy projects in areas where the Total Literacy
Programme has not been sanctioned to the District for implementation through Zilla Saksharta Samities.  During the
Monthly Monitoring Meetings as and when the issue regarding covering the whole State for literacy Programmes is
taken up, the State Government can decide as to whether to take up to projects on Total Literacy or to promote
Voluntary Agencies.
Recommendation
19.       The Committee feels that libraries are a must for neo-literates if their interest in education is to be sustained. 
The Committee finds that libraries have played a very important role in spreading literacy in Kerala. Similar efforts are
required in other parts of the country.  Community libraries can be made use of in generating interest in reading among
the neo-literates.
Action Taken
The importance of providing facilities of libraries and Reading Rooms for generating interest in reading among
the neo-literates has been recognised and  adequate financial provision has been made in the non-recurring and recurring
grants for Continuing Education centres under the Continuing Education (CE) programme.
Recommendation
21.2     While appreciating the monitoring mechanism for Adult Education, the Committee feels that involvement of
local MPs/MLAs in this task will prove to be more effective
Action Taken
The literacy  campaigns launched by the National Literacy Mission are being implemented in more than 450
districts around the country.  These campaigns have  become a people’s movement and people from all walks of life are
actively involved in various activities like mobilising learners, volunteers, environment building, training, material
preparation, monitoring, evaluation and so on.
In many campaign districts the local MPs, MLAs and other political leaders are taking keen interest in the
programme and they are closely associated with the various activities under this programme.  As members of State
Literacy Mission Authorities and Zilla Saksharta Samities (ZSS) , the local MPs and MLAs keep a vigil on the
implementation of various schemes.
CHAPTER-III
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT
HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
Recommendation
8.1  The Committee apprehends that until some radical measures are taken the target date may again have to be
extended.  There is a strong need of working out a mechanism of enrolment of adults, their retention and their
continuing education.  It must  be ensured that any adult enrolled is helped to reach the final stage of permanent
functional literacy.  Therefore, tracer study approach will have to be adopted.
Action Taken
National Literacy Mission has the objective of making 100 million persons literate in a time bound manner. 
Against this objective, the literacy campaigns, which is the principal strategy of the National Literacy Mission for
eradication of illiteracy, have been launched in 450 districts of the country.  As per the latest reports, approximately 130
million learners have been identified through survey, of which approximately 95 million persons were enrolled.  Out of
these, 73 million persons have so far been made literate under various schemes of the NLM.
The target of the National Literacy Mission which was set at 80 million persons to be covered in 345 districts by
1995 was revised to making 100 million persons functionally literate by the end of the 8
th   Five Year Plan i.e. the year
1996-97.  Keeping in view the progress made by the NLM, this target was reset in the year 1996 extending the date to
the year 1998-99.  Presently, the target stands reset to make 100 million persons literate in a time bound manner without
fixing any time schedule.

109th Report

     Against the objective of 100 million, NLM has been able to achieve 73% of the target which could be termed as quite
satisfactory.  In addition, the learners attending literacy centres, are still in the pipe line and this figure is certainly going
to cross the 100 million mark very shortly.
To revitalise and revamp the literacy campaigns in different districts, special strategies have been evolved by the
NLM which include involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions with literacy campaigns, more effective and result-
oriented monitoring, transparent evaluation systems, non-cash incentives to volunteers to enhance their level of
participation and linkages of literacy with other development programmes as well as programmes for the economic
well-being  of  the learners. 
Further Comments
On a specific query about  the  reasons for revising the target of the National Literacy Mission again and again,
the Department simply informed that the goal has now been redefined so as to attain full literacy i.e., a sustainable
thresh-hold level of 75 per cent literacy by 2005.   The progress made against the latest target was that upto March 2000,
number of districts covered under Total Literacy Campaigns was 559.  The number of persons made literate under
different programmes upto March 2000 was 84.0 million.
 The Department further clarified that  the figures regarding number of persons made literate were based on data
collected from monitoring reports of the literacy projects.  In order to obtain real picture on the ground as far as the
Nation as a whole and for individual states is concerned, the Department commissioned NSSO to carry out the required
exercise and bring out a consolidated picture of literacy as from the time of the last decennial census in 1991.
         The data now released at the end of the 53
rd round of survey indicates literacy rates in  the 7 + age group between
1991 and 1997 as well as that projected for 1998 as  shown below:

               Secondly, the urban-rural differential in literacy rates has shown a marked decline to 24% in 1997 as against 
28.4% in 1991.   Thirdly, and vitally important, the rise in female literacy between 1991 and 1997 has been 11%
whereas the male literacy rate for the same period has risen by 9%.  In the previous decade too, the female rate of
literacy had grown faster than the male rate (9.6% as against 7.8%).         
Comments  of the Committee
The Committee expresses its serious concern over setting an unrealistic target at the time of launching  of
National Literacy Mission in 1988.  The target data had to be extended from 1995 to 1996-97, from 1996-97 to 1998-
99.  As per the Action Taken Note submitted by the Department in August, 1999, target was reset to make 100 million
people literate in a time bound manner without fixing any time schedule.   However, the Committee finds that the goal
has been yet again redefined  so as to attain full literacy , i.e. a sustainable thresh hold level of 75%  literacy by 2005,  as
indicated in the reply given by the Department to the Questionnaire on ATN in September, 2000.   The Committee is
constrained to observe that the initial target of NLM, i.e. 80 million people by 1995 could be achieved only by March,
2000 (84 million).    Not only this, out of total 588 districts in the country,  Total Literacy Campaigns are yet to be 
launched in 32 districts.   The Committee notes that 53
rd round of NSSO survey commissioned by the Department was
meant to bring out a consolidated picture of literacy i.e. of +7 age group as from the time of the last decennial census in
1991.   The Committee fails to understand  as to how this survey can bring out the achievements under NLM which
covers non-literate persons in the age-group of 15 to 35 years. 
Recommendation
8.2       Against the total allocation of Rs.1400 crores for adult education during the 8
th   Plan, actual expenditure was
only Rs.718.14 crores.  Similarly, for 1997-98 although there was an allocation of Rs.129.81 crores , expenditure was
only Rs.84,48 crores.  The Committee expresses its deep concern over underutilsation of funds. It is true that in some of
the educationally backward states like Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, campaigns have lagged
behind leading to underutilisation of funds.  The Committee strongly feels that merely requesting such State

file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/109threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:20]
Governments to draw a time bound action plan for bringing uncovered districts under Total /Post Literacy Campaigns
will not serve the purpose.  What is required is a result oriented coordination between the Centre and the States.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should impress upon the States for effective implementation of
Adult Education Programme. The role of bureaucracy should recede and involvement of people should increase the
ownership level of the programme.  Strategy for this will have to be worked out.
Action Taken
In the report, it has been stated that against a total allocation of Rs.1400 crores,  only Rs.718.14 crores was
utilized.   Similarly for the year 1997-98 against an allocation of Rs.129.81 crores only Rs.84.48 crores was utilised.  It
may be submitted that apart from slow progress of the campaigns particularly in the Hindi speaking areas, the campaign
approach has reached a saturation  point where more release and /or utilization of funds may not help in the successful
implementation of the campaigns.   Of late, the National Literacy Mission has laid stress on consolidation of the existing
campaigns on ground rather than more and more expansion by way of more releases.  In addition to this community
participation has also gone up through contributions made to the implementing agencies by individuals as well as by
agencies in different areas for conducting various activities relating to the campaigns. This has a bearing on less
utilization of funds. 
As regards less expenditure by the National Literacy Mission, it may be stated that though Rs.1400 crores was
allocated for the 8
th  Five Year Plan , only a sum of Rs.953 crores was actually made available over a period of five
years.  In the case of less utilization of funds for the year 1997-98,  it may be submitted that due to non- finalisation of
revised enhanced norms for various schemes during the 9 th  Five Year Plan, the allocations had to be reduced at
appropriate stages of the financial year.  This resulted in less expenditure against the actual allocation.
The focus is now shifting towards decentralisation and devolving of powers on State Literacy Mission
Authorities (SLMAs) set up in different States.  The SLMAs  will be responsible not only for approval of literacy
projects like continuing education but also for actual implementation of the programme and its close monitoring .  State
level workshops have been held by the National Literacy Mission in several States to make aware the concerned
agencies of the role of SLMAs and clearly bring out as to how the literacy  programmes  would actually function.
Further Comments
The Department has informed the Committee  that in the revitalised National Literacy Mission, financial and
administrative powers have been decentralised to the State Literacy Mission Authorities (SLMAs).  SLMAs which have
been set-up in 18 States  have a two layer structure viz. Governing Council and Executive Council.  The State
Directorate of Adult Education serves as Secretariat.
           The State Literacy Mission Authorities are now specifically responsible for  the following:
-         Planning for literacy programmes in the State; fixing target dates for completing one phase of the programme and
launching new programmes.  Issuing guidelines for execution of State level.
-           Sanctioning Projects of Continuing Education: 
-           Sanctioning of Projects to NGOs:           
-           Monitoring of programmes:
-           Evaluation.
            The Department further informed that  the Director of Adult Education who is the member- secretary of the
SLMA in each State/UT is required to hold a monthly meeting on a fixed date.   The objectives of these meetings are to
review the progress of literacy campaigns and post literacy projects in various districts.  The focus of discussion is also
on assessment of qualitative aspects such as problems encountered in accelerating the pace of literacy campaign,
efficacy of corrective measures initiated in the past, activities planned for the coming month, and so on.   These
meetings are attended by secretaries of the Zila Saksharta Samities, Directors of State Resource Centres, State/Area
coordinators of the Bharat Gyan-Vigyan Samiti or representatives of the nodal voluntary agency and of Jan Shikshan
Sansthans. A representative from the National Literacy Mission or the Directorate of Adult Education is also present.
            The State Directorates scrutinise, analyse and compile the data from all the districts carefully and send
consolidated state reports to the central Directorate of Adult Education in the prescribed format.   National-level status
reports on literacy and post literacy are also compiled and published periodically.

.           The Committee was informed that  under the  three-step evaluation system of Literacy Programmes, self-
evaluation is a built-in feature of the literacy primers, concurrent and final evaluation is carried out by competent
evaluation agencies from outside the concerned district or State respectively.  The State Directorate is responsible for
nominating three evaluation agencies of which the district chooses one to conduct the concurrent evaluation.  Agencies
for external evaluation are nominated by NLM, but the SLMA keeps a close co-ordination and watch over progress and
results.
          As informed by the Department, recently, seven SLMAs- UP, MP, Rajasthan, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra
Pradesh & Maharashtra were visited by officers from NLM and qualitative and quantitative assessment of performance
made.  Criteria of performance appraisal were effectiveness of administration, management, planning, monitoring and
evaluation of the literacy programmes in the State.
Comments of the Committee
Despite the fact that the actual fund made available was less than that of allocated funds under 8th Five Year
Plan, the Committee finds that even the available fund  was not utilized upto the optimum level.    In Committee’s
view, major portion of allocation of funds under the programme is either wasted or misused.   The Committee,
therefore, feels that remedial steps need to be taken in this direction.  Decentralization of administrative and financial
powers to the State Literacy Mission Authorities (SLMAs) is a step in the right direction.    The Committee, however is
of the view that  the composition of SLMA  should be made in accordance with requirement of the state and  elected
representatives should  be involved in its activities. Besides, the monitoring of the programme in any state should be
done at the level of Chief Secretary periodically  and the D.C./D.M.  be made responsible for proper  implementation of
programmes under this scheme in his/her district.
Recommendation
9.1 The Committee, however is constrained  to note that PLCs have not taken off in the country in the real sense. 
Whereas 442 districts have been covered under TLC, Post Literacy Campaigns have been launched in only 229 districts
so far. 
Action Taken
            The progress of the literacy campaigns was not upto the mark in Hindi Speaking areas due to various factors. 
This has resulted in slow progress of post literacy campaigns throughout the country.  However, the present number of
districts where PLCs have been launched stands at 280 out of total of 450 districts.  In addition, 66 districts have also
launched the subsequent phase of continuing education after completion of the literacy phase.  It is expected to cover the
remaining districts under the PL as well as CE phase during the 9
th  Five Year Plan.  
 
Further Comments
In response to a query as to the factors responsible for the slow progress of literacy campaigns  in Hindi
speaking areas , the Department replied that  the reasons could be as follows:
1.         Low level of literacy: A small base to act as catalyst for Literacy Campaigns
2.         Lower Female Literacy Rates
3.     Inadequate Voluntary Teachers due to low literacy rate and social factors inhibiting Female       Literacy.
The Department also informed that  it has been indicated by the NSSO survey that during the period 1991-97, 
all the Hindi Speaking States have done exceptionally well. Rajasthan has shown dramatic improvement, pushing
forward from 38.55 per cent in 1991 to 55 per cent in 1997, a rise of 16.5 per cent. Uttar Pradesh registered a rise of
14.4 per cent, moving from 41.6 per cent to 56 per cent.  Bihar showed a gain of 10.5 per cent, rising from 38.5 per cent
to 49 per cent.  Himachal Pradesh has surged forward to take third position in the country, moving from 63.9 per cent to
77 per cent --a rise of 13.1 per cent.    The trend indicates that the Hindi Speaking States, though still below the National
average have been able to break the barriers and are surging ahead and it is expected that they would be able to match
the National level soon.
Recommendation
9.2  There is a gap of two to three years in the launching of TLC  and PLC in all the districts.  Thus the basic objective

109th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/109threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:20]
of PLC to provide opportunities of continuing education  to neo-literates so as to facilitate retention of their literacy
skills and to enable the learners to continue their learning beyond elementary literacy stands defeated.  The community,
therefore, recommends that the Department should impress upon all the states especially the educationally backward
states to launch PLCs  in the remaining districts so as to ensure  that benefits of literacy are sustained by the neo-
literates.
Action Taken
NLM’s  policy is to avoid any time lag between the completion of TLC and the subsequent launch of a PLC in a
district.   In order to achieve this, the districts are expected to formulate a Post Literacy Campaign during the currency
of the TLC itself .   However, it is true that in some districts, delay in launching PLC has occurred due to various
unavoidable reasons.   The State Governments have been advised to launch timely PLCs in various districts.
Further Comments
On a specific query as to   what steps are being taken to launch PLC in the remaining districts and  which are the
districts where  formulation of the PLC has not been done during the continuance of the TLC, itself, the Department
informed that Post-Literacy Campaigns have been launched in 352 districts in the country. In the revised policy for
NLM an integrated approach to Literacy has been launched which would enable the enormous illiteracy problem to be
tackled in a holistic manner.  By treating the imparting of functional literacy as a continuum rather than as a one-off
benefit for the illiterate person, progress of literacy efforts would be made goal-directed.  Literacy campaigns would
continue to run in those areas where there are large pools of residual illiteracy.  At the same time, for those who have
crossed the basic learning phase, programmes of consolidation, remediation, vocational skills, integration with life skills
and such other aspects are considered the basic unit.
         A district, while submitting their initial project, now also submits their strategy for post- literacy on the basis of
their anticipated target and projections of achievement.  The integrated proposal seeks to effectively bring the activities
of literacy campaigns under one ‘Literacy Project’ to achieve continuity, efficiency and convergence and to minimise
unnecessary time lag between the two, the Committee was informed.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee has been given to understand that as per the findings of 53
rd round of NSSO  Survey, during the
period 1991-97, all the Hindi speaking States have done exceptionally well.   The Committee would however, like to
point out that the literacy rate under NSSO  Surveys are based on 7+age  groupwhereas targeted group of NLM is 15 to
35 years age group.   The Committee notes that although considerable progress has been made in the launching of Post
Literacy Campaigns, gap between launching of Total Literacy Campaigns (TLCs) and Post Literacy Campaigns (PLCs)
still persists.   Position as in March, 2000 is that TLCs have been launched in 556 districts, and PLCs have been lunched
in 352 districts.   The Committee is constrained to observe that nine districts of Bihar are yet to be covered by TLCs
inspite of the Department vigorously pursuing the matter with the State Govt. and earmarking funds specially for these
districts.   The Committee notes that besides wide gap between launching of TLCs and PLCs in educationally backward
States, in NE States of Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Nagaland and Sikkim and also in J&K, not even one
district has been covered by PLCs so far.   The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that all such States
should be impressed upon to launch PLCs at the earliest in the districts not covered so far.
Recommendation
14.  The Committee, however, feels that  Government proposal  to sanction at least one Shramik Vidyapeeth (SVP) to
each district would not have the desired results. There might be many districts where there is no industry at all .  What is
required is to make , in the first instance, the existing 58 SVPs more purposeful, based on the area specific needs of the
working class. Evaluation of SVP Scheme, if not already done , may be initiated by the Department before further
expansion of the Scheme.
Action Taken
It has been proposed to sanction Shramik Vidyapeeth (SVP) for each district in due course of time keeping in
view the shift of focus of the revised scheme of Shramik Vidyapeeths from urban industrial workers to the neo-literates
and semi literates  and deprived sections of the society. The Expenditure Finance  Committee in its meeting held on
18.12.1998 has approved opening of 50 SVPs during the 9
th  Five Year Plan .  The Shramik Vidyapeeths, at present,

109th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/109threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:20]
functioning in the urban areas, will henceforth be  catering  to the needs  of the neo-literates, semi literates and other
deprived sections of people in urban and rural areas to help them acquire  some vocational skills or to upgrade their
vocational skill and income generating capacity . 
As per the revised scheme , the Shramik Vidyapeeths will concentrate more on continuing education in which
vocational education is a part. Enhanced role of the Shramik Vidyapeeths would be more or less to act as a district level
resource agency for vocational programmes.
The scheme has been evaluated by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences which gave valuable suggestions and
based on that a number of modifications have been carried out in the scheme.  As the scheme is in the threshold of a
change, further evaluation can be carried out after the scheme in the revised form is implemented  for some time.
Further Comments
         The Committee was informed that the Scheme of of Shramik Vidyapeeths was evaluated by the Tata Institute of
Social Sciences (TISS), Mumbai in 1993.  Some of the findings of the evaluation are as under:
·
        As long as the Sharmik Vidyapeeths remain committed to the deprived sections of the society with its tailor-made
programmes of polyvalent education, they have all the justification to exist as institutions outside the formal system
and deserve financial support from the Government;
·        The skill-oriented programmes of the Sharamik Vidyapeeths are largely directed towards enabling the beneficiaries
to be engaged in self-employment;
·        The Shramik Vidyapeeth scheme has the potential to equip individuals with the skills required to be gainfully
employed;
·        None of the existing organisational structures is in itself against the interests of the scheme of Shramik
Vidyapeeths.  Shramik Vidyapeeths can function effectively as autonomous, non-autonomous or semi-autonomous
institutions.
The Committee was further informed  that keeping in view the findings of the evaluation, scheme of  Shramik
Vidyapeeths has been  renamed as Scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansthan (JSS) or Institute of People’s Education with
increased focus on imparting vocational training to neo-literates.  Area of Operation of the JSS has been expanded to
cover both the urban and rural areas in the entire district where it is located.   Activities have been enlarged to function
as district repositories of vocational and technical skills under the Continuing Education Scheme.     JSS are to provide
academic and technical support to Zila Saksharata Samitis in taking up vocational and skill development programmes
for neo-literates and to organise equivalency programmes through the Open Learning System.
Comments  of the Committee
The Committee is of the view that adult persons are not merely interested in learning their alphabets.   They
would be only drawn towards this programme if there is a provision of some incentives and their money earning
capacity is also increased. The Committee notes that the revamped scheme of Shramik Vidyapeeths, now renamed as
scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansthan (JSS) approved by the Cabinet on 30.11.99 is under implementation  at present.  The
Committee has been given to understand that under this scheme, besides incentives, vocational education is being
imparted so as to enable the beneficiaries to get jobs.
The Committee finds that annual grants  for JSS have been considerably enhanced – from Rs. 12.30 lakh to Rs.
35 lakh for `A’ category city/ town, from Rs. 8 lakh to Rs. 30 lakh for `B’  category city/town and Rs. 25 lakh fixed for
`C’ category city/town.   Besides that considerable provision of non-recurring grant has also been made for vehicle,
equipment and building.  The Committee is of the view that due to the enhanced financial parameters laid down for the
scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansthan, an inbuilt effective monitoring mechanism with involvement of public
representatives is also required to be built up.  The Committee recommends  that evaluation of the scheme of JSS may
be carried out after some time so as to assess the impact of changes made therein.
Recommendation
17.1 The Committee feels that services of  VAs can be more gainfully employed if identification of really motivated
VAs is got done by State Governments.

Action Taken
In this regard in the EFC for the 9 th Five Year Plan it is proposed that 50% of the grants to the Voluntary
Agencies will be given by the State Literacy Mission Authorities for local projects.  State Literacy Mission Authorities
will be in a better position to screen Voluntary Agencies and also to monitor their performance.  At national level to
release the funds to Voluntary Agencies, the  credentials are checked and with lesser number of projects for monitoring,
the monitoring will be strengthened.
Further Comments
Since the scheme is implemented  with the support of NGOs/VAs , the Committee wanted to know as to what
were the sources of checking the credentials of voluntary agencies at national level.  In response,  the Department has
informed that  the credentials of voluntary agencies at national level are checked by following means:
·        Scrutiny of documents as to whether they have the requisite registration, constitution and experience.
·        Feedback from the State in which functioning regarding performance and credentials through SLMAs.
·        Feasibility study, especially in case of innovative projects by teams comprising of NLM, SLMA & established NGO
personnel.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is of the view  that most of the NGOs, particularly in the field of Adult Education, are not
performing well and all sorts of complaints have been received against them from various states.  The success of
implementation of a scheme/programme, to a great extent, depends upon the work done by good NGOs.   Therefore, the
selection of NGOs becomes very important.   The selection criteria for NGOs needs to be fool-proof so as to eliminate
fake NGOs without in anyway causing harassment to good NGOs.  The Committee is not sure about the effectiveness of
the above criteria in view of large number of complaints against NGOs.
The Committee  feels that high school students during their vacations can prove to be excellent instructors under
the Adult Education Programme.   The Committee has been given to understand that a special provision has been made
under the revamped programme to involve students as volunteers in Literacy Campaigns.   The Committee hopes that
this initiative would have a positive  impact.
Recommendation
20.1     The Committee, therefore, recommends that steps should be taken to ensure that Adult Education Programme is
taken up on a priority basis  by panchayats.  There is a specific responsibility of making the district fully literate as per
functional norms set by the NLM which may be given to Zilla Panchayats with total planning, implementation and
monitoring.  The funds for this as per requirements of the Zilla  Panchayat should be provided by the Central
Government from the Centrally Sponsored Schemes.  It must be made clear that this fund is in addition to the fund
allocated by the State Finance Commission.  The achievement of the target set by the Zilla Panchayat should be
externally evaluated and responsibility for any shortfall should be fixed on the concernedagency.  This will ensure the
responsibility and accountability coupled with decentralization of power and implementation.
Action Taken
Regarding the role of Panchayati Raj Institutions in the implementation of Literacy Campaigns, it may be stated
that wherever the elected Panchaytat Bodies exist, the implementing agencies  have been  advised to involve Panchayati
Raj functionaries in the actual implementation of the Campaigns.  Instructions have also been issued to reconstitute the
existing Zilla Saksharta Samities wherever PRIs  do not find a place in the Executive Committee  of the ZSS.  During
the 9
th Five Year Plan, the role of Panchayat Bodies in the implementation of Literacy Campaigns is proposed to be
specified more clearly so that they are made responsible for achievement of the overall objectives of the National
Literacy Mission.
Recommendation
20.2     The Committee was also given to  understand that there is a proposal to shift Collector Centric model to
alternative second – line of command to implement the campaigns,  through involvement of more and more non-
officials and voluntary agencies. The 

109th Report

Committee in this connection would like to suggest that the Kerala model may be experimented by making District
Panchayat President as the Chairman and District Collector as coordinator.
Action Taken
Wherever the elected Panchayat bodies exist, like in the States of West Bengal, Kerala  etc., the District
Panchayat President/Chairman of Zilla Parishad have been made as the Chairman of the Zilla Saksharta Samities and
the District Collector as the Executive Vice-Chairman,. This practice could be followed in other States also.
Further Comments
Specifying the role of Panchayat bodies, the Department informed that after the 73
rd Constitutional amendment,
responsibility of Adult Education rests with Zila Parishad/Zila Panchayat.  Panchayat elections have taken place in most
of the States and steps have been taken to nominate the elected representatives of the Panchayati Raj Institutions to the
literacy programmes and to integrate the Panchayat Raj structure more meaningfully with the Zila Saksharata Samiti
(ZSS).  In newly sanctioned districts, representation of Panchayat Raj Organisations at various levels is being ensured. 
Zila Saksharata Samities which were constituted before the election, people’s representatives at Panchayat, Block and
District level are being inducted by reconstituting the ZSS.  Panchayati Raj representatives are being imparted
orientation and sensitisation through workshops being held by the State Resource Centres and the National Literacy
Resource Centre at Mussoorie.
In response to a further query as to whether  the practice of Kerala and West Bengal of making  District
Panchayat President/Chairman of Zila Parishad, the Chairman of the Zila Saksharta Samities (ZSSs) and the District
collector as the Executive Vice-Chairman has been followed in any other State, the Department informed that in the
revised scheme for the nine Plan, the Literacy Programmes will continue to be implemented by the ZSS headed by the
Collector.  However, a democratically elected Chairman of the Zila Parishad may also head the ZSS in a State where a
full-fledged Panchayati Raj system has been established. The Zila Saksharta Samities have complete freedom to adopt
either of the systems, but no other State except West Bengal and Kerala have yet adopted a different pattern.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee feels that the matter has not been taken up in the right earnest.   It recommends that the
experience  of Kerala and West Bengal could be discussed/shared with other States and they could adopt the same if
they found it convenient and useful.
