REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       The Census of 2001 had indicated the population of India as 1027 million with 531 million males and 496
million females.    In the decade  1991-2001, nearly 181 million persons were added to the population of India.  
Population increased at an annual exponential growth rate of 1.93 percent in the decade.  As per the latest Sample
Registration System (SRS) estimates, the annual growth rate of population is 1.74% (1999).  
1.2       The eight States of U.P., Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Uttaranchal, Chhatisgarh and Orissa,
which currently constitute nearly 44% of the total population of India, are projected to comprise 48% of the total
population in 2016.   In other words, these States alone will contribute an anticipated 55% increase during the period
1996-2016.    Demographic outcome in these States will determine the timing and size of population at which India
achieves population stabilisation.
1.3       The three most significant factors that can curtail the growth of population are increase in the use of
contraceptives, improvement in the mother’s health and survival of children.  All the programmes of the Department of
Family Welfare are accordingly planned and being implemented for pursuing a combination of these three issues.
1.4       During the Tenth  Plan the main approach of family welfare programme will be:
(i)
                  To assess the needs for Reproductive and Child Health (RCH);
(ii)                To provide need based ,client centered and demand driven RCH care;
(iii)               To strengthen the infrastructure for service delivery and bridging the gap in essential infrastructure and
manpower;
(iv)              Providing additional assistance to poorly performing districts and ensuring uninterrupted supply of drugs
and equipments;  and

woman and BCG, Measles, DPT and Polio for infants have increased in comparison to the preceding year.
1.6       In respect of achievement of performance in Family Planning methods and to achieve the long term goals, the
following levels of contraceptives were achieved during 1996-97 to 2000-2001.

that in the case of sterilisation, the number of male sterilisation is much below the desired level and recommends that
the Department should take appropriate steps so that the participation of males is increased in Family Planning
methods.  
1.7       The Committee understands that under the Community Needs Assessment Approach (CNAA), an action plan is
prepared each year at the district level based  on the need assessment done by ANMs of Sub-Centre at village level.  In
the beginning of the financial year, the health worker will first complete the house-to-house survey.  Based on this
survey, Eligible Couple Register is updated by the ANM.  The Committee has been informed that the State Govts. are 
impressed from time to time to ensure that the Sub-Centre action is got prepared for each Sub-Centre in the State.  The
Committee has its own doubts about the implementation of this annual exercise, which is most essential for successful
implementation of Family Welfare Programme, specially in the remote and inaccessible areas.  The Committee strongly
feels that surprise inspections in the performing as well as non-performing districts by Central teams/dedicated
NGOs/Social Workers can bring out the ground reality.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
should initiate such an exercise in 2002-2003.

II          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1              The Committee has been informed that allocation for the Department for  2002-2003 is Rs. 4953.83 crores
against Rs. 4232.38 crores in BE 2001-2002 which was  reduced to Rs. 3721.67 crores at RE stage.   This represents  an
increase of Rs. 721.55 crores over the previous year.
2.2
              Commenting on the allocation, the Department submitted that the Annual Plan proposal for the year 2002-2003
was Rs. 7590.56 crores.  However, an allocation of Rs 4953.83 crores was approved by the Planning Commission.  As a
result of cut in plan proposal, funding of the infrastructural units in the States will be the most affected.   Besides that, 
other schemes like contractual appointments under RCH Programme, adolescent health care, supply of Dai kits,
promoting institutional deliveries, civil works at Sub Centres, urban slum project and strengthening of primary health
care infrastructure, may also be curtailed.
2.3
              The Committee  has also been given to understand that during 2001-2002, a cut of 710.00 crores (plan) was
proposed by the Ministry of Finance on the basis of expenditure  incurred by the Department till October, 2001
(51.19%).   However,  subsequently an assurance was given by the Ministry of Finance that if 75% expenditure was
incurred by the Department by December, 2001, the cut made in the outlay will be restored.    However, despite meeting
the targetted expenditure and the representations made at the highest level, the cut of Rs. 710 crores was only reduced to
Rs. 510 crores.  
2.4              The Committee agrees in principle with the Department's contention of there being no case for resorting to a cut
of Rs. 700.00 crores at the RE stage in 2001-2002 by the Ministry of Finance.  The Committee also notes that total plan
allocation of Rs. 3700.00 crores in 2001-2002 is anticipated to be utilised. Actual expenditure figures are not available
at present.  The Committee, however observes that during 2000-2001, against a higher projected requirement, plan
allocation was Rs. 3500.00 crores which was reduced to Rs. 3200.00 crores at the RE stage.  Actual expenditure was
even less i.e. Rs. 3071.35 crores.  The Committee strongly feels that inview of much higher allocation of Rs. 4930.00
crores in 2002-2003, the Department should ensure that funds allocated under various schemes are utilised optimally
and strictly as per the action plan to strengthen its case of higher allocation.
III        RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
3.1
              The Rural Family Welfare Centres were set up at all block level PHCs sanctioned upto 1.4.1980 to provide
Family Planning and MCH Services in rural areas.  There are 5435 such centres functioning in the Country.  Besides
that, to provide basic health and family welfare services to the rural population 1,37,311 Sub-Centres  are currently
functioning out of which 97,757 Sub-Centres were funded by the Department till now. 
3.2              The Committee was informed that a Consultative Committee consisting of the representatives of the Planning
Commission, Department of Expenditure, States of Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan was constituted by
the Department in 1998.   The Committee examined the SWAP proposal between Rural Family Welfare Centres and
Sub-Centres and strongly recommended that in view of the importance of the rural Sub-Centres for the Family Welfare
Programme, and as the Rural Family Welfare Centres have lost their original identity and have become part of primary
health centre complexes at the block level, the Department of Family Welfare should assume the responsibility of
funding all 1,37,311 existing Sub-Centres.   In exchange, for accepting this responsibility the States should take over the
financial liability of maintaining the Rural Family Welfare Centres  (RFWC) numbering 5435.
3.3       The Department  also informed that the main purpose of the SWAP is to streamline the system of financing the
Sub-Centres. As the Sub-Centres were established by Central Government and State Governments during different time
periods it is difficult to assess the impact of the programme run by the Department.   Therefore, there was a need to
bring all the Sub-Centres under one umbrella for effective monitoring of the programme.   The Planning Commission
insisted  that a consensus be developed among the States on the issue of swaping these responsibilities between the State
and Department of Family Welfare.     The Committee in its 101
st Report had also recommended that the issue needed
to be discussed with the States/UTs before any decision was taken in this regard.  The Committee, however, notes that a
decision has already been taken to implement the SWAP proposal from 1.4.2002.  Therefore there  is no proposal for

through Primary Health Infrastructure.  The overall goals of the programme are to reduce maternal and infant mortality
and morbidity and unwanted fertility and contribute thereto stabilization of population.

Commission, the allocation for polio activities and vaccines for routine immunization related activities which stands at
Rs. 376 crores and Rs. 141 crores respectively have been separated from the RCH Programme which in-turn resulted in
decreased allocation  for RCH Programme in BE 2002-2003.

VII       POST PARTUM PROGRAMME
Post Partum Programme is a maternity centered hospital based approach to Family Welfare Programme covering
550 Post Partum Centres at district level and 1012 Post Partum Centres at sub-district level hospitals.   The objective of
the programme is to provide antenatal,  natal and post-natal services to expectant mothers and also to provide Family
Planning Services, besides diagnosing early cases of cervical cancer.   An allocation of  Rs 135.00 crores was made for
Post Partum Programme in BE 2001-2002.   However, no allocation has been made for the year 2002-2003.   Giving
reasons, the Department has replied that the Planning Commission has decided to transfer the Post Partum Programme
to the States/UTs w.e.f. 1.4.2002.  The Committee would be interested to know as to the precise reasons that weighed in
favour of transfer of this Programme to the States/UTs.

8.1
              Allocation of Rs. 117.00 crores made under the head Free Distribution of Conventional Contraceptive in BE
2001-2002 has been increased to Rs. 181.80 crores in 2002-2003.  Explaining the reasons for increase,  the Department
has informed that due to increasing number of younger couples, the demand for condoms under free distribution from
the States has been increasing and   in order to meet the enhanced demand, increased budgetary provision has been
proposed.
8.2       The Department has further informed that as regards allocation of additional quantities of conventional
contraceptives in the States, these would be allocated proportionately in relation  to utilisation and demand of the
respective States.   The unmet need in condom under free supply scheme is nearly 30% whereas in Oral Contraceptive
Pill (OCP) it is around 10%.   Attempts will be made to fill up these gaps.   The additional allocation would be required
for the purchase of the raw material for OCP which is no more available under external assistance and the same has to
be met from domestic resources.
8.3       In regard to the quality of Nirodh, the Committee has been given to understand that  19% users have rated it
under free supply scheme as okay,  75% as good and 6% have rated as very good.    The Committee feels that the
quality of condoms goes a long way in its acceptance by the users.    The Committee is also of the view that poor quality
may lead to unwanted pregnancy and reproductive tract infections.    The Committee,  therefore, recommends that the
Department should ensure that only the best quality of latex is used in manufacturing of condoms.

11.2    The Committee feels that the problem of exponential growth of population is the mother of all the problems of

The Committee notes with satisfaction that the percentage of coverage in 2000-2001 in respect of TT for
pregnant woman and BCG, Measles, DPT and Polio for infants have increased in comparison to the preceding year.

The Committee notes that though there is a marginal increase in the case of sterilisation and C.C. users, the

            The Committee understands that under the Community Needs Assessment Approach (CNAA), an action plan is
prepared each year at the district level based  on the need assessment done by ANMs of Sub-Centre at village level.  In
the beginning of the financial year, the health worker will first complete the house-to-house survey.  Based on this
survey, Eligible Couple Register is updated by the ANM.  The Committee has been informed that the State Govts. are 
impressed from time to time to ensure that the Sub-Centre action is got prepared for each Sub-Centre in the State.  The
Committee has its own doubts about the implementation of this annual exercise, which is most essential for successful
implementation of Family Welfare Programme, specially in the remote and inaccessible areas.  The Committee strongly
feels that surprise inspections in the performing as well as non-performing districts by Central teams/dedicated
NGOs/Social Workers can bring out the ground reality.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
should initiate such an exercise in 2002-2003. (Para 1.7)

            The Committee is surprised to note that a final decision has already been taken by the Department inspite of
there being no consensus on this issue among the States.  According to the Department itself, outcome of
implementation of SWAP proposal will be that some states will be in an advantageous position by saving the funds and
some States in a disadvantageous position.  For example, as per the information made available to the Committee,
whereas additionalliability in the case of Chandigarh will be only Rs. 7 lakhs, for West Bengal it will be as high as Rs.
17.74 crores.  The Committee wonders about the fate of Rural Family Welfare Centres in view of no allocation being
made by the Department in BE 2002-2003.  The Committee would, therefore, like to emphasise that the issue of
compensating the affected states should be sorted out at the earliest.  (Para 3.4)
The Committee is sympathetic to  grievance of some of the State Governments  who will be placed
disadvantageously as a result of the proposal.  The Committee recommends that the Department should vigorously
pursue its proposal with the Planning Commission for compensating the affected states.   The Department should make
concerted efforts to fix a rational basis for distribution of liabilities amongst the State Governments so that no injustice
is done to any State.  (Para 3.5)
Given the tight financial position of the State Governments, the Committee feels that it is a great challenge for
them. (Para 3.6) 
The Committee is constrained to note that the major defaulting States in respect of setting up of Sub-Centres are
Bihar, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Meghalaya, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Delhi. In
respect of PHCs these are Assam, A.P., Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Nagaland,
Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Delhi.  As far as CHCs are concerned, Assam, A.P., Bihar, Haryana,
MadhyaPradesh, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Orissa, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal
and Delhi are the major defaulters. (Para 3.10)
The Committee is perturbed  to note that targets for setting up of Sub-Centres, PHCs and CHCs during Ninth
Plan seem to have been prescribed for namesake only.  The achievement level for the first four years of Ninth Plan
1997-2001 clearly indicates this assessment-
 Targets Achievement level (upto 2000-2001)
Sub-Centres 7686 1053
PHCs 1521 693
CHCs 2903 410
(Para 3.11)
The Committee recommends that the Department should take necessary steps to achieve the  target of setting up
of Sub-centres, PHCs and CHCs.  The Committee also fails  to understand as to how such a large number of states have
failed to achieve the target of setting up of Sub-centres, PHCs and CHCs and therefore recommends that the Department
should try to find out the reasons behind this phenomenon.  (Para 3.12)
The Committee also observes that in many States, the number of established Sub-Centres exceeds the projected
requirements as per 2002 projected population.  Financial liability with regard to all existing 1,37,311 Sub-Centres is to
be borne by the Central Govt. from 2002-2003.  The justification of bearing the expenditure in respect of excess Sub-
Centres set up in different States by the Centre needs to be explored from all aspects.  Specially in view of the fact that
proposal of the Department for financing the establishment of new Sub-Centres under the 100% Centrally Sponsored
Scheme is pending with the Ministry of Finance and shortage of Sub-Centres is there in large number of States. (Para
3.13)
The Committee laments at the lackadaisical approach of the Department in getting the data collected from
various States and desires that these may be obtained and  furnished to the Committee at the earliest .  (Para 3.15)
The Committee feels that  ANMs and LHVs are the persons responsible for delivering Family Welfare Services
to rural people and therefore recommends that the Department should make concerted efforts to get  the posts of ANMs
and LHVs  filled up at the earliest in respect of the weak performing states.  (Para 3.16)
IV        URBAN FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES

The Committee is of the view  that for improving outreach service delivery system in urban slums,
reorganisation of Urban Family Welfare Centres should be made at the earliest.    Therefore, the Committee
recommends that the Department should make adequate provision for reorganisation of Urban Family Welfare Centres
in 2002-2003. (Para 4.4)
V         REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH PROGRAMME (RCH)
The Committee notes with appreciation the rationalization done by the Department in restructuring the RCH
Programme and feels that the Department should, in the same vein carry similar rationalization/ restructuring,  
wherever possible, in respect of other programmes.     (Para 5.3)
The Committee feels that the underutilization of funds  by the State governments is quite alarming  as it reflects
that the Programme is not being implemented properly at the ground level. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Department should take up the matter with the concerned  States and try to find out the reasons behind under
utilization of funds by them and take necessary remedial measures. (Para 5.4)
The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction that the Department has not so far taken up the matter with the State
Govts even after almost a year has passed.   It desires that this may be done at the earliest and the outcome may be
intimated to it. (Para 5.5)
            Noting the efforts made by the Department, the Committee feels that though some progress has been made in
respect of Infant mortality rate, percentage of safe delivery etc.,   they are still very high in comparison to even a
number  of developing countries.   Some States like Assam, Bihar, M.P., U.P., Orissa and Rajasthan continue to perform
much below the National Average.   In view of this, the Committee recommends  that the Department should make
extra efforts to improve the performance in these states. (Para 5.8)
The Committee feels that the Department should approach the concerned States for bringing out the necessary
improvements/modifications in the schemes for a better implementation of the same. (Para 5.9)
The Committee recommends that the Department should pursue with the remaining States also.  Efforts should
also be made to extend this scheme to more districts. (Para 5.10)
VI        STRENGTHENING OF IMMUNISATION PROGRAMME AND ERADICATION OF POLIO
            The Committee is deeply anguished to find that a cut in the allocation at the RE stage was made due to delay in
procurement of equipment and stores.    The Committee feels that such delays seriously affect the implementation of
Family WelfareProgrammes.  It,  therefore, recommends that the  Department should inquire into as to whether this
delay could have been avoided and if so, the responsibility should be fixed in this regard.  It should also take extra
precaution so that such delays are avoided in future.  (Para 6.2)
In case of BCG vaccination and DPT Immunization the Committee is happy to note that the all India
achievement is more than 100%.  However, again Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland are the low-performing
States.   The same can be said about DPT Immunisation coverage.    (Para 6.3)
             The Committee observes that the States like Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya  and Nagaland continue to
perform much  below the national average over the years in all the immunization programmes.  Another disturbing
feature noticed by the Committee  is the downward trend in the percentage of coverage during the last three years of
Ninth Plan in respect of some States.  The Committee therefore, recommends that the Department should identify such
States as are performing below the national average and take special steps to strengthen the immunization scheme in
such States.  (Para 6.4)
VII       POST PARTUM PROGRAMME
The Committee would be interested to know as to the precise reasons that weighed in favour of transfer of this
Programme to the States/UTs.
VIII      DISTRIBUTION OF CONTRACEPTIVES
            In regard to the quality of Nirodh, the Committee has been given to understand that  19% users have rated it
under free supply scheme as okay,  75% as good and 6% have rated as very good.    The Committee feels that the
quality of condoms goes a long way in its acceptance by the users.    The Committee is also of the view that poor quality

may lead to unwanted pregnancy and reproductive tract infections.    The Committee,  therefore, recommends that the
Department should ensure that only the best quality of latex is used in manufacturing of condoms.  (Para 8.3)
IX        AREA PROJECTS
            The Committee is perturbed to note the reasons behind cut in RE 2001-2002.  The  Committee feels that reasons
like slow implementation of a Project and delay in finalization of cost bifurcation etc. reflect  administrative
inexpediency and therefore recommends that the Department should take necessary steps to avoid such procedural
delays in future.  It also gives an impression that the Project is not being effectively implemented. (Para 9.3)
X         INFORMATION EDUCATION AND COMMUNICATION
            The Committee notes with appreciation the steps taken by the Department in involving local people for IEC
activities.   The Committee, however, feels that such decentralisation of fund allocation sometimes result in
misuse/misappropriation  of funds and therefore recommends that the Department should keep a strict vigil on the
utilisation of funds by the district and local authorities. (Para 10.4)
XI       NEW INITIATIVES
           The Committee feels that the problem of exponential growth of population is the mother of all the problems of
this country. No matter howsoever, high is the growth rate of national economy it will be insufficient to meet the
economic needs of the people if the rate of population growth  is not arrested.  The Committee is of the considered
view that unless the factors which are contributory to the uncontrolled growth of population, such as illiteracy
particularly in woman, poverty etc. are appropriately addressed, we will have no escape from this unfortunate
situation.   All the political parties/groups owe their duty to the country to sit together and evolve a consensus in this
regard.  (Para 11.2)

            I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this 
Hundred – Eighteenth  Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.43) of the Department of
Indian Systems of Medicine & Homoeopathy,  Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the year 2002-2003.
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of Indian
Systems of Medicine & Homoeopathy, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and also heard the Secretary and other
Officials of that Department  on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held on 3
rd   April, 2002.

REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy was set up by the Government of India as an
independent Department in March, 1995 under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.  The main objective of the
Department is to provide focused attention for the proper development and  propagation of ISM&H, namely Ayurveda,
Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy and to fully utilise the potentials of these systems.
II          PERFORMANCE  DURING  NINTH FIVE  YEAR  PLAN
2.1       The thrust areas identified for intervention during the Ninth Plan period were as indicated below:-
Effective use of ISM&H systems for health for all and for better patient care system.
-
                      Upgradation of medical educational facilities and improvement in standards of ISM&H medical education.
-                      Focus on research and development efforts
-                      Increasing availability of raw material
-                      Setting up of National Institute for each system.
-                      Development/Strengthening of pharmacopoeial  laboratories and Strengthening of State Government
pharmacies
2.2       Keeping in view the thrust areas, the following schemes were prepared by the Department  for implementation
during the  plan period:-
-
                      Scheme for strengthening of Pharmacopoeia Committee on ISM
-                      Scheme of grant-in-aid for  development of ISM&H UG colleges
-                      Scheme of grant-in-aid for Re-orientation for in-service training programme

-                      Scheme of assistance to PG medical education in ISM&H
-                      Scheme of assistance to State Drug Testing Laboratories/Pharmacies
-                      Scheme of assistance for Extra-Mural Research Project through Research Institutions
-                      Setting up of Medicinal Plants Board
-                      Innovative Schemes for development of medicinal plants,
-                      Scheme on Information, Education and Communication
-                      Scheme of assistance for International Exchange Programme/Seminars/Workshops on ISM&H.
 
2.3              The plan allocation and utilization of funds during the Ninth Plan period (year wise)is indicated below:

2.4       From the above table, the Committee infers that  the  Department has fully utilised the allocated funds during the
first two  years of the Plan. Thereafter, the trend of BE allocation being reduced at RE stage and that too remaining
under-utilised started. The Committee was given to understand that tremendous increase in the Plan allocation for 2000-
01 as compared to previous year's allocation, put a strain on its absorption capacity. The Committee observes that
instead of there being any improvement in 2001-02, the last year of Ninth Plan, situation has worsened. The Committee
strongly feels that although the Department succeeded in getting enhanced allocation by projecting higher requirements
meant for expansion of ongoing Schemes and launching of many new Schemes, the Department failed to achieve both
the physical and financial targets during 2000-01 and 2001-02. The Committee notes that a large number of new
schemes were proposed to be launched during Ninth Plan period. However, so far as their implementation is concerned,
performance has been dismal.   In the last year of the Ninth Plan, i.e.2001-02, as many as eleven new schemes were
there, out of which some were yet to be finalised due to procedural bottlenecks and in the case of others, due to late
approval, schemes were yet to take off.
2.5       The Committee observes that as many as nineteen new schemes have been identified by the Department for
initiation during the Tenth Plan period. Scheme of CGHS Expansion in dispensaries is one of such Schemes. The
Committee is, however constrained to note that this Scheme was proposed to be launched during the Ninth Plan.  
However, for reasons unknown to the Committee, the Scheme was dropped during 1999-2000.  The Committee is
surprised to note that this Scheme is again included in the list of new schemes  to be launched during Tenth Plan.   In
contrast, fate of Schemes like 'Health for all through preventive and promotive Programme of ISMH', 'Speciality clinics
on ISMH',  ‘Indian Homoeopathy Pharmacy Council' and 'ISM Pharmacy Council’ is not known. The Committee hopes
that proper planning and preparatory exercise with regard to finalization and approval in respect of all these proposed
new schemes must have been done before making budget provision for the same in 2002-03. The Committee would like
to be enlightened in this regard.
III.      BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
            3.1       The total allocation both Plan  and Non-Plan taken together provided to the Department for the year
2001-2002 was Rs. 165.56 crores which was reduced to Rs. 134.84 crores at the RE stage.  However, the
Committee observes that while there has been minimal reduction in the non-Plan allocation at RE stage from
Rs.45.56 Crores to Rs. 44.84 Crores,  Plan allocation at the RE stage was reduced drastically from Rs. 120 crores
to Rs. 90 crores.  This year the Department has been allocated  Rs. 150 crores under Plan and Rs. 50.86 crores
under Non-Plan.
3.2
              The Committee notes that the Department has been given an increase of about 25% over the last year.  Asked to

256.66 crores, the Department received only Rs. 150.00 crores. It was clarified that  whereas it was sufficient for
continuing the existing and ongoing activities of the Department, the  new schemes and programmes projected in the
Tenth Plan would be affected to some extent.
3.3
              The Committee notes that the allocation at RE 2001-02 was reduced by the Department of Expenditure due to
insufficient utilization of the budget in first nine months,  owing   to a number of schemes not cleared or delay occurred
in receiving clearance of concerned Ministries.  The Secretary while deposing before the Committee also  confessed that
the Department of ISM&H being  a  new and small department, it had  to conceptualise new schemes and programmes
and steer them through various administrative and financial clearances from the Planning Commission and Department
of Expenditure and indeed faced a lot of difficulty in translating them into implementable schemes. This phenomenon,
the Secretary admitted has led to lesser utilization of funds. 
3.4       The Committee does not agree with the contention of the Secretary that the Department is new.  It is seven years
since the Department has been created for the very specific purpose of promoting and developing indigenous Health
systems.  The Committee, therefore, feels that without  the adequate  initiative  and support of the Department, these
systems will not develop and the purpose for which the Department has been created will get defeated.  The Committee,
is, therefore, of the opinion that the Department should make all out efforts to utilise the fund  earmarked for the
purposes  for which they are meant.

XI        NON-AVAILABILITY OF HERBS AND MEDICINAL PLANTS
11.1     The efficacy of most of the ISMH drugs is dependent upon the use of pure and genuine raw material obtained
from medicinal plants.  However, due to over exploitation, unscrupulous collection and denuding of forests, supplies
have been dwindling. 
11.2     Elaborating on the steps initiated in this regard, the Secretary informed the Committee that non-availability of
raw material of required purity and containing alkoids and essential oils etc. has been engaging the attention of the

            From the above table, the Committee infers that  the  Department has fully utilised the allocated funds during the

strongly feels that although the Department succeeded in getting enhanced allocation by projecting higher requirements
meant for expansion of ongoing Schemes and launching of many new Schemes, the Department failed to achieve both

initiation during the Tenth Plan period. Scheme of CGHS Expansion in dispensaries is one of such Schemes. The
Committee is, however constrained to note that this Scheme was proposed to be launched during the Ninth Plan.

lakhs out of Rs. 75 lakhs provided last year. Now the Department proposes to give Rs. one crore.     The Committee 
would  like to be apprised of the reason for lesser utilization by the Institute during 2001-02. The Committee is of the
view that concerted efforts should be made for optimum utilisation of funds during 2002-03.  The Committee desires
that PG courses proposed to be commenced in NIA, Jaipur and CCRAS, Jam Nagar be started  itself. (Para 4.3)
           
            The Committee notes that in spite of a number of initiatives being taken by the Department, not much
improvement seems to have been made. This is evident by the fact that no specific action-taken reports on 160
misleading advertisements forwarded to State Governments of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka,
Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, NCT of Delhi, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh have been received in spite of reminders
being sent to them. The Committee notes with serious concern that during 2001-02 (upto 14.2.02), 122 advertisements
were sent to the  Government of NCT of Delhi with no response forthcoming. This is indeed a sorry state of affairs. The
Committee enjoins upon the Department to vigorously pursue the matter with the concerned State Governments,
otherwise the efficacy of Ayuvedic medicines would be questioned.       The Committee would like to be apprised of the
initiatives taken and the results thereof within a period of three months. (Para 4.5)
The Committee notes that this proposal seems to have been initiated during 2000-01 and an expenditure of about
Rs.217 lakhs was incurred during 2001-02. The Committee feels that scrutiny of expression of interest may be
completed soon  and steps may be taken to establish it at the earliest. (Para 4.7)
            The Committee notes that the Department has taken adequate steps to popularise the system of  Ayurveda in
different countries.  The Committee hopes that such  initiatives will continue in  future also. (Para 4.11)
            The Committee feels that adequate steps have not been taken by the Government to provide ayurvedic treatment
facilities to the CGHS beneficiaries.  At the same time, no serious efforts are being made to strengthen the system as the
ayurvedic hospitals/centers continued to be under the Department of Health.  The Committee would, therefore,
recommend that all facilities of ayurvedic treatment should be transferred within a period of three months  to the
Department of Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy so as to ensure their proper management. Further, the
existing Government CGHS dispensaries/hospitals should be upgraded and private hospitals/dispensaries such as Arya
Vaidashala Kottakkal, Kerala, and its Delhi branch may also be brought under the facilities of CGHS beneficiaries.  The
Committee also feels that the Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy should be headed by a professional
adoctor(vaidya) at Secretary level rather than a civil servant who may not be adequately familiar with what kind of
policies need to be formulated in this area.  This will also facilitate taking decisions for cultivation of herbs which are
the basic raw-material for manufacturing  of all these medicines. (Para 4.15)
V.        HOMOEOPATHY
The Committee, however, notes that against an allocation of Rs. 4.00 Crores for NIH in 2001-02, expenditure
reported upto February,2002 is only Rs. 2.91 Crores. The Committee observes that all the proposed activities for the
year could not be activated. Like  Laboratories could not be modernised to the required level as targetted. Similarly, no
progress seems to have been made on the proposal for starting courses for Dispensers/Pharmacists/Nurses of the
Institute. What is a cause for  more serious concern  is the issue of increase of bed capacity from 60 to 100. The
Committee has been given to understand  that steps have been taken to enhance the bed capacity to 80 at the first stage
followed by 100 later. (Para 5.2)
The Committee notes that  in this connection cadre review committee had suggested creation of 44 posts in
various categories including teaching and non-teaching.  However, the Department proposes to create 47 posts.  The
Committee would like to know the reasons for creation of 3 extra posts by the Department on their own when an expert
committee has threadbare discussed the matter.  The Committee would also like to know whether these extra posts are
on the teaching side or  the non-teaching side. (Para 5.3)
VI.       UNANI
However, theCommittee regrets  to note that the Department is silent on the issue of increase in allocation and in

118th Report

what manner it  proposes to utilise the same.  The Committee, however, hopes  that the entire allocation would be
properly utilised by the Department. (Para 6.2)
The Committee desires that PG courses at the Institute may be started in 2002-2003. The Committee further
desires that the target for handing over the building may be sticked to.         (Para 6.3)
TheCommittee desires that the issue may be sorted out as quickly as possible, as it is pending  for quite a long
time. (Para 6.4)
VII       YOGA
The Committee is of the view that construction work of MDNIY should start without any further delay. (Para
7.1)
The Committee feels that no effective steps seem to have been taken in this regard and  desires that the
Department may pursue this issue  more vigorously with the Ministry of Human Resource Development . (Para 7.3)
VIII      NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF SIDDHA (NIS, CHENNAI)
The Committee is of the view that by publishing the efficacy of siddha medicines in vernacular  newspapers and
also by establishing more siddha dispensaries, the system can be made more popular. (Para  8.2)
IX        MEDICAL EDUCATION
The Committee feels that the Sub-Committee should finalise its recommendations at the earliest so as to address
to this problem urgently.  The Committee hopes that the Department would be benefited by the recommendations of the
Sub-committee in initiating appropriate legislative measures in this regard. (Para 9.3)
X         QUALITY CONTROL OF DRUGS
The Committee appreciates the steps taken in this regard.  However, the Committee feels that the
Pharmacopoieal work relating to Ayurveda needs to be further expedited, as only 40% has been done.  (Para 10.1)
The Committee notes that non-creation of new posts and non-filling of some posts are the two main reasons for
under-utilisation of funds. This situation has been continuing for the last few years. The Committee fails to understand
as to how in the absence of required staff, the primary task of testing/analysis of drugs is being carried out in these labs.
The Committee would like to be apprised about the required and sanctioned strength of posts and vacant posts in both
these labs. The Committee hopes that construction work in both the labs would be started at the earliest. (Para 10.2)
Welcoming this initiative, the Committee is of the view that Department must ensure that the Pharmacies which
are stocking  the homoeopathic medicines must be certified by a person having necessary qualifications.  (Para 10.3)
            The Committee would like to be apprised of the reasons as to why the states did not even approach the
Department for release of second instalment grants.  The Committee feels that the situation is ironical.  On the one hand,
the Department is willing to assist the states, while the States are not taking advantage of the same.  The Committee
feels that apparently something is wrong with the entire approach   which needs to be examined and suitable remedial
measures taken. (Para 10.5)
XI        NON-AVAILABILITY OF HERBS AND MEDICINAL PLANTS
The Committee is happy to note that about 17 States have set up state level Medicinal Plants Board. The
Committee desires that the Department should persuade rest of the States /UTs also to set up medicinal plant board at
the earliest to stop adulteration and to make optimum use of available resources in their respective states/UTs. (Para
11.2)
XII       PUBLICITY
            The Committee notes the steps taken in this regard.  The Committee feels that simply sending the folders on
Home remedies in Ayurveda and Unani to State Govts for distribution to Panchayats will not serve any purpose  unless
the folder is in vernacular language and the instructions printed in the folders are communicated properly. The
Committee, therefore, desires that a demonstration on how to prepare the home remedies may be held at the block level. 
The Committee also notes that a small booklet on ISMH for distribution in various fairs, conferences, seminars etc. has
been prepared and another detailed booklet giving in brief the status of the system including the achievements is under
print.    The Committee is of the view that these booklets should be widely circulated as and when printed and hopes

(Para 12.3)
XIII      NORTH EASTERN STATES
            The Committee hopes that the Research in Tribal areas and North Eastern States would be implemented in 2002-
2003.  The Committee finds that in the NE states of Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Sikkim,  not even
one ISM practitioner is registered and no ISM dispensary/hospital is located.   The Committee  strongly feels that
concerted efforts need to be made to strengthen the network of ISMH  system in NE  sector.   This might prove to be
another step in bringing the people of this remote region to the main stream. (Para 13.4)
XIV     CENTRAL REGISTER OF INDIAN MEDICINE
            The Committee observes that the Central Register pertaining to only six states i.e. Orissa, Andhra Pradesh,
Gujarat, Karnataka, Haryana and Tamil Nadu out of the eighteen states where practitioners of ISM are registered has
been prepared so far and that too for varying period of time.    The Committee urges upon the Department to expedite
the preparation of the Central register of Indian Medicare in respect of all the concerned States.

PREFACE
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this 
Hundred-Nineteenth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.50) of the Department of
Elementary Education and Literacy,  Ministry of Human Resource Development for the year 2002-2003.
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of
Elementary Education and Literacy, Ministry of Human Resource Development and also heard the Secretary and other
Officials of that Department  on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held on 27
th    March, 2002.
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on     24th    April, 2002.
 
 
 
NEW DELHI;
April  
24, 2002
Vaisakha 4, 1924 (Saka)
 
ARJUN SINGH
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Human Resource Development
 
             
REPORT
INTRODUCTION
1.1       An attempt to make Elementary Education a Fundamental Right and justiciable under the Constitution  shifting
it from Directive Principles of State Policy which is non-justiciable marks a bold initiative.  It shows the commitment of
the Nation to provide Education for all, priority being free and compulsory Elementary Education, coverage of children
with special needs, eradication of illiteracy, vocationalisation, women’s education and special focus on the education of
socially disadvantaged sections.  It is true that in the field of Elementary Education, progress towards Universalisation
of Elementary Education (UEE) has been made.  Concerted efforts have resulted in the manifold increase in institutions,
teachers, students.  National Family Health Survey-II (1998-99) indicates that 79 percent children in the age group of 6-
14 are attending school.  Even though there has been considerable improvement in the participation of girl children
belonging to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, religious and linguistic minorities, etc, the goal of UEE still remains
elusive. 
1.2       Approach Paper to the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002-2007) has also pointed out that “our performance in the field
of education is one of the most disappointing aspects  of our development strategy.  Out of approximately 200 million
children in the age group 6-14 years, only 120 million are in schools and net attendance in the primary level is only 66%
enrolment.  Therefore it has been suggested that the Tenth Plan should aim at a radical transformation in this situation. 
Education for All must be one of the primary  objectives of the Tenth Plan. 
II          ELEMENTARY EDUCATION STATUS
2.1       During the period 1950-51 to 1999-2000, the number of primary schools has increased three-fold and the
number of upper primary Schools by about 15 times.  Total enrolment at the Primary stage increased by 5.91 times,
from 19.2 million in 1950-51 to about 113.61 million in 1999-2000. Total enrolment at the upper primary level
increased by 13 time from 3.1 million in 1950-51 to 42.06 million in 1999-2000.  During this period, the growth rate of
girls’ enrolment at the elementary level was higher as compared to that of the boys. So far as retention level is
concerned, from 64.9 per cent at the primary level in 1960-61, the drop-out rate  decreased to 40.25 per cent in 1999-
2000 and from 78.3 per cent  in upper primary level in 1960-61, it decreased to 54.8 per cent in 1999-2000. However
what is discouraging is the fact that even though number of teachers has increased this has not kept pace with the growth
of enrolment.  From 1:24 in 1950-51 the Pupil Teacher Ratio (PTR) at primary education level worsened to about 1:43

119th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/119threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:26]
in 1999-2000.  Similarly from 1:20 at the Upper Primary level the PTR has gone to 1:38 in 1999-2000.  Proportionate
growth in the number of teachers is therefore essential for qualitative improvement in PTR.
2.2       Though participation of girls at all levels of school education has increased substantially, the Committee
observes that the proportion of girls enrolled both at the primary and upper primary levels continues to be lower than the
gross enrolment of boys. Vast disparities still exist amongst the States/UTs in terms of enrolment with educationally
backward States having a much lower GER than the all India average. Position is the same in respect of school retention
rate.   For example GER for Class I-V in Bihar and UP is 57.04 and 65.69 respectively.  Similarly drop-out rate on Bihar
and UP is 71.11 and 56.51 respectively.  Moreover in case of girls in general the dropout rates are as high as 42% and
58% at Primary and Upper Primary stage respectively.  The Committee observes that a number of schemes in
elementary education sector have been in operation which has resulted in considerable improvement in the overall
scenario. Inspite of that, quite a few problem areas like poor infrastructure in schools, improper distribution of teachers,
presence of single-teacher schools, inefficient teaching methods, etc. still remain. The Committee hopes that with the
launching of Sarva Shikisha Abhiyan, a composite scheme of elementary education, all-round improvement will occur. 
III        LITERACY RATES
3.1
              As per census 1951, literacy rate was 16.67%.  The overall national literacy rate in 2001 is at 65.38% as against
52.21% in 1991 recording an increase of 13.17 percentage points, which is the highest in any decade.  Growth of female
literacy was recorded more than male literacy.. Female literacy increased by 14.87 percentage points i.e. from 39.29% to
54.16% as compared to male literacy growth by 11.72 percentage points i.e. 64.1% to 75.85%.  The differential in male
female literacy rates has decreased from 24.84 percentage points in 1991 to 21.70  percentage points in 2001.  However,
female literacy rate in Bihar, Jharkhand, J&K, Arunachal Pradesh, UP, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Rajasthan is less than
50% as per census 2001.  For the first time,  there is a decline in absolute number of non-illiterates by 31.9 million. 
During 1991-2001, the population in 7+ age group increased by 171.6 million while 203.6 million additional persons
became literate.  All the States and Union Territories have not only shown increase in literacy rates during 1991-2001
but have achieved male literacy rates over 60%.As per the Department,  the rate of growth  of literacy is more in rural
areas than in urban areas. Between 1991 and 2001, rural literacy rates increased by 14.52% while urban literacy rates
went up by 6.98%,  thereby narrowing the urban-rural gap from 28.39% in 1991 to 20.85% in 2001.
3.2       Similarly, as  per NSSO 55
th  round (1999-2000), 53% of SCs are literate as compared to 37.41% in the 1991
Census.  49% of STs are literate as compared to 29.60% in the 1991 Census.  This has shown a somewhat positive
trend.  However, gender difference in Elementary Education, urban rural gap and low literacy among  SCs/STs and
among educational minorities still remain a cause of  concern for the Committee.  Effective monitoring and
implementation with a missionary zeal is, therefore, needed.
VI        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
4.1
              The Ninth Plan allocation for Elementary Education has been Rs. 16,369.59 crores.  However approved
allocation was Rs.11,963.41 crores.  Expenditure during Ninth Plan (upto 18 th March, 2002) was Rs. 14,225.58 crores. 
It will, thus be seen that there was a drastic cut in the approved allocation vis-à-vis the original allocation for the Ninth
Plan.  However, the expenditure exceeded the approved allocation. Similarly, for Adult Education, Ninth Plan allocation
was Rs. 630.39 crores and expenditure during the Plan (upto 18 th  March,  2002) was Rs. 517.00 crores.  If the
expenditure upto 18th March, 2002 on Adult Education is taken into consideration, it appears that full utilization of the
Ninth Plan allocation may not be possible. There is likely to be some saving under this head. The Tenth Plan
requirement based on Working Group Report for Elementary Education is Rs. 59,684.31 crores and for 2002-2003 it is
Rs.  11,502. 51 crores.  However, total budget provision for 2002-2003 for Elementary Education including allocation
for North East is Rs.  4667.00 crores. As regards Adult Education, Tenth Plan requirement based on Working Group
Report is Rs.  6339.50 crores and for 2002-2003 it is Rs. 918.10 crores.  However, Budget provision for 2002-2003 is
Rs.  233.00 crores only.
4.2       The Committee has been informed that the Department had projected a requirement of Rs.  9015.25 crores for
the Annual Plan 2002-2003 for elementary education sector, after discussions with the Planning Commission.
However,  the Planning Commission has provided an amount of Rs. 4667.00  crores only against the said minimum
requirement.  This drastic cut would affect adversely the targets which have been fixed for the year 2002-2003 in regard
to goal of Universalisation of Elementary Education.  In 2001-2002, an amount of Rs.  350 crores was cut out of the
approved Budget Estimate of Rs. 4000.00 crores though the Department had, in fact projected an additional requirement

119th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/119threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:17:26]
of Rs.  268 crores in the RE 2001-2002.
4.3       The Committee has observed over the years that for various schemes under Elementary Education budget
projected at BE stage is quite high which is drastically reduced at the RE stage.  However, what is more distressing is
that even this reduced allocation is not fully utilised.  The Committee is perturbed to note that in 2001-2002, there was
18% non-utilisation for Teacher’s training, 75%  in Education Guarantee Scheme, 75% in Shiksha Karmi Project, 67%
in Mahila Samakhya Programme ,  18%  in National Council of Teachers Education. The Secretary of the Department
while agreeing that in the previous years, the utilization of funds, as compared to the B.E. had been low, mentioned
basically two reasons for this. According to him, one was that the allocation itself got reduced during Revised Estimates.
The others reason was that the utilization certificates from the States/UTs were not forthcoming due to which further
releases of funds had to be stopped. He, however, hoped that in 2001-2002, full utilization would be made.
4.4       The Committee is of the view that successful implementation of a scheme can be undertaken with the
partnership of both the Central Government and State Governments/UTs. If the funds are released by the Centre to the
States/UTs and if the same are  not utilized/spent by them, utilization certificates are not furnished, the Centre would
have perhaps no option but to withhold further release, resulting in under-utilisation of funds. However, in certain cases,
the reason behind non-utilisation of funds by some States/UTs may be genuine, particularly financial crunch. In that
case, the Committee feels that the Department will have to give a thought to it and find some way out for such
States/UTs.
4.5       The Committee also observes that there is  no preparatory exercise before any scheme is introduced in the
Budget. It is the general practice that budgetary  allocation is made for a scheme pending necessary surveys and
clearances from various authorities. Sometimes, the entire financial year is over and the scheme is yet not approved.
This practice makes the entire budgetary exercise unrealistic leading to under-utilisation of funds. This state of affairs is
highly unsatisfactory and betrays total lack of commitment on the part of authorities.  The Committee, therefore,
reiterates its earlier recommendation given in the 103
rd Report that all procedural formalities should be completed
before including a scheme in the budget and would like to be apprised of the action taken in this behalf.
V         OPERATION BLACKBOARD
5.1       In pursuance of the NPE-1986, the scheme of Operation Blackboard was launched in 1987-88 with the aim of
improving the human and physical resources available in the primary schools of the country.  The Scheme consisted of
mainly three components.
a)
                  Provision of an additional teacher to single teacher primary school;
b)                  Provision of at least two classrooms in each primary school; and
c)                  provision for teaching learning equipment to all primary schools brought under the scheme.
5.2       In 1993-94 the Scheme of Operation Blackboard was extended to provide third teacher and third room to
primary schools wherever enrolment exceeds 100 and to cover upper primary schools through provision of additional
teachers and teaching learning equipment.  The Scheme is implemented through State Governments.  100% central
assistance is provided for appointment of additional teachers in upper primary schools and third teachers in primary
schools with enrolment exceeding 100.
5.3
              Under the Scheme, construction of school building is the responsibility of the State Governments/UTs. 
However, provision for construction of school building has been made under the programme of rural employment like
Jawahar Rozgar Yojna (JRY) and Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS).  The JRY has been restructured by the
Ministry of Rural Development renaming the Scheme as Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana.  Under the revised guidelines
effective from 1 st April, 1999, funding pattern is  75:25 between the Centre and the State, so far as rural development
funds are concerned for construction of school buildings under the Scheme of Operation Blackboard.
5.4
              The Committee was informed that from 1987-88 to 2001-2002 (as on 22.2.2002) funds have been sanctioned for
teaching learning equipment to 5,22,902 primary schools and 1,38,009 upper primary schools.  Similarly, 1,49,146 posts
of additional teachers for single teacher primary schools, 77,610 posts of additional teachers for upper primary schools
and 83,045 posts of third teacher to primary schools with enrolment exceeding 100 children have been sanctioned.  A
sum of Rs. 3,52,074.15 lakhs has been released to the State Governments/UTs so far since its inception in 1987-88. The
Scheme of Operation Blackboard will be subsumed in Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan from the year 2002-2003.  A sum of Rs.

119th Report

6500.00 lakhs has been allocated for residual work of the Scheme of Operation Blackboard for the year 2002-2003
mainly for meeting the committed liability of salary of teachers upto end of the Ninth Plan period.
5.5       The Committee has been given to understand that under the Scheme of Operation Blackboard during the entire
period of the Ninth Plan physical target fixed for third teachers for Primary Schools was 1,58,000.  Against this, the
posts of only 48,153 teachers were sanctioned.  Similarly, against the physical target of 1,23,624 upper primary schools,
90,420 posts of teachers were sanctioned. As regards additional teachers for upper primary schools against the physical
target of 1,23,624, only 40,730 posts could be sanctioned.   The Committee is  disturbed to note that for the states of
Haryana, Mizoram, Nagaland and West Bengal, even though 1204, 106, 161 and 2353 additional teachers for upper
primary schools were sanctioned respectively, not a single teacher was appointed in these States. In the case of Assam,
Maharashtra and Orissa against the sanctioned posts of 6730,10969 and 10023, only 2851, 7064 and 7741 teachers
respectively were appointed.  This shows that there has been a wide gap between the lofty targets fixed and actually
achieved.  This calls for a serious rethinking of our planning and implementation process. 
5.6       The Committee has been informed that the main reason for such a large number of vacancies of teachers under
Operation Blackboard is the reluctance on the part of State Governments to bear the financial liability in respect of
teachers’ salary after the Plan period  was over.  Different strategies were adopted by the States in this regard.  In some
States, recruitment rules for teachers were not framed.  There are other States where recruitment rules simply got
delayed due to obvious reasons. In some cases, funds were given to the State Governments, but they were not released
for this purpose in time.
5.7       The Committee notes that against Ninth Plan allocation of Rs.1955.04 crores under Operation Blackboard,
utilisation figures upto 18.03.02 are only Rs.1719.83 crores. Trend of under-utilisation of funds was due to unspent
balances lying with various State Governments due to one reason or other. The Committee has been informed that
during 2001-2002, amount of unspent balances was brought down from Rs.377 crores to Rs.228 crores as a result of
concerted efforts made by the State Governments. All the concerned State Governments have now been requested to
liquidate the unspent balances by June, 2002. The Committee is of the opinion that large number of vacant posts of
teachers and non-utilisation of funds for the various components of Operation Blackboard is a clear indication that the
Scheme has failed to achieve the targettted results. The Committee hopes that all these inherent shortcomings noticed
under the Scheme over a period of time must have assisted the Department in taking all the corrective measures in the
formulation and  implementation of SSA. 
VI        TEACHERS TRAINING PROGRAMME
6.1       The Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Restructuring and Reorganisation of Teacher Education was taken up in
1987 to create a viable institutional infrastructure, academic and technical resource base for orientation, training and
continuous upgradation of knowledge, competence and pedagogical skills of elementary school teachers in the country.  
    The Scheme envisages setting up of District Institutes of Education and Training in each district to provide academic
and resource support to elementary education teachers and non-formal and adult education instructors. It also envisages
establishment of CTEs/IASES to organize pre-service and in-service training for secondary teachers and provide
extension and resource support service to secondary schools.
6.2       The Committee was informed that the Planning Commission has agreed in  principle for continuation of the
Scheme as suggested by the Working Group on Elementary and Adult Education for Tenth Five Year Plan.  The
Working Group, however,  recommended some modifications in the Scheme  for qualitative improvement and
coordinated development in the field of Elementary Teacher Education with increased involvement of the States.  The
modifications suggested by the Working Group will be placed before the EFC and  Cabinet for approval in due course. 
Till that time, the Scheme is expected to continue in its present form.
6.3
              The budgetary provision of Rs. 220.00 crores in BE  2001-2002 for the Teacher Education Programme was
reduced to Rs. 180.00 crore in RE in view of longer time taken by the States to finalise the MOUs for effective
operation of the Scheme and also proposals from States for new institutions not  received as expected.  The Committee
notes that actual expenditure incurred upto 18.3.2002 is only Rs.164.60 crores.
6.4       The Committee is constrained to note that this under utilisation trend has been there during the entire Ninth Plan
period. Against total Ninth Plan  allocation  of Rs.954.59 crores, expenditure reported upto 18.3.02 is only Rs.754.66
crores. The main reason given for funds not being released is non-submission of requisite  information including the
approval of the appropriate authority by some States/UTs. As a result, physical targets fixed under the scheme for Ninth

VII       EDUCATION GUARANTEE SCHEME AND ALTERNATIVE & INNOVATIVE EDUCATION
(EGS&AIE)
7.1       Education Guarantee Scheme and Alternative and Innocative (EGS&AIE) is a part of the overall programme of
Universalisation of Elementary Education, i.e. the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan.  The revised scheme has three broad
strategies, namely,
a)         setting up of schools in school less habitations within a radius of one  k.m.;
b)         interventions for mainstreaming of `out-of-school’ children through bridge courses, back to  school
camps, etc.; and
c)         strategies for very specific, difficult groups of children who cannot be mainstreamed.
7.2
              Central and State Government would share the expenditure in the ratio  of 75.25. Per learner cost has been
increased from the existing Rs. 375/- to Rs. 845/- per annum for primary level and from Rs. 580/- to Rs. 1200/- per
annum for upper primary level.  Honorarium to Education Volunteers has been increased from the existing Rs. 200/-

overall cost ceilings) and monitor the projects under EGS&AIE have been delegated to the State Level Societies

7.4       One of the main strategies under EGS & AIE is setting up of schools in school-less habitations within a radius of
one km. As per the Sixth All India Educational Survey-1993, out of total number of 10,60,612 habitations, 1,76,523
habitations are school-less habitations. The Committee finds that NE States of Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya,
Mizoram, Tripura, Meghalaya, Sikkim and also Himachal Pradesh, J & K and A & N. Islands have maximum  number
of unserved habitations. The Committee observes that these States/UTs have not  identifed State level societies for
implementation of EGS & ATE so far. The Committee recommends that the Department should vigorously pursue with

VIII      NATIONAL PROGRAMME OF NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT TO PRIMARY EDUCATION (MID-DAY

8.1       The National Programme of Nutritional Support to Primary Education commonly known as Mid Day Meals
Scheme was launched in August, 1995.  The programme aims at covering  all students in classes (I-V) in Government,
Government aided and Local Body schools.  The objective of the Programme is to give a boost to Universalisation of
Primary Education and simultaneously impacting on nutritional status of  children in primary classes.
8.2       As per the guidelines, implementing agencies i.e. States/UTGovts/local bodies are to arrange for cooked/pre-
cooked food within two years of the commencement of the Programme in the area, subject to cooked meals being
wholesome and having calorific value equivalent to 100 gms.  wheat/rice.  As a prelude, a provision for distribution of
3kgs.  of foodgrains per student per month subject to 80% attendance has been stipulated till the institutional
arrangements for provision of cooked meals are available.
8.3       Foodgrains are allocated free of cost to States/UTs through FCI and the cost of this is being reimubursed at BPL
rate w.e.f. November, 2000 Costs of transportation is reimbursed to District Authorities/State Nodal Agencies for

Rs. 50 per quintal.  The cost of conversion of food-grains into cooked meal is met by the State
Governments/Implementing Agencies.
8.4       At present Gujarat, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Pondicherry are providing cooked meals.  89 tribal blocks of

IX        SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN (SSA)
9.1       The Scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) has evolved from the recommendations of the State Eduction
Ministers Conference held in October 1998, to pursue universal elementary education in a mission mode.  The goals of
SSA are as follows
1.
                  All 6-14 age children in school/EGS centre/bridge course by 2003;
2.                  All 6-14 age children complete five year primary education by 2007;
3.                  All 6-14 age children complete eight years of schooling by 2010;
4.                  Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis on education for   life;
5.                  Bridge all gender and social category gaps at primary stage by 2007 and at elementary education level
by 2010; and
6.                  Universal retention by 2010.
9.2       All existing schemes such as Operation Blackboard, Strengthening of Teacher Education, Non-Formal
Education now called EGS&AIE, National Programmes of Media Publicity an Advocacy for UEE, National Straegy for
ensuring greater participation of Women in Educational field will get subsumed in SSA in the Tenth Plan.  All
externally aided projects like Shiksha Karmi,  Lok Jumbish, DPEP, Mahila Samakhya & Joint GOI-UN Programme for
Primary Education will continue to be implemented in terms of their specific agreements with the concerned external
funding agencies and will form part of SSA during Tenth Plan.
9.3       The allocation for SSA is Rs. 500.00 crore in BE and RE 2001-2002.  Out of this  a sum of Rs. 51.65 crores has
been sanctioned for pre-project activities in 294 non DPEP districts and 54 DPEP districts in 30 States/UTs.  Besides,

the Project Approval Board for SSA has approved Districts Elementary Education Plans of 512 districts in 24 States and
one UT with a total outlay of Rs. 1106.26 crores.  The GOI share at 85% of this would be about Rs. 940.00 crores.  The
Ministry is, however, releasing only 50% of the GOI share i.e. about Rs. 470.00 crore as first instalment during 2001-
2002 as the plans were received in second half of the year.  In 2002-2003, Annual Work Plans would have to be

districts not covered so far would also be considered.  It would be possible to spend the entire sum of Rs. 1680 crores

9.4       The Committee has been informed that the main activities to be undertaken under this Programme in 2002-2003 
would be to continue with the interventions started in 2001-2002  and take up new activities in the districts to achieve
the goal of universalisation of elementary education.  Such activities would include the opening of new primary and
upper primary schools, and  construction of additional classrooms, school buildings, toilets and provision of drinking
water, training for community leaders including training for members of VECs, and supply of free text books, setting up
of Block Resource Centres and Cluster Resource Centres and innovative interventions targeted for girls and SC/ST
children.
9.5
              The Secretary in his presentation before the Committee stated that for the Tenth Plan, the Department had
projected a requirement of Rs. 32,500 crores before the Cabinet.  The Working Group, however, recommended Rs.
36,000/- crores against which the Planning Commission, at the discussion stage, agreed to Rs. 32,000/- crores.  The
Tenth Plan is yet to be finalized.  However, as per the Annual Plan for 2002-2003, which has been finalized, the
Department has got only Rs. 1512/- crores as against its requirement of Rs. 7150 crores.
9.6              It may be mentioned that the Tapas majumdar Committee (1999) has assessed an average annual additional
requirement of rs. 13700 crores , while the Parliamentary Standing Committee on HRD in its 63rd report on Constitution
(83rd Amendment ) Bill,1997 has estimated financial expenditure of Rs. 40,000 crores for five Years to implement the
obligation of the State to provide free and compulsory education to all citizens of the age of 6-14 years.  The 93 rd
Amendment of the Constitution has suggested a proposed provision of Rs. 9,800 crores per annum with total estimate of
Rs. 98,000 crores for 10 years to fulfil the obligation.
9.7              The proposed budget estimate of Rs. 4304.70 crores for Elementary Education and out of which only Rs. 1512
crores has been earmarked for Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) could hardly fulfill the declared objective of the 93 rd
Amendment Act.  In fact, the Government’s policy announcement both in and outside the Parliament that the Sarva
Shiksha Abhiyan would provide “all 6-14 age children in school/EGS centre/bridge course by 2003” may stand nullified
as the present allocation could not achieve the same within the next year.  So also the time limits for other stipulations of
the SSA, namely all 6-14 children complete five years of primary education by 2007 and all 6-14 children complete
eight years of schooling by 2010 have to be further extended, if the annual budgetary allocation under SSA is not
substantially raised.
9.8       The Committee observes that the funding pattern under SSA would be 75:25 in the Tenth Plan and 50:50
thereafter between the Centre and States.  The Committee has been given to understand that this pattern was fixed
through a consultative process after extensive discussion with the States.  A large number of States have submitted their
District Elementary Education Plans which indicates that these States have implicitly agreed to the above sharing
pattern.  The Committee, however, is not inclined to agree with the contention of the Department that States will be
better placed under SSA as compared to Operation Blackboard under which liability of teachers salary was transferred
to State Govt. at the end of the Plan period.  This is evident from the fact that already three States-UP, Assam and
Tripura have requested reconsideration of the sharing pattern.  The Committee feels that more such requests are bound
to follow.  The Committee therefore, recommends that viability of this funding pattern may again be reviewed,
particularly in the case of non-performing States as observed during the implementation of Operation Blackboard. 
X         DISTRICT PRIMARY EDUCATION PROGRAMME (DPEP)
10.1     The Centrally sponsored scheme of District Primary Education Programme (DPEP) was launched in 1994 as a
major initiative to revitalize the primary education system and to achieve the goal of universalisation of primary
education.  The Programme adopts a holistic approach to universalize access, retention and improved learning
achievement and to reduce disparities among social groups.  The Programme primarily aims at providing access to
primary education for all children, reducing primary drop-out rates to less than 10 per cent, increasing learning
achievement of primary school students by at least 25 per cent and reducing the gap among gender and social groups to

119th Report
